refuted_claims: The discovery hint that the TO-99 AM/BM/SM are out of production per TI E2E 2024 is contradicted. In 2024, TI E2E 1386960 said 'OPA627BU or TO-CAN package will be in stock shortly'. TO-99 status was changed to unclear.
'Revision A (April 2015)' is refuted. SBOS165A reads 'SEPTEMBER 2000-REVISED OCTOBER 2015'.
'Metal-can fakes put a DIP die inside the can' misstates Soomal, who says some fakes put an ordinary PDIP chip inside a metal shell.
corrections: SBOS165C is confirmed as current, with the header 'AUGUST 2000 - REVISED JANUARY 2025'. Rev B is dated April 2024, and the OPA627BU moved from preview to production in Rev C. The symlink entry was raised to high confidence.
The Difet references deleted, the OPA627BU preview added and the 'OPA6x7 Precision, High-Speed JFET' title are confirmed. The deletion and the BU preview are attributed to Rev B by inference.

Molded-package pins 1/5 as NC with trim for TO-99 only is confirmed via diyAudio 418419. TI's OPA132 E2E explanation (higher-precision manufacturing) was added. The silicon_changes confidence was raised to medium for the documentation change only; the die change remains unconfirmed.
OPA627AU status refined from TI E2E 1386960: still active but temporarily not packaged, with the OPA828ID as the suggested pin-to-pin replacement. OPA627AP is confirmed obsolete.
The OPA637 80 MHz GBW (G=10) and 135 V/us are confirmed. The OPA637 product folder is ACTIVE.

New datasheet copies added: ti.com symlink opa637.pdf; the SBOS165A diagram page; the TI.com.cn viewer; Burr-Brown-edition copies at audiophonics.fr, hifituning24.de, studylib and datasheetcatalog; the octopart OPA627BP copy; radiolocman OPA637; ciiva; and an OPA627-DIE datasheet on DigiKey. OPA627-DIE was added as a part number.
The Mouser, Cimarron and b-cdn copies were identified as freezing Rev A (Oct 2015), and the Carnegie copy as the Burr-Brown March 1998 edition.
The pin 1-5 trim-resistance fake check is flagged as invalid on new TI molded parts.
claims_confirmed: SBOS165C is current, with the header 'AUGUST 2000 - REVISED JANUARY 2025'. The Rev C history records the OPA627BU changing from preview to production and gives the Rev B date as April 2024 (https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/opa627.pdf).
The current title is 'OPA6x7 Precision, High-Speed JFET Operational Amplifiers' (https://www.ti.com/lit/gpn/OPA627 ; https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/opa637.pdf).
The revision history records that the Difet references were deleted and the OPA627BU preview device was added (https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/opa627.pdf).
SBOS165A reads 'SEPTEMBER 2000-REVISED OCTOBER 2015' and includes ESD ratings of HBM +/-2500 V and CDM +/-1000 V for SOIC (https://www.mouser.com/datasheet/2/405/opa627-406898.pdf).

The Rev A copy shows 'Trim 5 Trim 1' and 'Product Folder / Sample & Buy' (https://www.cimarrontechnology.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/opa627.pdf ; https://datasheets.b-cdn.net/files/OPA627AU-Texas-Instruments-datasheet-60566259.pdf).

Molded-package trim pins are now NC and offset adjustment applies to TO-99 only (https://www.diyaudio.com/community/threads/opa132-opa627-and-other-ti-bb-op-amps-no-longer-have-an-offset-trim-terminal.418419/).

TI attributes the NC trim pins on the OPA132 (from Rev C) to higher-precision manufacturing (https://e2e.ti.com/support/audio-group/audio/f/audio-forum/1517005/opa132-changed-opa132-pin-1-and-pin-8-from-offset-trim-to-nc).

In 2024, TI said the OPA627AU was still active but 'will not be packaged for now', named the OPA828ID as a pin-to-pin replacement, and said BU/TO-can stock would come shortly (https://e2e.ti.com/support/amplifiers-group/amplifiers/f/amplifiers-forum/1386960/opa627-is-the-opa627au-end-of-life).

OPA627AP is obsolete (https://www.digikey.com/en/products/detail/texas-instruments/OPA627AP/251165 ; https://e2e.ti.com/support/amplifiers-group/amplifiers/f/amplifiers-forum/1370897/opa627-opa627ap-product-problem).
OPA637: 80 MHz GBW at G=10, 135 V/us slew, product ACTIVE (https://www.ti.com/product/OPA637).
The OPA627BU and OPA637AU orderable pages exist (https://www.ti.com/product/OPA627/part-details/OPA627BU ; https://www.ti.com/product/OPA637/part-details/OPA637AU).
OPA627: 4.5 nV/rtHz at 10 kHz, 55 V/us, 100 uV max Vos, 0.8 uV/C, 5 pA max IB, +/-4.5 to +/-18 V (https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/opa627.pdf).

The Burr-Brown edition is 'Printed in U.S.A. March, 1998' and describes a dielectrically isolated complementary NPN/PNP process with laser-trimmed Difet input (https://instrumentation.obs.carnegiescience.edu/ccd/parts/OPA627.pdf ; https://www.audiophonics.fr/images2/8434/opa627.pdf).
No OPA627-specific PCN was found in TI/Mouser PCN search results (https://www.ti.com/quality-reliability/quality/product-change-notification.html).

families.tagline: The original CMoy chip: an 8 MHz, 20 V/us Burr-Brown FET-input part that runs well from a 9 V battery and has the soft 'BB sound' at entry-level cost.
families.technology: JFET (FET) input voltage-feedback op-amp. Burr-Brown design, datasheet origin January 1995 (Burr-Brown macromodel dated Feb 1996). TI datasheet SBOS054C (Aug 2024) changed them to NC, and a TI E2E engineer says the trim was 'eliminated in the new FAB change and design' due to an improved process.

SBOS054 revisions: A (revised June 2004), B (revised September 2015) and C (revised August 2024). Rev C changed OPA132 pins 1/8 from Offset Trim to NC. Per TI E2E, this followed a new-fab/design change with an improved process, affecting all package types. The PDIP singles (OPA132P/PA) and the PDIP quad (OPA4132PA) are obsolete; the SOIC parts are active. The TI PSpice model OPA132.LIB (Final 1.2, 05FEB2019) references SBOS054B.

reputation.summary: The op-amp of Chu Moy's original CMoy pocket headphone amp, and so the default in countless CMoy builds. Tangentsoft's CMoy guide recommends the OPA2132PA to beginners over the cheaper OPA2134PA because the series needs little voltage and rarely oscillates, and its lowest grade is adequate. The tangentsoft op-amp notes (also circulated as a Chinese translation on Soomal) call it a very good entry-level part: a natural, sweet Burr-Brown sound with few flaws, though not exciting. They heard it as identical to the OPA134 and about 5% behind the OPA627/637. The Head-Fi and diyAudio praise quotes come from discovery notes and were not re-verified.
sonic_descriptors: few flaws but not exciting (tangentsoft notes)
bass: with extra supply voltage the 132/134's bass turns boomy, while the OPA627's sounds more real (tangentsoft via translation; ambiguous)
sounds the same as the OPA134 (tangentsoft notes)
less resolving and less lively than the OPA228 when the 228 is stable (tangentsoft notes)
'a bit of magic reminiscent of the OPA627/637' (Head-Fi; unverified quote)
more neutral than the OPA2227 (Head-Fi; unverified)
typical_uses: CMoy and other 9 V battery pocket headphone amps
entry-level op-amp rolling in DACs, CD players and sound cards
portable and battery-powered audio (needs less voltage than the OPA134)
general audio line stages, filters and buffers
caveats: The Soomal Chinese article translates the tangentsoft notes; it is not an independent review.

TI parts built to SBOS054C (Aug 2024) and later are a new-fab die. The single OPA132 has pins 1/8 as NC, so an offset-null pot does nothing. Sonic or measured differences from Burr-Brown-era silicon are undocumented.
The DIP single (OPA132P/PA) and DIP quad (OPA4132PA) are obsolete. CMoy pages that say the 'OPA132 has been discontinued' mean the DIP; SOIC OPA132U/UA remain active.
Tangentsoft reports that the OPA134/OPA2134PA could distort or oscillate in circuits built for the 132, especially at low supply.
Russian DIY notes claim the OPA2132 handles low-impedance loads better than the OPA2134. This is folklore (low confidence).
Counterfeits are said to be common (discovery notes; low confidence). Buy from authorized distributors.
No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurement of the OPA132 was found.

silicon_changes.summary: TI moved the OPA132 to a new fab and design. A TI E2E engineer says the trim function 'has been eliminated in the new FAB change and design', with trim removed for all package types 'due to improved process'. Per a diyAudio thread on the 2024 datasheets, sibling parts OPA130, OPA131, OPA134 and the molded-package OPA627 got the same Offset Trim -> NC change; the TO-99 OPA627 keeps trim.

families.counterfeit_notes: No OPA132-specific counterfeit teardown or marking guide was found. The discovery notes say fakes are 'common, as with the OPA2134' (low confidence). Documented fakes of the sibling OPA2134 and of the OPA2604 are relabelled TL072-class dies, laser marks that wipe off with solvent, and ground tops. The PDIP single (OPA132P/PA) and PDIP quad (OPA4132PA) are obsolete, so 'new' DIP stock with recent date codes is suspect. The OPA4132PA itself was a genuine TI/BB part. A genuine pre-2024 single OPA132 responds to an offset-trim pot on pins 1/8; a new-fab TI part will not, so this is not a fake test for SBOS054C-era lots.

reputation.summary: Widely described as the archetypal 'laid-back Burr-Brown sound' and a common first op-amp upgrade in CMoy headphone amps, DAC output stages and sound cards. AudioKarma/Xonar users contrast its warmth with the more 'clinical' LME49720; some diyAudio members prefer it to the LM4562. Soomal reviewers call it warm-leaning (偏暖) and smooth (柔润); Japanese hobby reviewers treat it as a natural all-rounder. Measured differences are small: NwAvGuy found OPA2134, NE5532 and LM4562 near analyzer residual. TI positions the OPA1656 as its 'next generation OPA2134 and OPA2604 replacement'. (Reputation not re-searched in this pass.)
sonic_descriptors: fuller but looser bass than LM4562 (one user)
less dense and dynamic than OPA627 (Soomal; not re-read)
typical_uses: CMoy and portable headphone amps (tangentsoft CMoy guide lists OPA2134PA as an alternate)
DAC output stages (per Soomal): Aune X1S (OPA2134UA), Shanling H1.1, TempoTec Fantasia, Musway M1
Headphone amps (per Soomal): Topping NX3, a Lehmann-style desktop amp
PC sound cards and motherboard audio (Gigabyte G1.Sniper A88X; E-MU and Xonar op-amp rolling)
op-amp rolling in Fosi and similar amps
multimedia speakers (Soomal TP30 review)
caveats: Sonic claims are subjective; NwAvGuy's measurements put OPA2134, NE5532 and LM4562 essentially level.
FET-input: common-mode distortion in non-inverting stages with high source impedance (Self, Groner; from discovery notes, not re-verified).
DiyEden reports instability in circuits designed for OPA132 at low supply (single forum source).
Result depends on the circuit (Soomal found the G1.Sniper A88X harsh despite the OPA2134).
Minimum supply +/-2.5 V; input CM range stops 2.5 V above V- and 3.5 V below V+ (SBOS058B).
TI parts from about 2024-2025 on may be the new-fab die: pins 1/8 NC on OPA134, lower headroom/channel-separation specs, different ESD structures (see silicon_changes).
The '+/-18 V limit, 5 V/us slew' complaints refer to TI's NE5532 change, not the OPAx134.
Counterfeits are widespread, especially DIP-8 OPA2134PA.

silicon_changes.identification: Part number unchanged, no suffix. TI's internal die revision goes from A to B (per the PCN), but no marking difference is documented. Datasheet SBOS058B or later = new die (OPA134 pins 1/8 NC); SBOS058A or earlier = old die with trim. TI E2E: the practical way to tell is measurement (offset; pin impedance / ESD-diode behaviour differs between 2025 and 2018 date codes); mixed stock may ship until old inventory clears. BB-logo parts are very likely old die; TI-logo parts can be either.
silicon_changes.summary: TI moved the OPAx134 die to a new wafer fab under the same part numbers as part of its exit from 150 mm fabs. The new die has no external offset-trim function (internal laser trim), updated ESD structures, and revised datasheet specs. TI says moving fabs always shifts performance somewhat and that the datasheet now reflects the actual device. TI E2E attributes in-circuit-test and functional failures on 2025 date-code parts most likely to the new ESD structures. Hackaday (Jun 2026), diyAudio and Gearspace criticise the change and TI's 'no impact' wording.

spec_deltas.after: NC (do not connect); internally laser-trimmed. TI E2E says leaving an old trim network in place is harmless, while the datasheet warns not to connect.
1.0 mV per a third-party reading of SBOS058B (typ vs max unclear); TI product-page parametric still shows 2 mV max. Low confidence.

spec_deltas.after: Updated ESD structures; different measured pin impedances (2025 date code)

silicon_changes.audio_impact: Small on paper: about 2.3 dB less headroom before 0.01% THD+N, channel separation still very high (128 dB). No published old-vs-new THD, noise or listening comparison found. OPA134 trim circuits lose their adjustment. Japanese and Chinese hobby sources report no sonic change.
silicon_changes.compatibility_risk: medium: pin- and function-compatible for normal audio use per TI, but offset-trim circuits stop working, headroom is lower, and new ESD structures caused ICT/functional failures for at least one customer; old and new stock mixed with no marking difference.

families.counterfeit_notes: Fakes are widely reported, especially DIP-8 OPA2134PA from marketplaces. Discussions: TI E2E 1321243 ('OPA2134: Counterfeits?') and 534233; PedalPCB 'checking for fake OPA2134?'; diyAudio 377960; kokoro-navi 2011 write-up (fake OPA2134PA/OPA2604AP); fakes reported in an Aune mini USB DAC. Summaries describe relabelled TL072s or other noisier op-amps and differing lot-code formats. Forum checks: quiescent current (about 4-5 mA per amplifier), unity-gain follower AC test, noise and offset, and logo/font/laser marking/moulding vs known-genuine parts. These are forum methods, not a TI guide; TI advises authorized distributors. Genuine Burr-Brown-era OPA2134PA stock is sold by Rochester Electronics (authorized aftermarket). Caveat: since 2024-2025 genuine TI parts may be the new-fab die, so a higher offset or different ESD/impedance behaviour alone does not prove a fake.

families.name: TL071 / TL072 / TL074 (incl. TL07xH next-gen die)
families.tagline: TI's 1978 BiFET and the cheap JFET-input op-amp in countless mixers, synths, pedals and DAC filters. Enthusiasts use it as the baseline that "upgrade" op-amps are compared against.
families.technology: BiFET: JFET input stage with a bipolar output stage (legacy TI die, per SLOS080N). The TL07xH die (2020 onward) is described by TI only as 'FET-input' on a 'modern process'; a community claim that it is CMOS is unconfirmed. TL07xH inputs are diode-clamped to both rails and the common-mode range includes V+. TI PCN 20221219006.1 (21 Dec 2022) qualified the RFAB fab with a die revision and datasheet update for TL072/TL074 devices. From Rev U (Dec 2022) the plain C/AC/BC/I grades in non-PS/NS packages are specified with new-die values, and per Rev W (Jul 2025) they can come from either flow: legacy (CSO: SFAB) or latest (CSO: RFB).

reputation.summary: It is the ubiquitous low-cost BiFET. TI's datasheet (and the Diodes and JRC equivalents) calls it 'ideally suited for high-fidelity and audio preamplifier applications'. Hi-fi enthusiasts treat it as the stock or baseline part that upgrades (OPA2134, NE5532 and others) are judged against, not as a favourite in its own right. It is valued for its JFET input (high-impedance sources), low distortion at line level and low price. Its noise (18 nV/rtHz, legacy die) is considered acceptable in DAC low-pass filters, tone controls and crossovers, but not in low-impedance, high-gain stages. Douglas Self's EE Times series on op-amp selection reviews it among JFET-input types; a search summary says he uses TL072s where a DC servo is needed. NwAvGuy's op-amp measurements and Cycfi's op-amp shootout are frequently cited comparisons. It is standard in synth and Eurorack, guitar-pedal and pro-audio-mixer designs. Since 2024-2026, pedal and synth forums (PedalPCB, Mod Wiggler, the Gremblog) discuss TI's doubled noise spec.
sonic_descriptors: 'class-A output sound style' attributed to JFET op-amps (Soomal, CN; folklore)
'warm/smooth' (synth and pedal builders, per discovery notes; not verified)
adequate or neutral where noise is not critical (secondary summaries of Self/ESP; not quoted verbatim)
typical_uses: DAC low-pass filter and output stages (e.g. YBA Design WD202 uses a TI TL072 after an OPA2134 I/V stage, per Soomal)
PC sound cards and USB interfaces (TerraTec DMX 6 Fire USB, Tempotec Fantasia, Audioprobe Spartan Cue)
active speakers and headphone amps (ICON PX-T6A, DA&T HA-1)
DC servos in preamps (Self, per search summary)
Eurorack and synth VCF/LFO/BBD/mixer circuits
guitar pedals and buffers
active crossovers, EQ and tone-control stages in mixers
caveats: Legacy die phase reversal: TI Rev N says to keep single-supply inputs above 1 V to avoid the output going high, and to keep VCM >= V- + 4 V.
Legacy die needs 10 V total supply minimum (recommended 10-30 V in Rev V/W), so it is not usable at 5 V.
Output swing is only +/-10 V min into 2 kOhm at +/-15 V, so it is weak for 600-ohm or headphone loads.

Since PCN 20221219006.1 (first ship proposed 20 Mar 2023) and Rev U, the same TI part number can be the new die, with e_n 37 nV/rtHz (about 6 dB noisier at 1 kHz) but lower THD+N, faster slew and inputs that reach V+. Batch-to-batch sound or noise differences are possible.

A TI E2E thread reports TL074CDR date codes 2436, 2443 and 2522 failing a customer's functional test: the output swung to the -13 V rail where older parts stopped near -11.5 V, and ESD/protection structures changed.
TL071 in D/P packages no longer has offset-null pins (NC, 'Do not connect') per Rev W. Old boards with a trimmer on pins 1/5 lose the trim function.
New-die inputs are diode-clamped (differential input limited to VS+0.2 V, 10 mA). This can matter in comparator or clipper circuits that relied on the legacy die's wide differential range.

silicon_changes.when: Oct 2020 (SLOS080O, preview); production TL072H Jun 2021 (Rev R), TL071H Jul 2021 (Rev S)
silicon_changes.identification: The H is in the orderable (e.g. TL072HIDR, TL072HIPWR, TL072HIDDFR, TL074HIDR, TL071HIDBVR); I-grade (-40 to 125 C) only. Top marks per Rev W addendum: TL072HIDR 'TL072D', TL071HIDR 'TL071D', TL074HIDR 'TL074HID', TL072HIPWR '072HPW', TL072HIDDFR 'O72F', TL071HIDBVR 'T71V'. Rev W: 'If y = H, the die is manufactured on the latest flow (CSO: RFB)'.
silicon_changes.summary: A new die on a 'modern process', sold as the 'next-generation' TL07x. It has rail-inclusive (V+) common-mode input, diode-clamped inputs, lower Iq, higher GBW and slew, much lower Vos and Ib, and about 2x the voltage noise of the legacy die. TI now calls the family 'FET-input' rather than 'JFET-input'. The TI part page for TL072HIDR reads 40 V, 5 MHz, 4 mV, 20 V/us, in to V+.

spec_deltas.before: +/-5 to +/-15 V rec., 36 V abs max (30 V part-page headline)
V- +4 V to V+ (rec.), phase reversal near V-
spec_deltas.after: V- +1.5 V to V+, no phase reversal; inputs clamped (diff <= VS+0.2 V, 10 mA)

silicon_changes.audio_impact: About 6 dB higher voltage noise at 1 kHz hurts low-impedance, high-gain stages (mic/phono, low-Z filters). Distortion, slew, single-supply headroom and supply current improve. The flatter noise corner (37 at 1 kHz vs 21 at 10 kHz) means more low-frequency noise than the legacy spec.
silicon_changes.compatibility_risk: medium: signal pinout is identical for the dual and quad, but the noise doubles and TL071H SOIC has no offset-null pins. The input clamps and different CM limits can change behaviour in comparator or clipping circuits.

silicon_changes.when: PCN 20221219006.1 issued 21 Dec 2022 (samples until 20 Jan 2023; proposed first ship 20 Mar 2023); datasheet Rev U Dec 2022; nomenclature note and TL071 trim removal Rev W Jul 2025
silicon_changes.identification: The part number and top marking do not change (e.g. still 'TL072CP', 'TL072C'). PCN 20221219006.1 ('Qualification of new Fab site (RFAB) using qualified Process Technology, Die Revision, Datasheet update and additional Assembly site/BOM options') lists TL072 and TL074 devices; whether TL071 is listed was not confirmed. Inference: parts with date codes before about 2312 (Mar 2023) should be legacy die. A TI E2E thread shows TL074CDR date codes 2436, 2443 and 2522 behaving as the new process. Rev W: 'If y != H and y != M, the die is manufactured on the legacy flow (CSO: SFAB) or the latest flow (CSO: RFB)'. That RFB denotes RFAB is an inference. PS/NS-package orderables and TL07xM keep legacy-die specs. Bench check: about 0.94 vs 1.4 mA/ch Iq; 37 vs 18 nV/rtHz; the negative output swing reaches the rail.
silicon_changes.summary: Through PCN 20221219006.1 (Dec 2022), TI moved ordinary TL072/TL074 (and per the datasheet, TL071) C/AC/BC/I grades onto a revised die in the RFAB fab, with no part-number change. The new process has updated ESD structures and protection scheme. Since Rev U the datasheet specifies these parts with new-die values, and Rev W states either fab flow may ship and removes TL071 offset null on D/P packages. This confirms the community reports that 'TL072 now specs 37 nV' (PedalPCB, the Gremblog).

spec_deltas.parameter: Negative output saturation (E2E TL074CDR report, VCC- = -13 V)

spec_deltas.after: updated ESD structures and protection scheme (TI reply on E2E)

silicon_changes.audio_impact: Old boards re-populated with current-production TI TL072/TL074 may measure about 6 dB more hiss at 1 kHz but lower distortion. Output clipping levels differ, since the new die swings closer to the negative rail. Units may differ from each other because the die is mixed under one part number. Offset-trimmed TL071 designs lose the trim.
silicon_changes.compatibility_risk: medium: pin-compatible drop-in, but noise doubles and saturation and protection behaviour changed. At least one customer saw functional-test failures on new date codes (E2E). High risk for TL071 sockets that use the pins 1/5 offset trimmer.

families.counterfeit_notes: No counterfeits of the TL072 itself were documented; it is too cheap to be worth faking. The TL072 (and TL082) die is reportedly the usual body inside remarked premium audio parts, according to discovery notes; this session did not re-verify them. Examples: fake OPA2604s on Yahoo Auctions (a Japanese blog found 70 of 75 fake, including remarked TL072s); fake OPA2134s (PedalPCB, diyAudio and TI E2E threads); and a batch of fake OPA1612 that were TL082 dies. How to spot them: laser marks that wipe off with solvent, ground or reblacked tops, and wrong font or logo. On the bench, look for TL07x-like behaviour: roughly 1.4 mA/ch Iq, about 3 MHz GBW, and a noise floor far above the premium part's spec. Caution: a genuine TI TL072/TL074 shipped after PCN 20221219006.1 (from about Mar 2023) may be the new die, with 37 nV/rtHz, about 0.94 mA/ch and a different output swing. The E2E TL074CDR failures on date codes 2436/2443/2522 were genuine new-process parts, not fakes. Compare against Rev W sec 5.7, not the old 18 nV figure.

reputation.summary: Not a hi-fi favourite. Its fame comes from guitar pedals: the JRC4558D in the Ibanez TS-808 Tube Screamer (1979) and the BOSS SD-1. There, its modest slew rate and bandwidth are credited with a warm, mid-forward overdrive. In hi-fi it is the cheap default in 1980s–90s cassette/mini-system and budget audio boards. Chinese community sources such as Soomal rank it below the NE5532 and NJM4580 ('4558 < 5532/4580'), and swapping it out is a classic upgrade. Japanese pedal folklore prizes glossy JRC4558D parts (said to be from JRC's Saga plant) and Malaysian Raytheon 4558P parts. In Jazzcaster's TS test rig, glossy and matte parts produced nearly identical harmonics above 440 Hz, but the glossy part was clearly quieter, especially at high frequencies. The author judged that only 2–3 in 100 listeners could tell them apart.
sonic_descriptors: less clean than an NE5532 in the same socket (opinion in the Celine source)
plain budget baseline (Soomal: cheap JRC4558 vs better JRC4580)
typical_uses: Tube Screamer / TS9 / SD-1 overdrive pedals and clones
budget consumer audio: cassette decks, mini-systems, sound-card and USB-interface output stages
general-purpose filters and buffers on ±15 V or 9 V single supply
synth / Eurorack and retro-console audio stages (widely used as KiCad RC4558/NJM4558 symbol)
caveats: Slow (0.8–1.7 V/µs). Full-power bandwidth for 20 Vpp is only about 13–27 kHz (derived from datasheet slew).
Phase reversal when the common-mode input approaches V− (within about 1 V), per the TI datasheet and Chen Shuo.
Output specified only down to 2 kΩ (±10 V min). Not a headphone driver.
Bipolar input bias of 25–150 nA typ gives DC offset with high source impedances.
Supply: TI recommends ±5 to ±15 V; JRC operates from ±4 V.
Vendor dies differ (Raytheon, TI, JRC, and the NJM4558C), so 'a 4558' is not one sound or one spec.
Vintage-JRC NOS premiums attract fakes and relabels.

silicon_changes.vendor: Raytheon vs Texas Instruments vs JRC (second-source dies)
silicon_changes.when: Raytheon 1971; TI own document from March 1976; JRC by the late 1970s
silicon_changes.identification: Maker logo and prefix: Raytheon RC4558N/M (Raytheon logo); TI RC4558P/DR (TI logo; marking 'RC4558P' or 'R4558'); JRC/NJR NJM4558D marked 'JRC4558D' (JRC or NJR logo).
silicon_changes.summary: The same generic part number comes from different vendor designs. The three datasheets specify materially different typical figures, and the Raytheon schematic differs from the JRC equivalent-circuit drawing. That points to independent dies, not one die made under licence. No vendor states a die change within its own part.
silicon_changes.audio_impact: Small. All are 3 MHz, 741-class parts. TI's faster slew raises full-power bandwidth. Pedal users report tonal differences between TI RC4558P and JRC4558D in TS9-type circuits (folklore). In hi-fi use all are outclassed by the 5532 and 4580.
silicon_changes.compatibility_risk: low - same pinout, supply range and compensation. Differences are within a general-purpose tolerance.

silicon_changes.summary: Jazzcaster (a Japanese hobbyist site) says glossy JRC4558D/DD parts were made at JRC's Saga plant in Kyushu and matte parts are overseas production. That is a production-site change, not documented by the vendor. In its TS-circuit tests, harmonics above 440 Hz were almost identical and differences appeared only below 80 Hz, but the glossy part had clearly lower noise, especially at high frequencies. The vendor datasheet changes (Ver.2013 vs the old databook) are re-characterisation only.

families.counterfeit_notes: Premium-priced 'NOS vintage JRC4558D' listings, including glossy ('艶あり') parts on Japanese marketplaces, are often fakes or relabels (discovery notes). The NJM4558D DIP is reported discontinued, so expect more grey-market and remarked stock. Cheap JRC4558 parts are also confused with, or remarked as, the pin-compatible but much better JRC4580 (Soomal). A quick slew-rate or small-signal bandwidth check exposes a 4558 sold as a 4580: 4558 slew is about 1 V/µs and GBW about 3 MHz, far below a real 4580. Check that logo, font, finish, country of origin and date code are consistent (JRC logo on older parts, NJR later). Current TI parts carry the documented markings 'RC4558P', 'R4558' or 'R4558I', or the DGK codes YRP/YRS/YRU. Buy current production from authorized distributors.

families.name: AD8065 / AD8066 (single / dual FastFET JFET-input, 145 MHz)
families.tagline: Cheap, fast ADI JFET-input op-amp that CMoy/PIMETA battery-amp builders liked; Tangent placed its sound between the 'aggressive' AD8610 and the 'laid-back' OPA227/Burr-Brown sound.
families.technology: Voltage-feedback op amp with a laser-trimmed JFET input stage, built on ADI's XFCB (eXtra Fast Complementary Bipolar) process. The datasheet footnote says the AD8065/AD8066 is 'Protected by U.S. Patent No. 6,262,633', and the Theory of Operation calls the rail-to-rail output stage 'patented'; neither ties the patent to the process. The input is a cascoded N-channel JFET pair. When the common-mode voltage comes within about 3 V of +Vs, an auxiliary NPN pair takes over; this prevents phase reversal but raises Ib to tens of uA. The output is rail-to-rail, reaching within 0.5 V of either rail at up to 30 mA. Back-to-back input diodes limit the differential input to 1.8 V (absolute max). Unity-gain stable; the datasheet's model uses an open-loop crossover of 65 MHz.

reputation.summary:
A niche Head-Fi and CMoy favourite from the mid-2000s, not a top-tier audiophile legend. Tangent's op-amp notes, read via the DiyEden Chinese translation reposted on Soomal (dated 2005-02-17), give these figures and verdicts:
- Price: $4.21 (AD8065) and $5.38 (AD8066) at Digi-Key.
- Minimum supply: 4.0 V for 0.5 V into 33 Ohm, and 5.7 V for 2 V into 330 Ohm.
- Battery use: another good choice besides the AD823 and AD8610. It draws more current but needs less voltage, so the same battery setup can run longer.
- Sound: 'not aggressive, but not laid-back'. His summary recommends it if you find the AD8610 too aggressive and the OPA227 too laid-back. He adds: 'It's a bit veiled, which is expected given the chip's price.'
- Practical notes: SOIC only, so it needs an adapter, and it is rated only to 24 V (26.4 V max).
A 2024 GitHub CMoy build guide (spbkaizo/baudio) says: 'the AD823, AD8066, AD8620 are some of my faves'. Weaker, unverified evidence: Head-Fi thread titles compare it with the AD8620 ('AD8065/66 Opamps vs ad8620 ... wow....!'), and the discovery notes quote 'very delicate yet refined, with good bass, clear but smooth highs'. A Head-Fi Cmoy shoot-out reportedly preferred the OPA2228, and the Japanese blogger nabe reportedly rates it B+ with the LM4562 and OPA2604; none of these pages were re-read. No audio-band THD+N measurements (ASR, Groner) were found.
sonic_descriptors: neither aggressive nor laid-back; between the AD8610 and OPA227/Burr-Brown (Tangent)
good bass, clear but smooth highs (Head-Fi, unverified)
typical_uses: CMoy / PIMETA battery headphone amplifiers (low minimum supply voltage)
Op-amp rolling on SOIC-to-DIP adapters in headphone amps and DACs at supplies of +/-12 V or less
Line and headphone gain stages and buffers
Non-audio: photodiode preamps, ADC drivers, video buffers, instrument front ends
caveats: The maximum operating supply is 24 V total, with 26.4 V absolute max. Never fit it in +/-15 V or +/-18 V sockets: 30-36 V exceeds the absolute maximum.
It comes only in SOIC, MSOP and SOT-23, so audio use needs a DIP adapter. A 145 MHz part on an adapter can oscillate; decouple close to the pins.
It tolerates little capacitive load (20-25 pF for 30% overshoot at G=+1). Isolate cable or headphone loads with a series resistor.

The JFET input range ends about 2.6-3.3 V below +Vs. Beyond that the NPN stage takes over, Ib rises to tens of uA and the offset shifts. This can matter in unity-gain non-inverting stages at low supplies.
Back-to-back input diodes limit differential input to 1.8 V.
The 1/f noise corner is high (about 1.3-1.5 kHz): about 11 nV/rtHz at 1 kHz and about 33 nV/rtHz at 100 Hz (Fig. 21). That is worse in the audio band than the 7 nV/rtHz headline figure.
It draws 6.4 mA per amplifier. The datasheet warns that shorting the output 'will likely cause catastrophic failure'.
Ib grows about 1.7x per 10 C and about 5x from 5 V to 24 V supplies, which matters with high-impedance inputs at +/-12 V.
No audio-band THD+N specification; distortion is specified only as SFDR at 1 MHz and above.
Sonic reputation rests on 2003-2008 forum listening impressions, not measurements.

families.counterfeit_notes:
One direct report, low confidence (single user). In the Chinese '电子元件网店红黑榜' (component-shop red/black list), contributor BH2VGM blacklisted Taobao seller 联科达电子 (Shenzhen) on 2024-03-27: 'AD8066、AD8032等使用劣质运放重打标，性能极差' (AD8066, AD8032 etc. are remarked inferior op-amps; performance extremely poor). Source: GitHub wt01111/DigitialPancake server/seed/shop-seed.json.

How to spot fakes:
(1) No DIP-8 version exists. The Rev. D and Rev. L ordering guides list only SOIC-8, MSOP-8 and SOT-23-5, and Tangent (2005) noted the part was SOIC-only. A bare DIP-8 'AD8066' is fake, unless it is a SOIC chip on a visible adapter.
(2) Marking codes from the ordering guides:
- AD8066ARM (MSOP, leaded): H1B
- AD8066ARMZ: H7C
- AD8065ART (SOT-23): HRA
- AD8065ARTZ: HRA# (# = RoHS; top or bottom marked)
- AD8065WARTZ: H2F#
SOIC parts have no marking code in the guide; ADI normally prints the part number.
(3) Electrical checks from datasheet values: about 6.4 mA supply current per amplifier (about 12.8 mA per dual at +/-5 V), pA-level input bias current, about 180 V/us slew rate and 100+ MHz unity-gain bandwidth. A remarked generic bipolar op-amp would show nA-to-uA bias current, much lower slew and bandwidth, and a different Iq.
(4) The absolute maximum supply is 26.4 V. A part that 'survives' +/-15 V proves nothing and has been overstressed.

families.tagline: ADI's 1995 JFET-input, rail-to-rail-output dual that runs from 3 V. A CMoy/portable-amp favourite, rated for more bass impact and detail than OPA132/134 (Tangent).
families.technology: Original AD823: N-channel JFET input stage on ADI's complementary bipolar (CB) process, where PNP and NPN fT is 600-800 MHz. Uses a nested-integrator topology with Miller compensation (C1, C5) and a complementary common-emitter rail-to-rail output stage. Offset and drift are set by thin-film trimming. The input range extends 0.2 V below -Vs, and there is no phase inversion with inputs at the supply rails. Supply: 3-36 V single or ±1.5 to ±18 V. AD823A (2012) is a different die with the same dual pinout. It is built on the XFCB process (dielectrically isolated complementary bipolar with JFETs and thin-film resistors), uses a two-stage design with a folded-cascode first stage, has laser-trimmed thin-film resistors and a rail-to-rail output.

reputation.summary: A 2000s DIY headphone-amp favourite for battery-powered CMoy-style portables. Tangent (tangentsoft; confirmed through Soomal's Chinese translation) rated it slightly more impactful in the bass and more detailed than the OPA134/132, and ideal for battery amps because it runs on 3 V with rail-to-rail output. He also warned it can be too aggressive with already forward headphones, and that its roughly 15 mA output current is low against the roughly 40 mA typical of other op-amps. Soomal says the AD823 'is also considered' warm with good dynamics as a headphone amp; this reports general reputation, not a Soomal listening test. Soomal reports that earlier Graham Slee SOLO versions used it, and that it is fitted in the Colorfly C4 Pro and Hidizs AP100 DAPs (its role in the AP100 is unclear). No ASR, Samuel Groner or other independent measurements were checked in this pass.
sonic_descriptors: warm (偏暖; Soomal, citing general reputation)
'emotional', good with acoustic music (Head-Fi, per discovery notes; thread not verified)
typical_uses: Battery-powered CMoy / portable headphone amps (3 V single supply, rail-to-rail output)
Graham Slee SOLO headphone amp, earlier versions per Soomal (the SRG II unit examined had its op-amp marking sanded off)

DAP analog stage: Colorfly C4 Pro (Soomal teardown: 'the op-amp is the AD823'); Hidizs AP100 (Soomal teardown; Hidizs officially described the AD823 as the filter op-amp with OPA2613 driving the headphones, while Soomal's photo caption labels the AD823 as the headphone output, so its role is unconfirmed)
Op-amp rolling in DIY and commercial DAC/amps (e.g. suggested as an alternative in spbkaizo's CMOY design)
ADI's own 3 V stereo headphone-driver application circuit
caveats: Low output current: 15-17 mA linear, rated 0.5 V from the rails. Tangent notes most op-amps are rated around 40 mA, so it is weak for low-impedance headphones without a buffer.
Offset is much higher on ±15 V (3.5 mV max vs 0.8 mV at 5 V), which matters in DC-coupled stages.

Input overvoltage: if an input can exceed +VS by more than 300 mV, or signal is applied with the supplies off, use a series resistor (1 kΩ withstands 10 V of continuous overvoltage). ADI says the part is damaged if left in that state for more than 10 s.
About 20° phase margin driving 470 pF as a follower; add a series output resistor for capacitive loads or cables.
PDIP is available only as the original AD823ANZ. The AD823A redesign is SOIC/MSOP only.
Can sound too aggressive with already forward headphones or systems (Tangent).
AD823A Rev. B warns to use caution at a 30 V supply because excessive output current may overheat the part.
Reputation evidence is mostly subjective (Tangent, Chinese reviews, Head-Fi); no controlled measurements of audio performance were found.

revision_history.changes: Initial version.

Changes to Specifications and Ordering Guide; updated Outline Dimensions. The Pb-free parts AD823ARZ, ARZ-RL and ARZ-R7 appear ('Z = Pb-free part') alongside AD823AN, AR, AR-REEL and AR-REEL7. Absolute-max differential input voltage was ±1.2 V; θJA was given in a footnote (PDIP 90 °C/W, SOIC 160 °C/W). The ±15 V table (p.5) contained unit errors: Ib at TMAX in pA and Ios in nA.

Updated format. Changes to DC Performance (p.5, the ±15 V table), Outline Dimensions and Ordering Guide. Comparing A with E shows the ±15 V unit errors were corrected: Ib at TMAX is now 0.5/5 nA, Ios is 2/20 pA, and Ib at VCM = -10 V is 60 pA. Attributing this to Rev. B is inferred, because Rev. B is the only revision whose change log lists DC Performance. No numeric typ/min/max changes at 5 V or 3.3 V.

Changes to Table 4 (Absolute Maximum Ratings). The observed A-to-E difference is differential input voltage going from ±1.2 V to ±VS, with θJA moved to a separate Table 5. Attributing this to Rev. C is inferred from the change log.
Changes to Figure 34 (pulse response, CL = 470 pF) and Figure 36 (simplified schematic).

Changes to Theory of Operation (a word-level A-to-E diff shows editorial wording only, e.g. 'will occur' became 'occurs') and to the Ordering Guide. The ordering guide lists AD823ANZ, AR, AR-REEL, AR-REEL7, ARZ, ARZ-RL, ARZ-R7 and AD823AR-EBZ; leaded AD823AN is not listed (whether it was dropped in B or E is unknown). No electrical spec changes and no process change stated.
Initial version of the AD823A, a new XFCB-process part.
Added text to the Absolute Maximum Ratings section: 'Use the part with caution at the 30 V supply as excessive output current may overheat and damage the part.' Changes to Equation 8 (active filter).

silicon_changes.when: 2012 (AD823A datasheet Rev. A 5/12, Rev. B 6/12)
silicon_changes.identification: Separate part 'AD823A'. Order codes carry a double A (AD823AARZ vs the original AD823ARZ). Packages are SOIC_N and MSOP only, with MSOP branding H34. Datasheet doc D09439 is titled 'Wide Supply Dual, 17 MHz...'; the original is D00901 'Dual, 16 MHz...'. Hazard: the original AD823 datasheet (Rev. A) labels its A-grade spec column 'AD823A', and original SOIC codes are AD823AR/ARZ, so a listing that just says 'AD823A' is ambiguous. SOIC top-marking differences are unverified.
silicon_changes.summary: The original AD823's datasheet revisions show no die, process or fab change: Rev. 0 to E changes are format, unit typos, abs-max, figure, ordering and editorial only. Tables 1-3 values are numerically identical between Rev. A and Rev. E, and no PCN was found. ADI did create a materially different die under a near-identical name. The AD823A uses the XFCB dielectrically isolated complementary-bipolar process with a two-stage design (folded-cascode first stage). The original uses the CB process with a nested-integrator design. Pinout and supply range match, but specs, drive and package options differ.

spec_deltas.before: CB process, nested integrator, complementary common-emitter RRO
spec_deltas.after: XFCB (dielectrically isolated), two-stage with folded-cascode first stage, RRO

spec_deltas.parameter: Slew rate (5 V, G=-1, 4 V step)
Linear output current, 0.5 V from rails

spec_deltas.after: -108 dBc SFDR (G = -1, RF = RG = 4 kΩ); -99 dBc (G = +1, RL = 1 kΩ). Test conditions differ.

silicon_changes.audio_impact: No listening or measurement reports for the AD823A were found. On paper it fixes the AD823's main headphone weakness with about 2.5x the linear output current. It also has lower noise, higher slew and closed-loop output impedance below 0.01 Ω (versus below 0.2 Ω). Do not assume the praised AD823 sound carries over: the community reputation comes from the original CB-process part, mostly the PDIP AD823AN/ANZ.
silicon_changes.compatibility_risk: Medium. Same dual SOIC pinout and 3-36 V supply, but there is no DIP version, so DIP rollers need an adapter. Compensation and cap-load behaviour differ (the front page quotes 470 pF at 25% overshoot), input common-mode abs max is ±VS ± 0.7 V, and Rev. B warns of overheating from output current at a 30 V supply.

families.counterfeit_notes: No AD823-specific counterfeit reports were found; web search was unavailable, so forums were not checked. Soomal notes that the Graham Slee SOLO SRG II had its op-amp marking sanded off, possibly because the SOLO was often cloned; this is not an AD823 counterfeit report. The following are inferences, not documented reports. (1) Leaded AD823AN is absent from the Rev. E (11/11) ordering guide, so 'AD823AN' DIPs with recent-looking date codes deserve scrutiny. (2) The AD823A exists only in SOIC/MSOP, so any 'AD823A' DIP is either an original AD823AN/ANZ described loosely or a fake. (3) Marketplace listings often confuse the original AD823AR/ARZ (A grade) with the 2012 AD823AARZ die; check the full order code and the datasheet doc number (D00901 vs D09439). Buy from authorized distributors.

AD8620 / AD8610 (ADI precision JFET; Tangent, via Soomal's Chinese translation: 'a bit like the AD823 minus some of its excess aggressiveness'; SOIC only, 26 V operating / 27.3 V max)
AD8066 / AD8065 (ADI FET-input; frequent AD823 comparison on Head-Fi; Tangent: 24 V rated operating supply, 26.4 V max, SOIC only at the time)
OPA2132 / OPA2134 (TI/Burr-Brown FET-input audio duals; the usual reference comparison)
open_questions: The WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200 session cap), so no web query succeeded in either the research or the fact-check pass. Verification used the cached vendor PDFs (AD823 Rev. A and Rev. E, AD823A Rev. B) plus about 17 GitHub code searches. Vendor pages, distributor lifecycle data, the Head-Fi and diyAudio threads, and ASR were not read.
Is AD823 Rev. E (11/11) still ADI's current revision, or is there a Rev. F? A third-party note says Rev. E is current.

No copies were found of AD823 Rev. 0 (5/95), B (2/07), C (5/10) or D (6/10), or of AD823A Rev. A (5/12). Which revision first listed AD823ANZ and dropped AD823AN is unknown. The ±15 V unit fixes (Rev. B) and the Table 4 change (Rev. C) are attributed only from the change logs.
Lifecycle status (active/NRND/obsolete) of AD823ANZ, AD823AR/ARZ and AD823AARZ/AARMZ is unverified.
Does ADI officially position the AD823A as the AD823's replacement? The AD823A datasheet does not mention the AD823.
Top-marking differences between AD823 SOIC and AD823A SOIC are unknown; only the AD823A MSOP branding (H34) is documented.
No PCN or fab-transfer notice for the AD823 has been found in its roughly 30-year life.
What role does the AD823 play in the Hidizs AP100: output low-pass filter (Hidizs' claim, per Soomal) or headphone driver (Soomal's photo caption)?
The contents and measurements of the Head-Fi op-amp round-up thread (870832), the Head-Fi AD823/OPA2132/AD8066 review (242125) and the diyAudio AD823-vs-OPA2132 thread were not verified.
The AD823 datasheet's Theory of Operation quotes a '1 mV maximum' offset, while Table 1 gives 0.8 mV max at 5 V: a minor internal inconsistency present in both Rev. A and Rev. E.

reputation.summary: On Head-Fi, AD8599 is best known from the 'AD8599 is bloody good' thread, where op-amp rollers call it dynamic, vivacious, sparkling and 'alive'. One comparison thread calls it warmer than other Analog Devices op amps, with an accurate soundstage. Both come from discovery notes and were not re-read this run. Engineers use it as an ultralow-noise, ultralow-distortion bipolar dual. The discovery notes also say it is recommended as a low-noise alternative to the OPA1612 and LME49720, but that source is unverified. Confirmed uses in GitHub-hosted designs: the output amp of an MDAC (DAC8812) volume attenuator in a DIY preamp (FutureSharks preamp-two); the RX I/Q or AF preamp in Elecraft KX3 and KX2 SDR transceivers, next to the OPA2209; the I/Q baseband amp (U106) in the T41/Phoenix SDR; and precision low-noise instrumentation front ends. No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurements, and no Japanese or Chinese community impressions, could be retrieved.
sonic_descriptors: warmer than other Analog Devices op amps
typical_uses: Op-amp rolling in DAC and headphone-amp sockets (via SOIC-to-DIP adapter)
Output amplifier for multiplying-DAC (MDAC) volume attenuators in DIY preamps
Low-noise line and headphone preamplifier stages with low source impedance
SDR I/Q baseband and RX AF preamp stages (Elecraft KX3/KX2, T41/Phoenix SDR)

reputation.summary: Popular with Head-Fi and diyAudio op-amp rollers since the mid-2000s. Tangentsoft's 'Notes on Audio Op-Amps' (Warren Young; Chinese translation on DiyEden/Soomal, 2005) calls it the author's favourite chip, especially for battery amps. It likens the AD8610 to the AD823 without some of the aggressiveness and advises using it in laid-back rather than aggressive systems. ADI's AN-1429 (Rev. 0, 10/2016, David Guo) lists the AD8620 among ADI op-amps 'reputable with music fans', alongside the AD797, OP275 and ADA4627-1. Soomal teardowns confirm commercial use: the Topping NX5 (2016) runs 2x AD8610 plus BUF634, the Xuelin iHiFi990 (2017) uses 2x AD8610 as its DAC LPF, and the FiiO X7 MkII AM3A module (2017) uses an AD8620 preamp. Three sources were cited but not re-checked this session: Head-Fi threads praising the AD8620, a Leckerton blog post (AD8610 as its default output op-amp, OPA627 not clearly better in blind A/B), and a Japanese Zigsow review ('won't lose to the 627').
sonic_descriptors: AD823-like without some of its aggressiveness (Tangentsoft)
more detail and smoothness than AD843 (Tangentsoft via translation; wording ambiguous)
typical_uses: DAC output low-pass filter / I/V
headphone-amp gain stage, often with a BUF634 buffer (Topping NX5)
battery-powered portable headphone amps
op-amp rolling on SOIC-to-DIP adapters
precision/high-impedance instrumentation and photodiode amps
caveats: The operating supply is specified only to +/-13 V, with an absolute max of about 27.3 V total per Tangentsoft (not checked against ADI). It is not a drop-in for +/-15 V or higher rails.
The single comes in SOIC-8 or MSOP-8 and the dual in SOIC-8 only, so DIP-8 sockets need an adapter board.
Output current is about +/-30 mA. Designs driving low-impedance headphones often add a buffer (e.g. BUF634 in the Topping NX5), although Tangentsoft rated its drive as good for a battery amp.
Tangentsoft advises against pairing it with aggressive or bright systems.
No independent THD+N measurements (ASR, Samuel Groner) were found.
The Head-Fi, Leckerton, diyAudio and Zigsow reputation sources were not re-verified this session.

Ordering codes ADA4627-1BRZ, ADA4637-1BRZ and ADA4637-1ACPZ-R2/-R7/-RL were seen only in a third-party chip-catalogue sitemap. Confirm them in ADI's ordering guide, check whether a B-grade LFCSP exists, and check lifecycle status (NRND?).
ADI PCNs (fab or assembly transfer, die change) for either part were not searched. None are known.

The LTspice ChangeLog lists ADA4637 macro-model fixes on 04/17/21 (output-voltage limit) and 05/12/21 (open-loop gain/phase). These are simulation-model changes only and must not be read as silicon changes.
The SPICE model author tag 'HH / ADSJ' may refer to an ADI Japan design group; this is unverified.
No independent measurements (Samuel Groner distortion survey, Audio Science Review) have been located.

reputation.summary: NOT VERIFIED: no web search was available, and forum and measurement sites were not reached. The discovery notes describe the LF353 as a vintage BiFET dual in 1980s-90s consumer and synth gear, called smooth or warm by some listeners and ordinary by measurement-minded reviewers. The datasheets make it a TL072-class part: 16-18 nV/rtHz and 3-4 MHz. TI lists 'Pro Audio Mixers' among its applications, and National specified THD <0.02%. Its appeal is originality in restorations, not performance.
typical_uses: pro audio mixers (TI SLOS012C application list)
preamp, tone-control and filter stages in vintage gear (discovery notes, unverified)
synthesizer and modular CV/VCO/VCF circuits (e.g. open4Umodular subosc BOM 'LF353 or TL072')
active filters, integrators, sample-and-hold, D/A converters (TI and National datasheets)
budget Chinese DACs (a Xiang Sheng DAC-01A review lists OPA2604 x1 and LF353N x2; low confidence)
caveats: Noisier than bipolar audio duals: 16-18 nV/rtHz vs about 5 nV/rtHz for an NE5532. It matters with low-impedance sources.
Offset up to 10 mV (13 mV over temperature), so DC-coupled stages need trimming, a servo or a coupling capacitor.
National documents phase reversal: taking either input below the negative common-mode limit forces the output high (no latch). Keep inputs at least 3-4 V above V-. TI SLOS012C does not mention it.
TI recommends +/-3.5 V minimum, while National says zener biasing gives normal operation from +/-6 V. Commercial 0-70 °C only.
Output specified only into 2 k/10 k loads, so not for 600-ohm or headphone loads.
Specs differ by vendor (TI 3 MHz/18 nV; National 4 MHz/16 nV; ST 4 MHz/15 nV). An 'LF353' from another maker is not the same part.
Never let an input go below the negative supply: National warns this can destroy the unit.

families.counterfeit_notes: No LF353-specific counterfeit reports were verified (no web search available). It is a very cheap commodity part, so remarking pays little, but recycled or remarked DIP pulls from marketplace sellers are common for all classic op-amps. Buy TI, ST or onsemi stock from authorised distributors. Current TI parts are marked LF353P (PDIP) or LF353 (SOIC) per TI's addendum. 'LF353AN/BN' or TO-99 'LF353H' parts are genuine National grades from before 2000; offers of them as new production are suspect. When TI stopped using the NS logo on ex-National parts was not verified, so date-code rules for National-marked parts are unconfirmed.

reputation.summary: A cult op-amp-rolling pick rather than a mainstream audio part, and opinion is split. JP: nabe's Chu-Moy comparison ranked the LM6172 'straightest' (least coloured), ahead of the OP275, and found the OPA627AP muddied detail. A Zigsow reviewer calls the LM6172IN/NOPB 'simply a high-speed stone'. Other JP listeners are negative: a goo blog post is titled 'LM6172 無駄買いですよ' (a wasted purchase), and other reports call it light in the bass and treble-leaning, or less resolving than the LM4562/LME49720 as a buffer. diyAudio posters call the LM6171/6172 'very detailed and neutral'. Head-Fi has dedicated threads (Mind the LM6171/2; OPA637 vs LM6171 mini shoot-out; LM6172's sound signature; LM6171 vs OPA604 vs OPA627) with mixed impressions, from neutral and clean to 'too thick/sombre' or 'technical, slightly cold'. The Chinese DiyEden/Soomal notes (2005) are a translation of an English first-person CMoy op-amp test that cites headwize threads; they are not independent CN opinion. Those notes say it has more powerful bass than the OPA132/134, a subtle but real difference from the OPA134PA at 15 V, and is better than the OPA132/134 at low supply. They also say it turns soft and round rather than harsh when starved of supply, and is not for beginners. Commercial use: per a Soomal teardown, the Shanling H1.1 DAC (2013) uses LM6171s in its headphone module. A search summary reports a CMoy test that ranked the LM6172 lowest in noise floor against the LM4562, NE5532, OPA2277, OPA2134 and OPA2132; it apparently comes from a UIUC Physics 406 student report, but that attribution is unconfirmed. No ASR or Groner measurement was found.
sonic_descriptors: more powerful bass than OPA132/134 (DiyEden translation)
soft and very round when supply-starved, not harsh (DiyEden translation)
light / weak bass, treble-leaning (some JP listeners)
typical_uses: Op-amp rolling in Chu-Moy/CMoy headphone amps
Headphone output stage (Shanling H1.1 DAC uses the LM6171)
DAC I/V or output stages in DIY builds
Video and high-speed signal paths, ADC drivers (original target market)
caveats: Layout- and stability-sensitive ('cranky' per AMB forum and Head-Fi). Needs tight decoupling and a suitable circuit; risky in sockets and adapters.
Not beginner-friendly; the result depends heavily on the surrounding circuit (DiyEden translation).
Opinion is split: praise (nabe, diyAudio) sits beside clearly negative JP reviews (goo blog 'wasted purchase', light bass) and mixed Head-Fi impressions.
Bass descriptions conflict: JP reports light bass, the translated CMoy notes report powerful bass.
The DiyEden/Soomal translation wrongly calls it a 'high-speed FET-input' op-amp. The LM6171/6172 is bipolar.
All praise is subjective listening; there are no vendor audio-THD claims aimed at audio users.

families.tagline: National's 44 V member of the LM4562/LME49720 audio series: 2.7 nV/√Hz, 0.00003% THD+N, ±22 V rails. Used in Sony PHA-2/PHA-3 and Gustard DACs and preamps.
families.technology: Bipolar voltage-feedback op-amp, unity-gain stable. LME49860 is the dual. LME49870 is the single: distributor and datasheet mirrors title it '44V Single High Performance, High Fidelity Audio Operational Amplifier' (National, later TI). Whether it uses the same die as the LME49860 is not confirmed. Supply is ±2.5 V to ±22 V, with a 46 V absolute maximum. Inputs are bipolar: IB 10 nA typ, differential input impedance 30 kΩ. A TI E2E thread titled 'LME49710, LME49720 and LME49860 Differential Input Diodes' covers the input clamp diodes. The datasheet lists SOIC-8 (D) and PDIP-8 (P) packages; TI's Nov-2025 addendum lists only the SOIC. SNAS389C does not use National's 'Overture' brand for this part.

reputation.summary: Seen as the high-voltage (±22 V) member of National's LM4562/LME49720 audio series, with the same headline numbers (2.7 nV/√Hz, 0.00003% THD+N, 55 MHz) and more rail headroom. Forum summaries describe it as refined, detailed and wide-staged: in a head-fi round-up it sat between OPA2604 and AD823 in character, with a better soundstage than either. On diyAudio it is a 'very good all-rounder' with slightly 'synthetic' highs. In a VentureCraft Vantam swap test, Soomal found it firmer and more tense than MUSES02 while still warm, with springier bass, no muddy mid-bass, a wider upper-mid stage and more 3D vocals, and recommended it for speaker systems. Japanese blog summaries praise its clarity across the whole band and its refined highs; others find it plain. Opinion is split on whether it differs audibly from LME49720/LM4562. Nearly all of this is forum and blog opinion, not controlled listening tests.
sonic_descriptors: between OPA2604 and AD823 in character, more refined and detailed, better soundstage than either (head-fi round-up, via search summary)
very good all-rounder: powerful bass, good soundstage, detailed highs (diyAudio 'Best Sounding DUAL opamps', via search summary)
更硬朗，有张力 (firmer, more tension) but still warm; springier bass and no muddy mid-bass vs MUSES02; wider upper-mid stage, more 3D vocals (Soomal Vantam review)
clarity across the whole band, good coherence and resolution, refined highs that are never unpleasant (JP blogs, via search summary)
flat or plain with decent resolution; 'lacking' to some (JP, via search summary)
less coloured than NJM2114DD; one JP review heard little difference from LME49990 (JP search summaries)
some rank it LM4562 < LME49720HA < LME49860; others hear no difference (head-fi)
typical_uses: DAC output and filter stages (Gustard A18: four LME49860 duals, per the Frieve-A review)
Balanced preamps (Gustard P26: two socketed duals, moved to SO-8 on a socket adapter after DIP-8 was discontinued)
Portable DAC/amp voltage-gain stages: Sony PHA-2 (final analog output) and Sony PHA-3 (voltage gain and gain switch), per Soomal
Socketed pre stage in VentureCraft SoundDroid Vantam (stock LME49860; a MUSES02 version was also offered), per Soomal
Input op-amp in the Luxman/Stereo LXA-OT1 kit (low confidence: the sara-mac page title reads as a swap to LME49860NA)
Op-amp rolling in DIP-8 sockets; pro-audio line drivers and receivers on ±18 to ±22 V rails; RIAA phono preamps and active filters (datasheet applications)
caveats: 55 MHz GBW: capacitive loads above 100 pF must be isolated with a series resistor (datasheet). DIY notes flag socket parasitics, decoupling and CL peaking.

The 1.6 pA/√Hz current noise means the 2.7 nV/√Hz advantage is lost in high-impedance (≈20 kΩ) networks (i_n × R ≈ 32 nV/√Hz), so it needs low-impedance feedback. IB of 10 nA typ / 72 nA max also adds DC offset there.
Quiescent current of about 10.5 mA per package at ±22 V means heat and battery drain in portables.
DIP-8 (NA/NOPB) and SOIC tube (MA/NOPB) went obsolete after a 28-Sep-2016 LTB (per E2E summary). Only SOIC tape-and-reel remains, and DIP sockets need an adapter.
Differential input diodes (TI E2E 337068) conduct under large differential input, so it is not suitable as a comparator.
Popcorn/low-frequency noise (TI E2E 415907) and EM-field sensitivity reports concern the sibling LM4562/LME49720, not specifically the LME49860.
Sound reports are subjective and often whole-device impressions. Soomal found the PHA-3 soft and restrained despite its LME49860s.

families.counterfeit_notes:
No counterfeit report specific to the LME49860 was found, so the risk here is inferred. LME49860NA/NOPB (PDIP), LME49860MA/NOPB and LME49870MA/NOPB are obsolete: DigiKey lists them so, and a TI E2E 456802 summary gives an LTB of 28 Sep 2016. Any 'new' DIP LME49860NA or LME49870 is therefore old stock at best. Fakes of sibling parts are documented: a fake 'LME49720NA' (diyAudio 386852) and a fake LME49710 (tinytransistors.net, 2022). The discovery note that remarked LME49860s have been reported was not confirmed. How to check:
(1) Genuine current SOIC parts are marked 'L49860' over 'MA' (TI addendum) with a logo and lot code. National-logo parts are older stock.
(2) Total Iq should be about 10.2-10.5 mA per package at ±18-22 V.
(3) THD+N should sit near analyzer residual, e_n about 2.7 nV/√Hz and GBW about 55 MHz.
(4) Do not first power-test suspect parts at ±22 V: a remarked 36 V-class part would exceed its absolute maximum.
(5) Buy SOIC LME49860MAX/NOPB from authorized distributors.
alternatives: LME49720 / LM4562 (same National series and headline specs, but ±17 V max; the LME49720 MA/NA also went EOL in 2016)
OPA1602 (TI's suggested replacement for LME49720 in the EOL discussion; OPA1611 was suggested for LME49710). ±18 V class, so it does not suit ±22 V rails.
OPA1612 (dual of OPA1611; a distributor cross-reference names OPA1612AID as the LME49860MA/NOPB replacement; ±18 V class)
OPA2227P (a distributor cross-reference names it as the LME49860NA/NOPB PDIP replacement; ±18 V class)
OPA2604 (FET-input dual rated to about ±24 V, one of the few rolling candidates that tolerates ±22 V rails)
OPA1656 (modern CMOS-input low-distortion dual, ±18 V class)
LME49870 (the 44 V single sibling; obsolete since the 2016 LTB)
NE5532 (the classic it replaces in sockets; ±22 V is its absolute maximum, not its operating rating)

families.name: LME49990 (National Overture E-Series / TI ultra-low-noise bipolar single)
families.tagline: National's Dec 2009 Overture E-Series flagship single (0.9 nV/rtHz, 0.00001% THD+N), rolled as an AD797/LT1028 rival in phono and DAC stages.
families.technology: Bipolar-input, voltage-feedback single op-amp from National's LME 'Overture E-Series' audio line. The datasheet title is 'Ultra-low Distortion, Ultra-low Noise Operational Amplifier'. Front-page specs: 0.9 nV/rtHz typ and 1.3 nV/rtHz max at 1 kHz, 1/f corner 43 Hz, THD+N 0.00001% (AV=1, 3 Vrms, 1 kHz, 600 ohm), GBW 110 MHz, slew rate 22 V/us, supply range +/-5 V to +/-18 V, output current +/-27 mA. The only package is SOIC-8 (LME49990MA).

reputation.summary: A cult-favourite single among op-amp rollers and low-noise designers. In the diyAudio thread 'LME49990 audio op amp - better than AD797?', a long-time AD797 fan reportedly called it the 'winner by a mile' (per discovery notes, not re-checked). In Soomal's 2020 Creative AE-9 test, the reviewer called it the highest-end single of the series. It made the hybrid fast roll-off filter mode sound more refined, but the reviewer judged the LME49710 better value. Zigsow lists it with the AD797, THS4631 and LT1115 as a famous single and praises its resolution. Aurorasound frames it as National's rival to the LT1028A/OPA627A. Engineers are cooler. In EEVblog #541 the 'outperforming the 797' line came from a viewer's letter. Dave Jones himself called the datasheet an 'audiophile wank alert' and found the noise curves 'not hugely better' than the AD797's. TI's own E2E answer is that there is no exact replacement; the OPA1611/1612 are the closest. Douglas Self gives it sections in 'The Design of Active Crossovers' (2nd ed.), including one on its common-mode distortion.
sonic_descriptors: very extended bass (diyAudio, per discovery notes)
high resolution: harmonies and reverb tails fully revealed (Zigsow)
harsh and thin when under-bypassed (Japanese users)
typical_uses: MC/MM phono preamplifiers (DIY)
DAC and sound-card output/filter stages, e.g. Creative Sound Blaster AE-9 op-amp swaps
low-impedance, low-noise preamps and measurement front-ends (e.g. suggested for an HP 35670A front-end in EEVblog #541)
op-amp rolling in DIP-8 sockets via SOIC-to-DIP adapter boards
caveats: Obsolete: TI first made it NRND under a process end of life, and distributors now list it Obsolete. Supply is NOS or grey market only.
SOIC-8 only, so DIP sockets need an adapter. The extra lead length matters for a part with 110 MHz GBW; this is a general layout concern, not a specific report.
Japanese users say it needs 10 uF or more of local supply bypassing, and that with only 0.1 uF it sounds harsh and thin. This is forum folklore, not a datasheet statement.
Its measured noise advantage over the AD797 is small (EEVblog #541), so do not over-read the headline 0.88/0.9 nV figure.
It pays off in low-impedance circuits. Douglas Self treats its common-mode distortion separately, so check non-inverting and follower use.
TI's suggested replacement, the OPA1611, has nearly as low distortion, but its THD rises more at high frequency (TI E2E, per search summary).
Costs more than the sibling LME49710. Soomal judged the LME49710 better value in the AE-9.

families.counterfeit_notes: No documented counterfeit or remarked LME49990 reports turned up. Risk is still elevated. The part is Obsolete (TI process end of life), single-source and SOIC-only, and it trades as NOS or grey-market stock, often pre-soldered on SOIC-to-DIP adapters (e.g. BrownDog boards on Yahoo! Auctions), where the marking is hard to inspect. Buy traceable stock. Check the laser marking (National or TI logo, 'LME49990'/'MA'). Also measure quiescent current (about 9 mA typ per distributor data) and noise; a remarked cheaper bipolar part would show clearly more than about 0.9 nV/rtHz at 1 kHz.

families.name: LT1028 / LT1128 (single ultralow-noise bipolar, 0.85 nV/√Hz)
families.tagline: A 0.85 nV/√Hz bipolar single from Linear Tech. It has long been the benchmark for MC, tape-head and mic head-amps, and it is a cult pick for op-amp rolling (e.g., Xonar I/V stages).
families.technology: Bipolar single op amp. The input stage runs at nearly 1 mA collector current, so voltage noise is very low but current noise is high. Bias-current cancellation holds IB to about 25 nA typ; the cancellation injects correlated current noise, which is rejected only when the source resistances are matched. The LT1028 is decompensated: stable at gain >= +2 or -1, 75 MHz GBW. The LT1128 is the unity-gain-stable version, 20 MHz GBW. Pin 5 is an over-compensation terminal and pins 1/8 are VOS trim. The inputs have back-to-back protection diodes with no series resistors.

Bipolar, nearly 1 mA collector current. Back-to-back input diodes with no limiting resistors: limit current to 25 mA if the differential input exceeds +/-1.8 V. The optimum source resistance is about e_n/i_n = 850 ohm at 1 kHz (computed from typ values). Datasheet Table 1 names the LT1028/LT1128 as LT's lowest-noise choice for 0-400 ohm sources at 10 Hz and up to 4 kohm at 1 kHz. Because of bias-current cancellation, unmatched source resistance above about 1 kohm adds cancellation noise.

The LT1028 is stable at closed-loop gain > +2 or -1 (about 50 deg phase margin at 6 dB). As a follower it needs parallel RC feedback (CF < 68 pF) or source resistance. A large CF can oscillate unless RS2 >= 500 ohm. The LT1128 is unity-gain stable. A capacitor from pin 5 (over-comp) to the output cuts noise bandwidth and improves capacitive-load drive.
Rev C (10/14) corrected the right-hand (non-A-grade) Electrical Characteristics column and changed TJMAX to 150 C for S8/SW. Non-A limits printed in Rev B or earlier copies may therefore be wrong.

reputation.summary: Hi-Fi enthusiasts and engineers treat the LT1028 as the reference ultralow-noise bipolar op amp for very low source impedances: MC phono head amps, tape heads and dynamic mics. Its own datasheet shows MAG phono and tape-head preamps. One diyAudio poster calls it 'the only real Linear Technology star' among audio op amps, and the same thread lists it among the best VFB op amps. It is a popular I/V pick when rolling Asus Xonar Essence ST/STX op amps. Japanese Dr.DAC users call it monitor-like and not fussy about sources. Aurorasound presented NS's LME49990 as a challenger to the LT1028A. The 1993 rec.audio Audio FAQ already called it 'very well received' for phono, head-amp and mic preamps. Engineers note its high current noise and a noise bump around 400 kHz. The community sonic claims come from earlier discovery searches and were not re-verified in this run.
typical_uses: MC phono head amp / pre-preamp
MM phono and tape-head preamps (datasheet application circuits)
low-impedance microphone preamps
DAC I/V stage (e.g., Asus Xonar Essence ST/STX op-amp rolling)
op-amp rolling in Dr.DAC-type DACs and headphone amps
low-noise measurement preamps, TIAs, laser current drivers
caveats: The LT1028 is NOT unity-gain stable (gain >= +2 or -1). It can oscillate as a follower, unity buffer or I/V stage with a large feedback cap. Use the LT1128 or follow the datasheet RC/RS2 rules. With 75 MHz GBW it is sensitive to socket and adapter layout.

High input bias current (+/-25 nA) and current noise (1 pA/rtHz at 1 kHz, 4.7 at 10 Hz). With source impedances well above about 1 kohm (about 400 ohm at 10 Hz per the datasheet table), current noise dominates and another part is better. Bias-current cancellation adds noise when the source resistances at the two inputs are unmatched.

High supply current: 7.4 mA typ, 9.5-10.5 mA max at 25 C, and up to 12.5 mA max (non-A, -40 to 85 C). It runs warm and loads small supplies. It is specified at +/-15 V, and PSRR is specified from +/-4 V.
Single only, with no dual version. Dual sockets need adapters, which adds oscillation risk.
Pin 5 is an over-compensation pin and pins 1/8 are VOS trim. Check that the host board leaves pin 5 open or uses it correctly. The SW16 package has a different pinout.
Input diodes have no series resistors. Large differential transients (for example slew overload in unity-gain use) need input current limiting.
There is a noise bump around 400 kHz in the HF noise curve. It is inaudible but raises integrated wideband noise (Libbrecht & Hall 1993 and Seck et al. 2016, as cited in P. Baus's PhD thesis).

families.counterfeit_notes:
No specific counterfeit reports were located. Web search was unavailable, and a GitHub code search for LT1028 counterfeit/fake/remarked returned nothing. The discovery notes flag cheap marketplace listings as of doubtful origin (low confidence). Identification per Rev D:
- SO-8 parts are top-marked '1028' / '1128' (plus date and lot code).
- PDIP and SW16 parts carry the full part number (e.g., 'LT1028ACN8').
- The temperature grade appears on the shipping-container label.
- #PBF / #TRPBF / #TRMPBF are orderable suffixes, not package markings.
- AM/M grades and the H (TO-5) and J8 (CERDIP) packages are obsolete, so 'new' metal-can or ceramic parts are old stock or fakes.
Quick bench checks at +/-15 V:
- A genuine part draws about 7.4 mA (9.5 mA max A grade, 10.5 mA non-A, at 25 C).
- Its 1 kHz noise should be at or below 1.1-1.2 nV/rtHz.
- A remarked generic bipolar op amp would typically show about 3 nV/rtHz or more.
alternatives: AD797 (ADI): about 0.9 nV/rtHz bipolar single with high output drive and a very low-distortion reputation. It is the usual head-to-head rival. Seck et al. (via Baus) found lower integrated wideband noise than the LT1028, which has a 400 kHz bump.
LT1115 (Linear/ADI): 0.9 nV/rtHz audio-optimised sibling, marketed by LT as an ultralow-noise, low-distortion audio op amp.
LT1128 (same datasheet): use it where unity-gain stability is needed (buffers, some I/V stages).
OPA1611 / OPA211 (TI): about 1.1 nV/rtHz bipolar, unity-gain stable, modern supply range. OPA1612 is the dual.
LME49990 (National/TI, discontinued): 0.9 nV/rtHz, positioned by Aurorasound as a challenger to the LT1028A.
ADA4898-1/-2 (ADI): 0.9 nV/rtHz, unity-gain stable, dual available. Much lower open-loop gain (about 0.14 V/uV) than the LT1028.

families.name: LT1363 / LT1364 / LT1365 (single/dual/quad 70 MHz, 1000 V/us C-Load bipolar)
families.tagline: Linear's 1994 70 MHz, 1000 V/us C-Load bipolar dual. A cheap Japanese favourite called fast and transparent; English forums are split between 'magic' and 'coloured'.
families.technology: Complementary bipolar process (Linear Technology's own). Voltage-feedback amplifier that slews like a current-feedback one: each input is a complementary NPN/PNP emitter follower driving a ~500 ohm resistor (R1), the currents are mirrored into a high-impedance gain node, and the output stage is a pair of complementary followers. The NPN and PNP base currents cancel to first order, so input bias current can be either polarity. C-Load compensation places an RC network across the output stage; it is bootstrapped under light loads and adds compensation under capacitive or low-impedance loads, so the part is stable with any capacitive load. Slew rate scales with input step size, so it is highest at low gain (tested at AV = -2).

reputation.summary: Reputation is mixed. It rests on forum and blog listening reports, re-checked here only through search-result summaries captured earlier in this session; no independent measurements (ASR, Samuel Groner) were checked. English-language posts call it the 'magic' op-amp: dynamic and involving (though tonally 'rounded'), with 'much greater transparency and less grain'. They rank it with the AD8610 as an OPA627 alternative with a different flavour. A diyAudio 'best sounding opamps' thread describes it as heavily coloured and euphonic, simplifying the music and able to 'kill nuances' in high-quality systems. The same thread says it suits delta-sigma DAC filters and low-impedance headphones. Some listeners prefer the lower-bias LT1358 (same circuit). In Japan it is a popular value pick: Akizuki sells the LT1364CN8#PBF for under 1,000 yen. Bloggers call it fast and uncoloured, with precise imaging, a 'tight, lean-muscled' sound and clean treble without harshness. One blogger found it lighter in bass than the MUSE8820. A Zigsow review is titled 'cool sound, hot chip'. Zigsow opinions go both ways: one reviewer prefers its transparency to the OPA627AU, while another review puts the OPA627AP in a different league. Mineden says it covers the OPA2604's thin midrange. A 2023 pooq.biz post tries to recreate it with discrete parts.
sonic_descriptors: cool sound (while the chip runs hot)
typical_uses: DAC I/V, output filter and buffer stages (delta-sigma DACs)
op-amp rolling in DACs, headphone amps and sound cards (Xonar/Prodigy buffers; listed among swap options in the Maverick TubeMagic D1 FAQ)
line buffers and cable drivers (datasheet application)
video/RF amplification and fast data-acquisition buffers (datasheet)
caveats: Mixed reputation. English forum views range from 'magic' and transparent to 'heavily coloured', and it can 'kill nuances' in high-end systems. Japanese reviews are mostly positive but still mixed against the OPA627.
Runs hot: 6.3 mA typ (7.5 max) per amplifier. A DIP-8 dual at +/-15 V dissipates about 0.38 W, a rise of about 50 C at 130 C/W, which matches the 'hot chip' remark.

70 MHz GBW makes it sensitive to layout, sockets and decoupling. The datasheet asks for 0.01-0.1 uF RF-quality bypass close to the pins, plus CF > RG*CIN/RF when feedback resistors exceed 5 kohm. One Japanese DIY builder's GitHub design notes (indare/pcb_work) rank it the most layout-sensitive part in their stock. They predict, by analysis rather than measurement, ringing or oscillation with 47k/10k feedback and only 0.1 uF decoupling in a DIP socket.

High input bias current (0.6 uA typ, 2 uA max, either polarity) produces large DC offsets with high-value bias or feedback resistors (about 200 mV worst case with 100 kohm). Use balanced source impedances or AC coupling.
Voltage noise of 9 nV/rtHz is higher than the NE5532 or LM4562, with a 1/f corner of roughly 600-700 Hz per graph G05. It is a poor choice for low-impedance, high-gain or phono stages.
Do not use as a comparator or with sustained differential input: supply current rises to tens of mA and the part may be damaged.
C-grade parts are only guaranteed to meet specifications from 0 to 70 C.
Slew rate depends on input level and is highest at low closed-loop gain.

families.name: LT1468 / LT1469 (single/dual 90 MHz, 22 V/µs, 16-bit-accurate bipolar precision op-amp)
families.tagline: Linear Tech's 16-bit-settling precision op-amp built for DAC I/V: 5 nV/√Hz, 90 MHz, ±15 V, very low distortion. A measurement-minded I/V and filter choice.
families.technology: Bipolar, single-stage precision high-speed op-amp. The datasheet says it is 'a single stage amplifier with an optimal thermal layout'. It uses input bias-current cancellation, and only the inverting-input bias current is trimmed (at zero common-mode voltage), so the part is tailored for inverting (I/V) use. Each input has a 100 Ω series resistor, and back-to-back diodes sit across the input-device bases. LT1468 and LT1469 are unity-gain stable. The -2 versions (LT1468-2, LT1469-2) are stable only at AV ≥ 2, with 200 MHz GBW and 30 V/µs per the Rev B related-parts table.

reputation.summary: Linear's datasheet calls the LT1469 'the optimum choice' for high-accuracy uses such as DAC current-to-voltage conversion and ADC buffers. It also shows an 'Ultralow Distortion Balanced Audio Line Driver' measured at 0.00025% THD+N (with an LT1364 supplying output current). Among DIY-audio users it is described as a 'best on paper' pick for DAC I/V and filter stages. Per discovery notes, diyAudio members found it as clean as the OPA627 but quieter and more neutral, and Head-Fi DAC-output threads recommend it alongside the LT1361, LT1364 and LT1122. Samuel Groner's distortion survey reportedly shows very low common-mode distortion. None of these community or survey claims could be re-checked this run (WebSearch budget exhausted), so they are unverified folklore-level claims. Only the datasheet statements are confirmed.
typical_uses: I/V conversion for current-output DACs (datasheet front-page LTC1597 example)
DAC post-filter / active reconstruction filters
ADC input buffer / driver (datasheet LTC1604 example)
balanced line driver (datasheet parallel-composite circuit with LT1364)
op-amp rolling in DAC output stages (community, unverified)
caveats: The -2 variants (LT1468-2 / LT1469-2) are stable only at gain ≥ 2 and may oscillate in unity-gain buffer sockets. Check the suffix.
Phase reversal (datasheet): if an input comes within 0.5 V of the positive supply, the output reverses phase.

Layout-sensitive. The datasheet asks for a ground plane, short leads, RF-quality 0.01-0.1 µF bypass capacitors in parallel with 1-10 µF low-ESR capacitors, and guard rings for best DC. Socket adapters and long leads likely raise the oscillation risk (general inference, not a datasheet statement).

Input-capacitance pole: for RF > 2k use CF > RG·CIN/RF. When DC noise gain is one with a large RF, CF should be ≥ CIN, and a DAC can add 'many tens of pF'. The datasheet's LTC1597 I/V uses 15 pF across 12k for optimum nulling.
Capacitive load is limited to 100 pF at unity gain and 300 pF at gain -1. Beyond that, use a series output resistor plus a feedback capacitor (datasheet Fig. 3).

Because of bias-current cancellation, the datasheet says balanced source resistances are NOT recommended: they degrade DC accuracy and raise noise. The noninverting-input IB is untrimmed (±40 nA max).
Modest output current (±22 mA typ). The datasheet line driver adds an LT1364 to drive 600 Ω.
Draws about 4.1 mA per amplifier at ±15 V (up to 6.5 mA over temperature), so it runs warmer than low-power audio duals.
Needs a proper split supply: specified at ±5 V and ±15 V, with ±4.5 V the guaranteed minimum.

Simulation: older LTspice IV symbols (mirrored on GitHub) describe LT1468-2 and LT1469-2 as '90MHz, 22V/µs', and the LT1469 and LT1469-2 symbols reference the single-channel LT1468 and LT1468-2 models. ADI fixed the LT1468-2 label on 01/23/21.

families.technology: JFET-input single op-amp. The datasheet graphs show asymmetric drive at ±15 V: about +12.6 V but only about -10 V into 50 Ω.
