reputation.summary: Launched in March 2017 as New JRC's MUSES flagship single. Launch press (Stereo Sound: 'Will it reach the summit of op-amps?'; EE Times Japan) focused on the two-die design and the 0.00003% THD. Head-Fi Opamp-thread posters (seen as search summaries, not full threads) credit its midrange and a deliberately 'slow' presentation that gives vocals and instruments physical presence and holography. They call it neutral with a slightly darker tone than the OPA828 or AD797BRZ, and one poster found the OPA828 emotionally flat on vocals by comparison. Posters describe the later MUSES05 as a refinement with more speed, resolution and air, and the MUSES03 as having more body. They also rate the MUSES03 less resolving than the Burson V7 Vivid. The PHILE WEB MUSES05 launch report credits the MUSES05 with deeper staging. Views are not unanimous: a Japanese blogger could not tell the MUSES03D from the MUSES05 in a Quad405 copy amp. No independent bench measurements (ASR, Samuel Groner) were found.
sonic_descriptors: midrange strength; a deliberately 'slow' sound that gives vocals and instruments physical presence and holography (Head-Fi Opamp thread, via search summary)
power and presence projected by vocalists (diyAudio/Head-Fi, via search summary)
neutral, with a slightly darker tone than the OPA828 or AD797BRZ (Head-Fi, via search summary)
more body, but less air, speed and resolution, than the MUSES05 (Head-Fi Opamp thread)
less resolving than the Burson V7 Vivid (Head-Fi Opamp thread)
less three-dimensional depth than the MUSES05 (PHILE WEB MUSES05 launch listening report)
typical_uses: I/V conversion after DACs (datasheet application list)
preamps, line amps and active filters (datasheet)
headphone amps (datasheet list; 250 mA peak abs-max output, which community posts say is well above the 30–100 mA typical of rivals)
op-amp rolling with two singles on a dual-DIP8 adapter in DACs and headphone amps (hobbyist use)
caveats: Single channel, DIP8 only: a dual socket needs two parts on an adapter, which adds height and lead length.
Iq is 5.8 mA typ and 10 mA max per amplifier, so a two-part adapter can draw 20 mA per socket. Check regulators and heat.
Minimum supply is ±3.5 V and abs max is ±19 V. Differential input abs max is only ±6 V.
The output is asymmetric under heavy load: about -10 V into 50 Ω and about -6 V at 250 mA on the negative side, against about +12.6/+12.8 V on the positive side (datasheet graphs).
Peak output abs max is 250 mA. The datasheet recommends a series protection resistor (e.g. ≥90 Ω at 18 V) where a short is possible.
Slew rate is asymmetric on the datasheet graph: about 37 V/µs rising versus about 102 V/µs falling.
Vos is 1.0 mV typ with no max. Ib is several hundred pA at 85 °C and reaches the nA range above about 90 °C.
Listening impressions are subjective and mixed: one blogger heard no clear difference from the MUSES05.
Discontinued by Oct 2023. Stock is scarce, much of the remaining supply trades on auction and marketplace sites, and counterfeits of MUSES parts are reported.

families.counterfeit_notes: Vendor, datasheet Ver.4.2 p.10: counterfeit MUSES parts circulate worldwide and are often visually indistinguishable from genuine ones. NJR says to buy only through its sales offices or authorized distributors. Genuine reference points from the datasheet: marking '03' (ordering table; alldatasheet marking page); package DIP8(MUSES), body 8.8 × 6.4 mm, OFC lead frame; Sn-2Bi plating; 470 mg; shipped in carbon sticks of 10. Since the 2023 EOL, much of the remaining supply is on auction and marketplace sites (Yahoo! Auctions and aucfan listings seen), where fakes are the main risk. Hobbyist warning (maimai-audio blog 'オペアンプの偽物に注意しよう！', medium-low confidence): it names MUSES01/02/03 among models needing caution, especially units priced far below list or appearing in quantity after production ended. The nw-electric blog (2019) recommends slew-rate measurement as the most effective generic fake test; for MUSES03 the reference values are SR+ about 37 and SR- about 102 V/µs, Iq about 5.8 mA. The 'MUSES03D' name on Akizuki stock is a retailer catalog name, not a sign of a fake. No decap or teardown evidence was found.
alternatives: MUSES05 (Nisshinbo): the successor flagship JFET single, two-chip and fully balanced; general sale from Feb 2022. Its production was reported halted over a process-material shortage (nw-electric 2024-06), and a search summary also calls it discontinued, so check its current status.

MUSES01 (NJR/Nisshinbo): JFET-input dual in the MUSES line
OPA627 (TI/Burr-Brown): the legacy JFET-single benchmark, heavily counterfeited

reputation.summary: Often called the 'budget MUSES02' and treated as the value way into the MUSES sound. Japanese blog reviews (tanupon2000, 音フェチの世界, guiblo/zigsow, new_western_elec) describe it as close to MUSES02 with slightly thinner lines. They report full, deep bass and a crisp, forward presentation, with the extreme treble slightly softened. One LT1364 comparison calls it warmer, with more bass. Head-Fi posters (the Opamp thread and the Burson V6 Classic round-up) called it 'least opamp-sounding', tube-like and wide-staged; one heard no difference from MUSES02 in an LPF position. Rankings put it above NJM4580/NJM8801 and below newer or JFET parts: new_western_elec (2025) ranked OPA2604 < MUSES8820 < MUSES8920 < NL8802 < NL8902. OEM uses include the TEAC AP-507 (MUSES8820E), the Ibanez BT Mini and the VentureCraft VALOQ.
sonic_descriptors: close to MUSES02 but thinner lines
typical_uses: Drop-in upgrade for NJM4580/NE5532 sockets in DACs, CD players and preamps
Op-amp rolling in socketed DIP-8 headphone amps and DACs
DIY preamp, line and LPF stages
OEM: TEAC AP-507 (MUSES8820E), Ibanez BT Mini bass pedal, VentureCraft VALOQ
caveats: All praise is subjective listening impressions. No ASR or Samuel Groner bench data was found, and the Head-Fi round-up's measurement values were not captured.
The 'least opamp-sounding / almost as good as OPA627' quotes may come from the Opamp thread rather than the Burson V6 round-up, which has no OPA627.
Bipolar input: bias current is 100 nA typ / 500 nA max, far above FET parts such as MUSES8920. Watch high source impedances and DC-coupled pots.
Output drive, stability and full electrical tables were not read. Check the datasheet before driving headphones directly.
Counterfeits are documented for MUSES01, MUSES02 and MUSES8920D; no MUSES8820-specific case was found.

families.counterfeit_notes: No documented MUSES8820-specific fake was found. Fakes are documented for sibling MUSES parts: MUSES01 and MUSES02 fakes posted by @fakecomponents on X, including a MUSES02 fake passed off as an Akizuki purchase with thin, wrong top-marking digits, and a MUSES8920D fake reported by new_western_elec (2023-11). MUSES parts in general are reported as frequent counterfeit targets on AliExpress. Practical checks: buy from DigiKey, Mouser or Japanese retailers (Akizuki, Kyohritsu eleshop, Marutsu); treat prices far below the roughly ¥1,100 retail price for MUSES8820D with suspicion; compare the top-marking font, logo and lot code with a known-genuine part; and measure input bias current (100 nA typ / 500 nA max) or supply current against the datasheet. Logo or marking differences between New JRC-era and Nisshinbo-era lots are unverified.

families.name: NJM2068 / JRC2068 (low-noise bipolar dual, New JRC → Nisshinbo)
families.tagline: A cheap, quiet JRC bipolar dual. NwAvGuy used it for the O2's gain stage, and it is common in E-MU audio interfaces and in Japanese CD and AV gear.
families.technology: Bipolar dual op-amp with the standard 4558 dual pinout. NJR's own SPICE macro-model uses a PNP input pair. Internally compensated. The noise-selected D-rank grades (DD/MD/LD) have a guaranteed maximum equivalent input noise.

reputation.summary: NwAvGuy measured the NJM2068 for the Objective2 (O2) and chose it for the gain stage. By his account it was quieter than the NE5532, LM4562 and OPA2134 at lower supply current, and it cost well under a dollar. That made it a favourite with the measurement-minded DIY community. The DIY SmartStand amp also copies the O2's NJM2068 gain stage with an NJM4556A output. In China, Soomal reviews found it in E-MU interfaces (0202/0204/0404/1212m), the Musiland X-Sword II and ooAoo sound cards, and many mid-range CD players. Soomal describes it as very low noise and high resolution, with a neutral, plain sound. Japanese op-amp swappers treat it as the classic quiet JRC dual, calling it relaxed with ample bass. Pro and MI gear uses it too: the Roland VG-99 input stage and GK-3 pickup (per h-milz), Yamaha and Pioneer AV and car units, and cheap MM phono preamps such as FX-Audio. The sound descriptors are community impressions, not measurements.
sonic_descriptors: very low noise (噪声很小; Soomal)
typical_uses: O2 (Objective2) headphone amp gain stage
E-MU 0202/0204/0404/1212m audio interfaces
Chinese PC sound cards (Musiland X-Sword II, ooAoo SQ710 II/SQ717a)
mid-range Japanese CD players and AV receivers (e.g. Yamaha YSP-600 uses NJM2068MD-TE2)
car audio (Pioneer KEX-M8406ZT, NJM2068MD)
MM phono / RIAA preamps (FX-Audio BOX-01/BOX-02)
guitar-synth/pro-audio input stages (Roland VG-99, GK-3 per h-milz)
active monitor speakers (ICON PX-T6A per Soomal)
caveats: Vendor notice: capacitive loads can cause oscillation. Add about 50 Ohm in series with the output (Ver.2011-03-18 p.2).
Minimum supply is +/-4 V (8 V total), so it is unsuitable for 5 V single-supply or USB-powered designs.
The '27 MHz' headline figure is GB at 10 kHz. The unity-gain frequency is only 5.5 MHz, so it is not comparable with other vendors' GBW numbers.
No noise-current or nV/rtHz spec, and input bias current is relatively high (150 nA typ, 1 uA max). Keep source and feedback impedances low.
Output current is not specified, and specs are given for loads of 2 kOhm and above. It is not a headphone driver: the O2 pairs it with NJM4556A outputs.

jh4vaj's pop-noise comparison found the standard NJM2068D had less turn-on pop than the noise-selected NJM2068DD. Both were among the low-pop group; NJM4558DD had the least. This is a single blog measurement.
A note.com blog (gokurakugadget) reports NJM2068D oscillating abnormally in an audio preamp. It is a single user report; see the vendor capacitive-load notice.

families.counterfeit_notes: No NJM2068-specific counterfeit or remarking reports were found in a limited web search. Generic Amazon and eBay listings sell 'NJM2068M SOP8 JRC2068' in lots of 5-10 from unnamed sellers. As with other popular 'JRC' audio duals, such marketplace parts carry a general risk of being remarked. Buy from authorized distributors (Mouser, DigiKey, Akizuki). A 'DD'/'MD' marking only means noise-selected, not a different die, so a big price premium for 'DD' from unknown sellers deserves suspicion. Check the logo style, lot codes and package: genuine DMP8 has a 5.3 mm-wide body, not a 3.9 mm JEDEC SOIC, even though listings call it 'SOP8'.

reputation.summary: A mid-tier Japanese audio dual, marketed by JRC as an improved NJM5532 and perceived that way. JP DIY reviews of NJM2114DD are mostly positive: a Zigsow review is titled 'same price class as NE5532 but better sound', and reviewers describe clear, firm bass and more clarity than NJM2068. Opinion is not unanimous: one JP comparison ranks NJM2114 (with NJM4580) C-rank, below NE5532, LM4562 and OPA2134 (B-rank). Internationally it is best known as the stock JRC2114(D) in the Creative X-Fi Titanium HD, Zx, ZxR, X7 and AE-9, the ASUS Xonar Essence STX, the Gigabyte Z170X-Gaming G1 and the TempoTec DAII Plus. Soomal considers it a neutral buffer/I-V part. No independent measurements were found.
sonic_descriptors: 'Same price class as NE5532 but better sound' (Zigsow NJM2114DD review title)
clear, firm bass with relatively subdued highs (JP NJM2114DD reviews, via search summary)
not bass-heavy like NJM5532; drier than OPA2134; slightly more coloured than LME49860 (JP reviews, via search summary)
'higher-performance 2068: wins on information and clarity' (JP comparison, via search summary)
'JRC2114对声音影响较小': has relatively little effect on the sound (Soomal AE-9 review, 2020)
typical_uses: Creative Sound Blaster X-Fi Titanium HD (2010): socketed JRC2114D, presumed filter and I/V, with LME49710 singles (Soomal)
Creative Sound Blaster ZxR (2013): socketed NJM2114D + LME49710 on front channels, SMD JRC2114 on others. Creative spec: 'Headphone Op-Amps (Swappable) NJM2114D', TPA6120A2 driver.
Creative Sound Blaster Zx (2013) and Sound Blaster X7 (2015, JRC2114D + LME49710) (Soomal)
Creative Sound Blaster AE-9 (2020): socketed JRC2114 buffer with NE5534 singles; SMD JRC2114 + L49720 on sub-channels (Soomal)
ASUS Xonar Essence STX (2009): socketed 2114D used as the I/V converter (Soomal)
E-MU 0202 USB (Soomal teardown, 2010); Gigabyte Z170X-Gaming G1 onboard audio (2015); TempoTec Fantasia DAII Plus DAC, two 2114D as I/V (2017)
I/V stage in some Philips / Marantz CD players (head-fi opamp thread p.113; models unverified, low confidence)
Drop-in NJM5532 / NJM2068 / NJM4580 swap in Japanese headphone amps, USB-DAC filters and cassette decks
caveats: Soomal's AE-9 review (2020-04-15) says op-amps on Creative's EARLIER cards were already good, so swapping brought almost no improvement. It calls the AE-9's stock NE5534 singles puzzling, and advises that users wanting a different sound should upgrade the two singles (LME49710 for continuity) rather than the JRC2114.
Mixed JP rankings: one comparison surfaced by search ranks it C-rank, below NE5532. The page was not pinned; the candidate is nabe.adiary.jp/opamp-compare.

Availability: a 2023 JP blog reports that Nisshinbo made it a maintenance (pre-EOL, not for new designs) product. Marutsu has ended sales of NJM2114D and Mouser shows NJM2114L as obsolete. Expect shrinking authorised stock and more grey-market parts.

No objective measurements (ASR, Groner, jh4vaj) were found. Treat it as a 5532-class bipolar NPN-input part: input bias current and source impedance matter, and with 13 MHz GBW and 15 V/µs it needs sensible decoupling and layout.

families.name: NJM4556 / NJM4556A (dual high-output-current bipolar, 70 mA)
families.tagline: JRC's 70 mA dual that drives 150 ohm loads directly. It is the paralleled output stage of NwAvGuy's O2 and a staple of Japanese DIY headphone amps.
families.technology: Bipolar dual op-amp with a high-current output stage (+/-70 mA into 150 ohm at +/-10.5 V). The input differential pair is PNP in the datasheet equivalent circuit, in NJR's own PSpice macromodels (Version 1 and 2) and in the 2007 Bee Technologies model. Supply is +/-2 V to +/-18 V. The datasheet says it combines many NJM4558 features with 150 ohm drive capability. The Japanese search summary describes it as a 4558 with a reinforced output stage. On the typical curve at +/-15 V, the output sources about 100 mA and sinks about 200 mA before swing collapses.

reputation.summary: It is valued for current drive rather than for a distinctive sound. NwAvGuy used NJM4556A in the current-gain (output) stage of the Objective2 (O2), with both halves paralleled per channel. An earlier search summary of his 'O2 Details' page paraphrased him as saying no other dual DIP8 op-amp delivered as much current at as low distortion ('killed everything else'); this pass did not re-confirm that wording. The O2 made it a default DIY headphone driver, reused in O2/ODA derivatives, Eurorack headphone modules and other projects. Japanese DIY sources call it a standard (定番) headphone-amp chip, and say it sounds surprisingly good for about 30 yen. One Japanese listening comparison (audio-simulation.net, 2019) found it more energetic but rougher in texture than the NJM4580. It also appears in commercial gear: one 2018 owner's Behringer UCA202 had a 4556A, and the Roland AC-90 uses NJM4556AM in its phones amp.
sonic_descriptors: energetic / lively (vs NJM4580; single Japanese listening test)
surprisingly good for the price (Japanese DIY summary)
clean, low-distortion current drive (NwAvGuy O2 testing)
typical_uses: O2 / ODA headphone amp output stage (paralleled sections)
DIY and kit headphone amps in Japan (e.g. aitendo kits)
Eurorack headphone and line-out modules (NJM4556AV)
USB audio interface headphone outputs (one 2018 teardown of a Behringer UCA202)
instrument-amp phones outputs (Roland AC-90, NJM4556AM)
line drivers into 150-600 ohm loads
caveats: The DIP8 (NJM4556AD) and SIP8 (AL) versions are NRND per the March 2025 Nisshinbo datasheet. A maintenance-product (保守品) designation was reported in April 2023. The SMD AM and AV versions continue.
The SMD packages are JRC DMP8 (wider body than a 3.9 mm JEDEC SOIC-8) and SSOP8, so footprints differ.
Package dissipation limits are low (DMP8 300 mW, SSOP8 250 mW), and quiescent current is 9 mA typ per package. Derate for high rails and low-impedance headphones.
Speed is modest (3 V/us, 8 MHz). The typical THD at 20 kHz rises steeply with output level (about 0.2% at 10 Vrms into 200 ohm).
High offset (6 mV max) and bias current (500 nA max) matter in DC-coupled designs like the O2.
Its reputation rests on drive capability rather than a distinctive sound. The sonic descriptors come from single listening reports.

A '4556' on vintage boards may be NEC's uPC4556. That part is decompensated (stable only at gain >= 20 dB), so it is not a substitute for an NJM4556 in a unity-gain buffer. It may also be a Yamaha house-marked part.

silicon_changes.audio_impact: A uPC4556 placed in an NJM4556 socket at unity or low gain (e.g. the O2 output buffer) risks oscillation, and its heavy-load drive is unknown. An NJM4556A replacing a uPC4556 in a high-gain vintage stage would lose bandwidth and slew.

families.counterfeit_notes: No counterfeit or remarking reports for NJM4556/NJM4556A were found; search coverage was limited. eBay listings of NJM4556AD advertised as '"Original" JRC' show that DIP stock now circulates on the grey market after the NRND notice; the 2023 保守品 report and the March 2025 datasheet both mark AD/AL as NRND. Remarked 4558/4559-class duals would not deliver 70 mA (unverified risk). Salvaged vintage '4556' parts may be NEC uPC4556, a decompensated part that is unstable at unity gain and not an equivalent, or Yamaha house-marked YM4556 parts. A practical check: at +/-15 V a genuine NJM4556A should hold about +/-11 V into 150 ohm (datasheet min +/-10.5 V), draw about 9 mA per package, and be stable as a unity-gain follower. Buy from authorized Nisshinbo distributors.

families.name: OP27 / OP37 (PMI/ADI low-noise precision bipolar; OP37 = decompensated, gain ≥5)
families.tagline: PMI's c.1980 3 nV/√Hz zener-trimmed precision bipolar op-amp, long used in phono, tape-head and mic preamps; ADI's datasheet still carries those audio circuits.
families.technology: Monolithic bipolar, single channel. The NPN input stage runs at high quiescent current for low e_n. It has input bias-current cancellation, back-to-back input clamp diodes without series resistors, and on-chip zener-zap offset trim at wafer test. OP27 is unity-gain stable (8 MHz, 2.8 V/µs). OP37 is the same design decompensated for closed-loop gain ≥5 (63 MHz, 17 V/µs); the datasheet schematics are identical.
manufacturers: Analog Devices (acquired PMI c.1990; current source)
Linear Technology (OP-27/OP-37/OP-227/OP-237 second source per LTC 1990 databook references in LTC SPICE models; now ADI)
Texas Instruments (unconfirmed second source; evidence is only 1989 MicroSim-generated macromodels filed in a third-party 'ti' folder; low confidence)

lineage.notes: OP37 Rev B says its audio applications text was 'abstracted from a PMI article in the 12/20/80 issue of Electronic Design magazine', so the parts existed by December 1980. The datasheet positions the part as OP07 offset and drift plus low noise and speed, and says zener-zap trimming has proven itself 'over many years of production history'. ADI's OP27 SPICE macromodel header reads '12/90, Rev. B, JCB / PMI' (JCB is the model author, not necessarily the chip designer). The chip designer is not verified this run.

The PMI macromodel is headed 'Copyright 1990 by Analog Devices, Inc.'. OP27 datasheet revisions run Rev 0 → A (9/01) → B → C (1/03) → D (9/05) → E (12/05) → F (5/06); OP37 runs Rev 0 → A (2/02) → B (12/02). Later revisions not verified. reputation.summary: The reputation is mostly pro-audio and engineering, not 'op-amp rolling'. PMI and ADI pitched the OP27/OP37 at professional audio: the datasheet cites ±10 V into 600 Ω with low distortion and shows RIAA phono, NAB tape-head and transformerless and transformer-coupled mic preamps. A 1990s hobbyist audio FAQ (Atari ST diskmag) says 'The OP-27, OP-37, LT1028, and LT1115 are very well received for phono preamps, head amplifiers, and microphone preamplifiers' and lists the OP-27 among good audio singles, without the 'highly recommended' star. Douglas Self's 'The Design of Active Crossovers' (2nd ed.) has a section titled 'The OP27 Opamp'; its content was not read this run. The diyAudio quotes ('a classic', 'nice forgotten opamp') come from discovery notes and were not re-read. No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurements were verified.
sonic_descriptors: 'nice forgotten opamp' for phono (diyAudio, via discovery notes; unverified)
'very well received' for phono, head-amp and mic preamps (1990s Atari ST diskmag audio FAQ)
typical_uses: MM phono RIAA preamps (datasheet Figure 41)
Microphone preamps, transformerless (OP37 at 50 dB) or transformer-coupled (OP27)
Tape-head (NAB) playback preamps
Low-noise gain stages from low source impedance (<1–3 kΩ)
Precision instrumentation and ADC drivers
caveats: OP37 is decompensated and stable only at gain ≥5. ADI warns that an unplugged mic input (100% feedback) can oscillate and suggests a dummy resistor Rp.

Bias-current cancellation raises current noise (1.7 pA/√Hz at 10 Hz) and gives poor IB matching. ADI: 'The noise advantage of the OP27 disappears when high source resistors are used.' For low-frequency work the OP07 is better above about 3 kΩ source resistance.
OP27 slew rate is low (2.8 V/µs), and the 8 MHz GBW causes RIAA equalisation errors at gains above 40 dB (datasheet). Self's comments on the OP27 were not verified.
The unprotected input diodes conduct when the differential input exceeds 0.7 V. Fast large pulses in unity-gain buffers pull current: use Rf ≥ 500 Ω, plus 20–50 pF across Rf when Rf > 2 kΩ.
Best linearity when peak output current is below ±10 mA (OP37 datasheet, 'Optimizing Linearity').
Single channel only: needs an adapter for dual-op-amp sockets. Draws about 3 mA per amplifier.

families.counterfeit_notes: No OP27/OP37-specific counterfeit or remarking reports were verified (web search unavailable this run). General guidance only: genuine current parts carry ADI Pb-free codes (e.g. OP27GPZ/GSZ). Treat cheap marketplace 'OP27' parts with PMI or old LTC markings, or new-looking CERDIP/TO-99 A-grade parts, with suspicion. A quick check is the ~3 mA supply current (90 mW typ at ±15 V) and the ~3 nV/√Hz noise floor with a low source impedance; a relabelled generic op-amp will be much noisier.

OP227 / OP237 (dual OP27 / dual OP37, if still available)
LT1115 and AD797: listed alongside the OP-27 in 1990s audio op-amp guides for phono and mic use
Modern low-noise bipolar singles in the standard single-op-amp pinout (e.g. OPA1611): pinout match not verified this run

families.name: OP275 (dual 'Butler' bipolar/JFET audio op-amp, Analog Devices)
families.tagline: ADI's audio dual with its 'Butler' bipolar+JFET input. China's classic 'warm, tube-like' op-amp and Musiland's house part; ADI says music fans rate it.
families.technology: Dual voltage-feedback op-amp with ADI's 'Butler Amplifier' input stage, which combines bipolar and JFET transistors. It is unity-gain stable. ADI's claim, repeated on a 1999 German product page and in EEVblog #738, is that it was the first op-amp with a Butler front-end. The design came from the PMI (Precision Monolithics) group: the SPICE macro-models are credited 'JCB / PMI' and carry an Analog Devices copyright of 1992 and 1995. Analog Devices is the only maker; there are no second sources.

reputation.summary: OP275 was ADI's audio-targeted dual. ADI's AN-1429 (Rev. 0, by David Guo) says ADI op-amps 'are reputable with music fans, like the AD797, OP275, AD8620, and ADA4627-1'. In the Chinese community (Soomal) it is the textbook 'warm, tube-like' op-amp. It was Musiland's signature part, confirmed in Soomal teardowns and reviews: Long March II (2007), MD10 (2007), Monitor 01 US and 02 US (2009), 01 PS (2010, with TPA6120), MD11 (2010), HP11 (2010/11, ahead of LME49600 buffers), MD30 (2011) and MD12 (2014, marked OP275G). In 2009 it cost nearly 20 RMB, about 20x an NE5532. Soomal's RMAA plots of OP275 products show a spray of low-level harmonics that do not affect the score. Soomal links these to the warm sound but says it has no direct proof, and it notes that some OP275 cards sounded neutral. Other confirmed OEM uses: Denon DVD-A1 (with NE5532 and OP37) and DVD-2900, the Yamaha DME32, the Apogee Mini-DAC, the HiFiMAN HM-602 filter stage, and the TempoTec DAII Plus headphone stage (with TPA6120A). Japanese hobbyist rankings (nabe, Zigsow) reportedly praise its balanced, 'straight' sound, but this was not verified this run.
sonic_descriptors: tube-like, valve-amp style (胆味 / 胆机风格)
warmth without losing treble (Soomal, Monitor 01 US)
'straight' or balanced (Japanese reviews; unverified this run)
typical_uses: DAC post-filter and output stage in Chinese USB DACs and sound cards (Musiland Monitor and MD series)
headphone-amp gain stage in front of a current buffer (Musiland HP11 with LME49600; Monitor 01 PS and TempoTec DAII Plus with TPA6120)
analog stages of DVD-Audio/SACD players (Denon DVD-A1, DVD-2900)
pro-audio DSP and converters (Yamaha DME32, Apogee Mini-DAC)
DAP analog filter (HiFiMAN HM-602)
op-amp rolling in socketed sound cards and motherboards (Soomal tried it on the Gigabyte G1.Sniper A88X)
guitar pedals (a forum trace of MXR MC402 Rev E, via third-party notes)
caveats: Needs at least ±4.5 V (9 V total) supplies, so it does not suit low-voltage single-cell circuits.
Weak as a headphone driver on its own: Soomal says one OP275 cannot drive a 300 Ω HD580 with authority, so products pair it with buffers.
Measurements show a series of low-level harmonics (Soomal RMAA), so it is not a lowest-distortion choice by modern standards.
The sound depends on the implementation: Soomal found some OP275 cards neutral.
Expensive relative to NE5532/4580. Musiland used CLC2059 in the cheaper 01 Mini (2009) and MC33079 in 03 US and 03 PS (2011), but still used OP275G in the MD12 (2014).
'Warm/tube-like' is subjective community reputation; Soomal says it has no direct proof that the harmonics cause it.
Counterfeits are rumoured, but no specific report was confirmed.

families.counterfeit_notes: No concrete counterfeit report was found. A full-text search of all 29 Soomal posts that mention OP275 found no fake or remarked-part report; the only 'sanded chips' note concerned other ICs in the Apogee Mini-DAC. OP275 was sold in China as a premium upgrade op-amp (nearly 20 RMB each in 2009, about 20x an NE5532), which is the usual profile for remarked parts. Genuine parts are marked 'OP275G' on top (Soomal MD12 photo; EEVblog #738 reads '275G'). Buy OP275GPZ (DIP) or OP275GSZ (SOIC) from authorized distributors. A heuristic, not from a vendor: a relabelled NE5532/4558-class die would measure differently, so compare supply current (about 2 to 2.5 mA per amplifier), slew rate (22 V/µs) and GBW (9 MHz) against the datasheet. The GP to GPZ and GS to GSZ suffix change is the RoHS package transition; no evidence of a die change was found.

families.name: OPA111 / OPA2111 (Burr-Brown Difet low-noise precision, single/dual)
families.tagline: Burr-Brown low-noise Difet precision op-amp. TI's OPA627 datasheet measures itself against 'the popular OPA111', and Japanese hobbyists prize the metal-can OPA2111AM.
families.technology: Burr-Brown Difet (dielectrically isolated JFET-input) precision op-amp. TI product titles, as captured in a 2013 model index: OPA111 'Low Noise Precision Difet Operational Amplifier' and OPA2111 'Dual Low-Noise Difet Operational Amplifier'. Burr-Brown's own 1990 PSpice macromodels (OPA111 REV.A 10/12/90, OPA2111 REV.A 10/15/90) give the same values for both parts: GBW = 1/(2π·RD1·C2) ≈ 2.0 MHz, SR = ISS/C2 = 2 V/µs and Avol ≈ 1.78e6 (125 dB). A third-party aggregated SPICE library labels it 'JFET, Low Noise 8nV/RTHz'. Input bias current is in the low-pA range.

reputation.summary: A niche cult part among vintage-op-amp rollers, and a well-known pA-bias, low-noise instrumentation front end. Vendor context: TI's OPA627/637 datasheet benchmarks against 'the popular OPA111'. Japan: hobby blogs praise the metal-can OPA2111AM. One reported a swap from OPA827 that gave less bass emphasis, clearer vocals and a wider soundstage; others describe a warm, analog sound and a 'veil lifted'. A Zigsow reviewer found the plastic OPA2111KP harder-sounding and slightly more fatiguing than the OPA2134. China: in a 2016 HiFiMAN review, Soomal groups OPA111 with OPA627/OPA637 as BB Difet parts. It says OPA627/637 have much better treble resolution than the older OPA111/OPA2107, and that Difet op-amps in general sound warm, full and relaxed. That is a class generalisation, not an OPA111 listening test. On Head-Fi, a poster lists OPA2111KP among favourite duals (and wrongly calls it CMOS). No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurements were found.

families.counterfeit_notes: No documented counterfeit reports for OPA111/OPA2111 were found. The risk is structural: TI reportedly lists OPA2111 as in discontinuation, and supply is NOS or broker stock. A 2023 Italian broker record shows 50 OPA2111KP bought at €18 each and resold at €35. eBay listings market the KP as 'Audio Grade', and metal-can AM parts carry cult prices. These conditions invite remarked cheaper duals. Practical checks (general advice, not vendor guidance): (1) look for a Burr-Brown logo, a plausible pre-2000 or early TI-era date code, and marking that matches the grade and package (M = TO-99 metal can, P = plastic DIP); (2) measure input bias current. Genuine Difet parts are in the low-pA range per the model tables (0.5–3 pA typ), so a remarked bipolar op-amp (nA-level Ib) or a generic JFET part (tens of pA) is easy to spot; (3) GBW should be about 2 MHz and slew rate about 2 V/µs. An NE5532-class or TL07x-class remark would slew much faster.

families.name: OPA1622 (dual bipolar-input, high-output-current headphone-driver op-amp)
families.tagline: TI's 2015 dual bipolar headphone driver: 2.8 nV/rtHz, -119.2 dB THD+N at 100 mW into 32 ohms, +145/-130 mA drive. Widely used in Chinese DAPs and phones.
families.technology: Dual bipolar-input SoundPlus audio op-amp, with "Burr-Brown Audio" branding on the datasheet. It uses a single gain stage: a high-gain transconductance input stage feeding a unity-gain high-current output stage. It has a dedicated GND reference pin, to which the compensation capacitors and the enable logic are referenced, plus an EN/shutdown pin (5 uA per channel) and thermal shutdown at 175 C. It comes only in a VSON-10 (DRC) 3x3 mm package with a copper leadframe and an exposed pad that must be tied to V-.

reputation.summary: OPA1622 is a purpose-built headphone driver. It combines very low THD+N into 16-32 ohm loads, 2.8 nV/rtHz noise and high output current on 2.6 mA/ch, which suits battery gear. Teardown and review notes list it in FiiO (X7 AM3 module, X3 III, M9), Lotoo (PAW S1, Paw Gold Touch 4.4 mm output, PAW6000) and HiBy (R3 Pro II, R6 Pro Max) players, vivo Xplay6, Smartisan M1L, and Xiaomi MSM8996 phones, whose kernels carry a 'ti,opa1622' driver. DIYers built the AmpCasq integrated headamp around it (diyAudio / headphones.com). Some Japanese hobby blogs describe its sound as clear and fast, with tight bass. All community praise and device lists come from discovery notes and GitHub mirrors and were not re-verified by web search.
typical_uses: headphone output driver in DAPs, USB dongles and phones
DAC differential-to-single-ended converter plus headphone driver (TI reference design TIDUAW1, unconfirmed)
balanced (4.4 mm / 2.5 mm) headphone outputs, one device per leg
DIY integrated headamp (AmpCasq)
high-current line/buffer stage after a DAC low-pass filter
op-amp rolling on VSON-10-to-DIP-8 adapter boards (e.g. Audiophonics OPA1622 DIP8 unit)
caveats: Only available in VSON-10 3x3 mm with an exposed pad that must be soldered to V-, never ground. There is no DIP/SOIC version, so socket use needs an adapter.

Non-standard pinout with GND (pin 3) and EN (pin 8) pins, so it is not drop-in for standard dual op-amp footprints. A DIP-8 socket has no ground pin, so adapters must synthesize GND/EN. PSRR may suffer because the compensation capacitors are referenced to GND (inference from the datasheet).
EN must not float or sit on a high-Z GPIO, or the amp stays disabled. EN thresholds (0.78/0.82 V) are referenced to the GND pin. The output is NOT high-impedance in shutdown.
Output drive is limited to about +145/-130 mA. In TI's circuit that gives 150 mW into 32 ohm and 95 mW into 16 ohm before clipping, so one device per leg cannot deliver watt-class power.
Thermal: RthetaJA is 47.6 C/W and the part shuts down at 175 C, then cycles on and off while the fault persists. High rails driving low-ohm loads need copper under the pad.
Asymmetric supply ramp-up can cause audible pops. TI advises holding EN low while the rails ramp.
Minimum supply is +/-2 V.
Differential input clamp diodes (+/-0.5 V) can conduct in G=+1 circuits with fast inputs, so limit input current to 10 mA.

families.counterfeit_notes: No specific counterfeit or remarked-OPA1622 reports were found. Genuine parts are VSON-10 (DRC) with the top marking 'O1622', per the TI package addendum and alldatasheet marking page, plus the TI logo and a lot-trace code. The part ships on 250- or 3000-unit reels. The '.B' orderable suffix (OPA1622IDRCR.B) that appears in newer TI listings is a variant TI calls identical to OPA1622IDRCR, not a different die. In the hobby op-amp-rolling market it is usually pre-soldered on VSON-10-to-DIP-8 adapter boards (e.g. the iancanada adapter kit, Audiophonics 'OPA1622 Dual OPA DIP8'), where the chip cannot be inspected and GND/EN wiring varies. Buy bare parts from authorized distributors and inspect adapter boards for the O1622 marking. In 2021-era shortages OPA1622IDRCR was scarce enough that people wrote TI-store stock monitors (noxue/ticom), a typical setting for grey-market substitutes.

reputation.summary: TI's JFET-input SoundPlus family, pitched at OPA2134-class uses but with far lower datasheet distortion. Soomal describes a 'typical OPA1642 style': the whole sound is refined and balanced, with mild, delicate mids and relaxed bass. Paired with the OPA1662 (FiiO E17K) Soomal hears the 'BB' character: relaxed, grand, full dynamics, warm overall. Review sites list it as the DAC low-pass-filter or line buffer in many portable and desktop products (e.g. FiiO X3K/X3 II/X5 III/M11/E17K/K13 R2R, Lotoo PAW Gold, Astell&Kern AK380, HiBy RS6, Apogee Element 24/Groove, EarMen CH-Amp). In DIY it is the core of the 'OPA Alice' phantom-powered electret mic (Hackaday 2020), where its low quiescent current is the selling point. DIY DAC builders also pick it for its voltage-independent input capacitance. No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurement of the bare op-amp was checked.
sonic_descriptors: mild, fine mids (中频温和而细腻)
relaxed, grand, full dynamics, warm overall (松弛大气, 动态饱满, 偏暖; FiiO E17K with OPA1662)
typical_uses: DAC post-filter (LPF) and I/V stages in DAPs and USB DACs
line-out buffers
phantom-powered electret/condenser mic preamps (OPA Alice mic)
phono (RIAA) preamps
high-impedance piezo/guitar buffers
active filters, tone controls, mixing consoles (TI target applications)
caveats: Surface-mount only (SOIC, VSSOP, TSSOP). Op-amp rolling into DIP-8 sockets needs an adapter board (e.g. the Audiophonics OPA1642 DIP-8 adapter).
The common-mode input range stops 3.5 V below V+. Below ±3.5 V supplies it does not include midsupply, which limits low-voltage single-supply unity-gain buffers.

Not a headphone or 600 Ω driver. TI warns that 600 Ω at full supply can trip the current limit (ISC +36/-30 mA) and advises keeping output current under about 13 mA (2.8 kΩ minimum at 36 V single supply).
Capacitive-load overshoot: the datasheet recommends 24-51 Ω output isolation (Figs 19-20).
Offset is 1 mV typ / 3.5 mV max, higher than precision parts. DC-coupled outputs may need trimming or a servo.
VSSOP-8 θJA is 180 °C/W. A shorted output at ±18 V dissipates over 600 mW.
Soomal's sound descriptions are of whole devices, not the op-amp in isolation.

families.counterfeit_notes: This run's limited searches found no OPA164x-specific counterfeit reports. Two facts from the datasheet help screen parts. First, TI never offered the family in DIP, only SOIC-8 (D), VSSOP-8 (DGK), SOIC-14 and TSSOP-14, so any one-piece DIP-8 body marked OPA1642 is not a genuine TI package. Legitimate DIP-8 versions are SOIC parts on adapter boards, such as the one Audiophonics sells. Second, the genuine top markings per the 2026 TI addendum are O1641A, O1642A and O1644A on SOIC and TSSOP, and 1641 or 1642 on VSSOP, plus the TI logo and lot code. The realistic risk is remarked generic JFET duals sold on DIP adapters. Buy from authorized distributors.

reputation.summary: TI's own E2E FAQ presents the OPA1656 as the next-generation replacement for the OPA2134 and OPA2604 and calls it the lowest-voltage-noise high-voltage CMOS op-amp on the market (vendor claim). Hi-Fi and DIY users treat it as the modern, transparent, low-distortion FET-input Burr-Brown part. Community reports from the discovery sweep (not re-checked this run): in an ASR input-shorted phono noise test the roughly €5 OPA1656 matched the roughly €33 MUSES02; a Fosi ZA3 user said it 'basically wipes the floor' with Burson V7 Classic modules; Japanese listeners call it clean and balanced, with less colouration than the OPA2134; one SQ5J DAC test picked it for the I/V stage for a 'very modern' presentation; diyAudio and AMB threads discuss it as an OPA1612 substitute.
sonic_descriptors: low colouration and less harsh than OPA2134
OPA1655: high fidelity, smooth voices and instruments, slightly treble-leaning, good value (Japanese listening summary, low confidence)
typical_uses: DAC I/V and output/filter stages
headphone-amp gain and line stages (100 mA output; TI FAQ recommends it as a headphone driver)
high-gain microphone preamps (TI FAQ)
MM phono preamps (datasheet application 8.2.1; fA-level current noise suits high source impedance)
op-amp rolling on SOIC-to-DIP8 adapters (Fosi and similar)
measurement and ADC front-end buffers
active tone controls and guitar/XLR interfaces (datasheet examples)
caveats: Packages are SOIC-8 only for the OPA1656 (SOIC-8 and SOT-23-5 for the OPA1655). There is no DIP, so rolling needs third-party adapter boards of variable quality and unknown origin.

It is fast (53 MHz GBW, 20 MHz unity-gain bandwidth), so socket and adapter parasitics and poor decoupling can cause ringing or oscillation. The datasheet rates capacitive load drive at 100 pF and shows RISO of 25-50 Ω taming overshoot. The oscillation risk in sockets is an engineering inference, not a documented incident.
The marketed 2.9 nV/rtHz is measured at 10 kHz. The datasheet gives 4.3 nV/rtHz at 1 kHz and 11.8 nV/rtHz at 100 Hz (CMOS 1/f noise), so bipolar parts are quieter in low-impedance circuits.
Maximum supply is 36 V (±18 V; absolute max 40 V), so it is not a drop-in for OPA2604 circuits running ±20-24 V rails.
The input is not rail-to-rail: VCM tops out at (V+) - 2.25 V, which limits follower headroom on low rails.
Iq is 3.9 mA per channel typical (4.6 mA max), about 7.8 mA per dual package.

families.name: OPA2107 (Burr-Brown/TI precision Difet JFET-input dual)
families.tagline: Burr-Brown Difet JFET dual (about 4.5 MHz, 18 V/us) that op-amp rollers call warm and full. HiFiMAN paired it with the OPA627 in its HM-801 and HM-901 players.
families.technology: Dual JFET-input op-amp on Burr-Brown's Difet (dielectrically isolated FET) process. The Burr-Brown macromodel (Rev A, 10/17/90) uses a P-channel JFET input pair (.MODEL JX PJF). Its elements give a GBW of 4.5 MHz (GA/(2*pi*C2)), a slew rate of 18 V/us (ISS/C2), CMRR of 100 dB and an Aol of about 100 dB. It is the faster sibling of the OPA2111 Difet dual: the same 1996 EWB library gives the OPA2111 2 MHz and 2 V/us against 4-4.5 MHz and 18 V/us for the OPA2107.

part_numbers.status: unknown (discovery lenses say obsolete; not verified)
part_numbers.notes: 8-pin plastic DIP (Burr-Brown suffix P). Listed in the 1996 Electronics Workbench (EWB) Burr-Brown model libraries. c't Lab's AD16-8 parts list calls for 'OPA2107A DIL'. This is the version used for op-amp rolling.

Probably TO-99 metal can (inferred from Burr-Brown's M-suffix convention). Seen only in the 1996 EWB Burr-Brown model libraries.

Probably the TO-99 high grade. Both EWB files give it Aol 100,000 (vs 63,000) and about half the bias and offset current. BURR_BR1.LIB also gives Vos 50 uV (vs 100 uV) and CMRR 100 dB, but BUR_BRWN.M15 lists Vos 100 uV for the BM too.
TO-99, presumably the military-temperature (S) grade. Seen only in the 1996 EWB libraries.

lineage.notes: The Burr-Brown PSpice macromodel header reads 'CREATED USING PARTS RELEASE 4.03 ON 10/17/90', REV.A, so the part existed by October 1990. An enhanced OPA2107E model was 'REVISED 3/21/92 BCB' to add input bias-current correction and current and voltage noise. In KiCad BBOPA.LIB the plain model is named OPA2107B. The 1996 EWB libraries list the AM, AP, AU, BM and SM grades. The Burr-Brown PDS number and first-release date were not found.

The TI PSpice model is literature SBOM045. The werner2101/spicelib TI checksum list shows 'ti/pspice_models/opa2107/sbom045.zip', confirmed by direct fetch. HiFiMAN designed it into the HM-801 (2009), HM-602 (2010), HM-601LE (on sale in 2014) and HM-901 (2013). No second sources are known.

reputation.summary: A cult favourite from the Head-Fi op-amp-rolling era. Head-Fi and diyAudio threads, Japanese blogs and Zigsow reviews reportedly call it warm, full and 'tube-like', with a detailed midrange and non-fatiguing highs; those forum pages were not re-checked in this pass. Soomal (2016) groups it with the warm, full, spacious 'DiFET' sound (a group where Soomal also puts the OPA2134 and OPA2604) and says the OPA627/637 clearly beat the older OPA111 and OPA2107 on treble resolution. Soomal's 2013 HM-901 review admits its reviewers had not heard the OPA2107 in any other device. HiFiMAN used it in the HM-801 (with OPA627), HM-602 (headphone stage, with an OP275/OPA2604 LPF), HM-601LE (OP275, OPA2604, OPA2107) and HM-901 (OPA627 + OPA2107 in the LPF). c't Lab (Heise, 2007) specifies it, or an AD712, as the input amplifier of its AD16-8 ADC card, and calls it 'weit besser' (far better) than a TL072 for the 16-bit DA12-8 variant. Tangent's bench notes give only supply headroom and price for it, with no listening verdict. No independent measurements (ASR, Samuel Groner) were found.
typical_uses: DAC low-pass filter (HiFiMAN HM-901, with OPA627)
DAP analogue stage (HiFiMAN HM-801, with OPA627)
Portable headphone-amp stage (HiFiMAN HM-602 and HM-601LE)
Op-amp rolling in DACs and preamps (DIP-8 OPA2107AP)
Precision high-impedance instrumentation (c't Lab AD16-8 ADC input amp; recommended over TL072 in the 16-bit DA12-8)
caveats: Needs a fairly high supply: Tangent measured a 10.6 V minimum to meet his headphone-drive tests (OPA627: 6.8/9.8 V), so it is a poor choice for low-voltage battery CMoy builds.
Modest output current (about 40 mA limit per the models), so buffer it for low-impedance headphones.
It was expensive even when current ($12.25 per dual at Digi-Key in the Tangent notes). It is now largely secondary-market stock, and its obsolete status is unverified.
Most sonic praise is forum or blog impression. Soomal says it had not heard the part outside the HM-901, and its 'DiFET sound' grouping also covers non-Difet parts (OPA2134).
Counterfeit and remark risk on NOS or pulled parts (flagged by the discovery lenses, unverified).
Soomal's folklore that fab origin (Taiwan vs Southeast Asia) changes the sound refers to OPA627/637, not the OPA2107.

families.counterfeit_notes: No OPA2107-specific counterfeit report was found or verified. The discovery lenses flag a high risk of remarked fakes because supply is now NOS or pulled stock (low confidence). General checks: see whether the logo era (BB vs TI) matches the date code, and look at marking quality and package moulding. On the bench, a genuine part should show pA-level input bias current (JFET input), about 18 V/us slew and about 4.5 MHz GBW (model values). A remarked bipolar part will show nA-level or higher bias current. A remarked generic JFET dual will usually be noisier and may slew or settle differently.

families.name: OPA827 (single low-noise precision JFET-input)
families.tagline: TI's 2006 single JFET op-amp (4 nV/√Hz, 22 MHz) that DIYers treat as the modern OPA627: a DAC I/V favourite, called 'successor to the legendary stone' in a Japanese review.
families.technology: JFET-input precision voltage-feedback op-amp. Supply ±4 V to ±18 V (8 to 36 V total), abs max 40 V. Specified from -40 °C to +125 °C. Packages: SOIC-8 (D) and VSSOP/MSOP-8 (DGK). Input common-mode range and output swing are not rail-to-rail: both reach only to within 3 V of each rail. Only the single ever reached production. Early SBOS376 revisions (2006 to 2008) were titled 'OPA827, OPA2827' and announced a dual OPA2827 as Product Preview. That is why the datasheet says 'OPA827 series' and carried 'Mixed Status'. The 2013 orderables list has no OPA2827, and no evidence was found that it ever shipped. Before Rev G (Feb 2012) the datasheet also listed a high grade, OPA827I. reputation.summary: Hi-Fi DIYers treat it as the cheaper modern successor to the OPA627. They use it mostly as a DAC I/V converter and in socket-rolled line and headphone stages on SOIC-to-DIP adapters. In Xonar Essence ST/STX I/V discussions it is named with LT1361, LT1028 and OPA627 as the best I/V choices. Impressions conflict. English-forum posts gathered by an earlier sweep (not re-read) call it almost neutral, clean and more dynamic and less fickle than the OPA627. A diyAudio 'Best Sounding DUAL opamps' thread describes it as bass-centric, dark, warm and laid-back, with an impressive soundstage. In Japan two Zigsow reviews carry the titles 'The strongest lineage' and 'Successor to the legendary stone', the stone being the OPA627. TI's datasheet supports audio use (-128 dB THD+N at 3 Vrms/600 Ω; 'professional audio applications'). No ASR or Samuel Groner measurement was found.
sonic_descriptors: very clean, clear and fluid (lens note)
more dynamic and less fickle than OPA627 (lens note)
bass-centric; deep, dark, warm, laid-back (diyAudio dual-opamps thread)
more assertive low end than OPA2111 (one Japanese swap report)
typical_uses: DAC current-to-voltage (I/V) stage, e.g. socket rolling in Asus Xonar Essence ST/STX I/V positions
Portable DAC/headphone-amp op-amp swaps on DIP-8 adapters (e.g. a 2015 Fostex HP-A4 OPA827 swap blog)
Line-level buffers and preamps
Engineering (datasheet application list): 16- to 18-bit ADC drivers, DAC output buffers, transimpedance amps, filters, precision ±10 V front ends, professional audio
caveats: SMD only (SOIC-8 / VSSOP-8), so socket use needs a DIP-8 adapter. It is single channel, so a dual socket needs two parts on a 2-in-1 adapter.
Not rail-to-rail: input CM range and output swing reach only to within 3 V of each rail. On ±5 V rails usable swing is only about ±2 V.
4.8 mA typ (5.2 mA max) quiescent current per channel, and it needs at least ±4 V (8 V total).
22 MHz GBW on adapter boards: keep supply decoupling at the chip (general practice, not a documented failure report).
Listener impressions conflict (neutral/clean vs dark/warm/bass-centric). Several descriptors come from lens summaries, not first-hand re-reads.
DC precision: a PhD thesis (PatrickBaus) saw non-symmetric cubic INL with OPA827 as an ADC buffer, and a 2019 blog shows higher 1/f noise than the OPA227 near DC.
JFET bias current rises steeply with temperature (±5 nA max at 125 °C vs ±10 pA at 25 °C).
Costs much more than common audio duals.

families.counterfeit_notes: No OPA827-specific counterfeit or remarking report surfaced, but no search this run targeted counterfeits. Genuine TI markings per the SBOS376H package addendum (Oct 2013): SOIC-8 (D) reads 'OPA / 827 / A' plus logo and lot/date code; VSSOP-8 (DGK) reads 'NSP'. DGK lead finish may be NiPdAu or NiPdAuAg. TI has only ever listed the D and DGK packages, so a DIP-8 'OPA827' is not a genuine TI package. The OPA2827 dual never went beyond Product Preview, so any 'OPA2827' offered for sale is suspect. The part is often sold pre-soldered on adapters by marketplace sellers, and its benchmark OPA627 is among the most-faked audio op-amps. Buy from TI or authorised distributors, and check Iq (4.8 mA typ) and slew rate (at least 20 V/us).

families.name: OPA828 / OPA2828 (45 MHz, 150 V/us SiGe JFET-input, "next-generation OPA627/OPA827")
families.tagline: TI's 2018 fast JFET-input op-amp (4 nV/rtHz, 45 MHz, 150 V/us, -130 dB THD+N). DIY rollers put it on DIP adapters as a modern OPA627 and describe it as very neutral and spacious.
families.technology: JFET-input (BiFET). The datasheet says it is built on TI's "high-voltage, SiGe-complementary, JFET-bipolar process technology" (also called a "SiGe precision, high-speed, high-voltage, BiFET wafer process") and that "patented wafer processing techniques" reduce JFET gate-region noise. Offset voltage is laser-trimmed at two temperatures; offset drift and quiescent current are also trimmed. It has a proprietary slew-boost circuit that fires on large input differential voltage, plus an overload power limiter that turns slew-boost off after about 300 ns. There are no anti-parallel diodes across the inputs ('MUX-friendly'), so the differential input can reach the full supply, but the inputs are diode-clamped to the rails. It is specified at G=+1 (57 deg phase margin with CL=30 pF).

part_numbers.notes: SOIC-8 (D), tube of 75. Top marking 'OPA828'. D-package spec set. Pins 1, 5 and 8 are NC; there are no offset-null pins. Shown as Active in both the 17-Jun-2025 and 9-Nov-2025 package addenda of SBOS671D. The original 2018 package.
SOIC-8 (D), 2500-piece tape and reel. Marking 'OPA828'. Mouser P/N 595-OPA828IDR appears in the Mouser field of the stefaweb Q17-Mini-3.0 and Q17-TURBO-2.0 KiCad schematics.
SOIC-8 (D) tube, G4 orderable variant. Marking 'OPA828'. Active per the 2025 addenda.

HVSSOP-8 PowerPAD (DGN): 2500 on T&R (R) or 250 on T&R (T). Top marking '2RAJ'. Added as preview in Rev C (Oct 2022) and moved to production in Rev D (Dec 2022). Has its own, tighter DC spec set (Vos, drift, Ib) but a lower CMRR than the D package.

The dual exists only in HVSSOP-8 PowerPAD (DGN); SBOS671D lists no SOIC or DIP dual. Top marking '2QGJ'. Standard dual pinout (OUT A=1, V-=4, OUT B=7, V+=8). The pad is isolated (>10 Mohm) from the die; TI says to solder it and tie it to V- or GND. It has its own product folder (ti.com/product/OPA2828, linked from the datasheet). It first appears in Rev C (preview) and reached production in Rev D (Dec 2022). A Rev-B-era (2019) text copy of the datasheet lists the single only.

reputation.summary: Among DIY and op-amp-rolling hobbyists the OPA828 is treated as the modern high-speed successor to the OPA627, which matches TI's own 'next generation OPA627 and OPA827' positioning. Discovery searches found a diyAudio 'OPA828/OPA2828 vs OPA627' thread, threads on RIAA and OPA828+LME49600 builds, and Japanese 2026 roundups (maimai-audio) that describe it as an elegant, low-colour, spacious FET all-rounder. Those forum and blog sources were not re-verified in this pass. GitHub-verified uses: the open-source Q17 power amplifier replaced OPA1641 with OPA828 in U1 'for JFET lovers' and reports 0 mV output DC offset with OPA828 vs 1 mV with OPA1611. A Japanese DIY board (indare/pcb_work) keeps OPA828 on a two-singles DIP module and rates it easy to try as-is. A 2025 instrumentation project picked it over the OPA627/637 on price (about $7 vs about $30). On measurements, the datasheet gives -130 dB THD+N into 600 ohm and 10 kohm and 137 dB CCIF IMD. No independent Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner op-amp measurement was located.
typical_uses: DAC I/V conversion and post-filter / output stages
line buffers and preamps
RIAA phono preamps
headphone amps with a separate buffer (OPA828 + LME49600)
power-amplifier input/error-amp stage (Q17 amplifier)
op-amp rolling on SOIC-to-DIP adapter modules (two singles on a dual-DIP adapter, or OPA2828 on a PowerPAD-capable adapter)
caveats: No DIP package exists. The single comes in SOIC-8 or HVSSOP-8 and the dual only in HVSSOP-8 PowerPAD, so socketed use needs adapter boards, which add parasitics. TI says to solder the DGN exposed pad and tie it to V- or GND.

This is a fast part (45 MHz GBW, 150 V/us, 57 deg phase margin at CL=30 pF). TI says to isolate heavier capacitive loads with a small series resistor, for example 50 ohm. Layout, decoupling and adapter parasitics matter. The indare/pcb_work datasheet review puts it in its 'layout-sensitive' group, but well below LT1364, and rates it relatively well-behaved. The review reports no oscillation.

Slew-boost engages when the inputs are driven far apart. TI warns this 'can distort the signal' and advises keeping the inputs close together where low distortion is needed (relevant to clipping and overload, not normal linear closed-loop use).

Minimum supply is +/-4 V (8 V). Common-mode range is only (V-)+2.5 V to (V+)-3.5 V and the output needs 0.9 V typical (1.2 V max) of headroom from each rail, so it is unsuitable for 5 V or low-voltage portable gear.

It draws 5.5 mA per channel (about 165 mW/ch at +/-15 V). With the SOIC RthJA of 121.5 C/W that is roughly a 20 C self-rise. JFET bias current rises steeply with temperature (max +/-400 pA at 0-85C, +/-3 nA at 125C), which matters in very high-impedance stages. A two-single adapter draws about 11 mA.
Output current is +/-30 mA linear (50 mA short-circuit): fine for 600 ohm and above, but it is not a stand-alone low-impedance headphone driver.
The inputs have no anti-parallel protection diodes. Differential input up to the supply is allowed, but the inputs are diode-clamped to the rails, so limit input current to 10 mA.

silicon_changes.summary: This is a package extension, not a documented die change. TI added a thermally enhanced DGN package for the single and introduced the dual OPA2828 in DGN only. The DGN parts carry a separate, tighter DC spec set than the SOIC OPA828. TI does not state that a new die, process or fab is involved, and no PCN was found. The SOIC (D) part appears to keep its original 2018 specification: TI's Rev C log lists no D-limit change, the Rev-B-era features text shows the same D typicals (50 uV, 0.45 uV/C, 1 pA), and the Rev-B-based PSpice model uses 0.45 uV/C drift. Whether the DGN part uses revised silicon or only a different trim, test or package flow is unknown. AC specs (noise, GBW, slew rate, THD+N) are common to both packages.

spec_deltas.parameter: Input bias and offset current typ / max @25C
spec_deltas.after: DGN: +/-0.2 pA / +/-5 pA (front page says 0.1 pA)

silicon_changes.audio_impact: Negligible for audio. The deltas are DC precision (offset, drift, bias) and a few dB of CMRR; noise, GBW, slew rate and THD+N are specified identically. The DGN runs cooler because of the PowerPAD, which also keeps JFET bias current lower. The main practical impact is packaging: the dual needs a PowerPAD-capable adapter.
silicon_changes.compatibility_risk: low - the parts use different footprints, suffixes and markings, so they cannot be confused. The SOIC D variant is unchanged per the revision history. Only the OPA2828 is restricted to HVSSOP-8 with an exposed pad that should be soldered.

families.counterfeit_notes: No OPA828 or OPA2828 counterfeits were documented in the sources available; web search was unavailable in both the research and verification passes, so this is unconfirmed either way. Authenticity facts from TI's 2025 package addenda: (1) TI makes no DIP-8 version of either part, so any 'OPA828' or 'OPA2828' DIP must be an adapter board; a DIP-8 IC body laser-marked OPA828/OPA2828 is not a TI package. (2) The OPA2828 exists only in HVSSOP-8 (DGN) with top marking '2QGJ', so an SOIC-8 or DIP body marked 'OPA2828' is suspect. (3) A genuine SOIC OPA828 is marked 'OPA828' and a DGN OPA828 '2RAJ', each with possible logo and lot-trace marks. The OPA627, which it replaces in rolling circles, is heavily counterfeited. The OPA828 is much cheaper (a 2025 project note puts it at about $7 vs about $30 for OPA627/637), which lowers the incentive to fake it, but adapter modules are usually bought from marketplaces. Inspect the chip marking on any adapter and, where possible, check slew rate (~150 V/us) and pA-level bias current.

families.name: OPA211 / OPA2211 (1.1 nV/√Hz bipolar precision, single / dual)
families.tagline: TI's 1.1 nV/√Hz, 45 MHz (G = 1) bipolar precision op-amp. Head-Fi rollers found the OPA2211A more open than the LM4562, and Shanling product copy lists it in DAC low-pass stages.
families.technology: Bipolar-input precision voltage-feedback op-amp. It is unity-gain stable, has a rail-to-rail output and back-to-back differential input protection diodes, and its EMI rejection (EMIRR) is characterized. It runs on 4.5–36 V. On the single OPA211, pin 8 is Shutdown (active high) in the VSSOP (DGK) and SON (DRG) packages and NC in SOIC-8 (D). The dual comes only in SMD packages: SO-8 PowerPAD (DDA) and 3×3 mm SON (DRG). TI does not name the fab process.

reputation.summary: A well-regarded modern bipolar part for rolling and for DAC output stages. The evidence is forum and blog impressions (read through search summaries), not published measurements. Head-Fi rollers preferred the OPA211 to most other parts, including the LM/LME chips. One Head-Fi post found the OPA2211A 'more open, yet not harsh' in the highs than the LM4562, with a 'natural roundness and warmth'. One listener found female vocals a bit 'creamy'. Japanese reviewers call the OPA2211 versatile, with resolution and power in balance and a wider sense of space. They find it clearer than the OPA2134 and drier than the OPA627. A zigsow review says it suits some genres better than others. On the SQ5J DAC blog, an OPA1656 I/V stage followed by an OPA2211 differential stage gave a 'very modern' sound. Third-party retail copy of Shanling products (mirrored on GitHub) lists the OPA2211 in the M6 Pro 21 LPF. The same copy places it in the EM7 LPF and in an OPA2211+BD139/BD140 amplifier stage. No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurement could be checked, because web search was unavailable.
typical_uses: DAC differential / summing and low-pass filter stages
DAC post-filter in Shanling products (M6 Pro 21 LPF; EM7 LPF and amp stage, per third-party retail copy)
headphone-amp and DAC op-amp rolling via SOIC/PowerPAD-to-DIP adapters
low-impedance, low-noise gain stages: sources below ~2 kΩ per TI, ADC drivers, and SR560-style LNAs as a unity-gain-stable stand-in for the OP37/LT1028
caveats: SMD only. The dual comes in SO-8 PowerPAD (DDA) or SON-8, so a DIP socket needs an adapter. The datasheet says the exposed pad 'must be connected to V–' (not ground), and soldering it improves heat dissipation and gives specified performance. On the single SON it is 'required'. Check how the adapter connects the pad.

On the VSSOP and SON singles, pin 8 is Shutdown (active high). The datasheet says it 'must be connected to a valid high or low voltage or driven, and not left open-circuit'. Rev L shows pin 8 as NC on the SOIC-8 single, so a SOIC single on a standard adapter is safe.
The back-to-back differential input diodes can conduct on fast, large steps at G = 1. Input current must then be limited to 10 mA, and the series resistor that does this adds noise.

Current noise is 1.7 pA/√Hz. TI (SBOS377L §8.1.3) positions the OPAx211 for source impedances below 2 kΩ. It suggests the OPA227 for 10–100 kΩ and a FET part such as the OPA132 above 100 kΩ. The OPA828 datasheet (Fig. 7-7) makes the same comparison against the OPA828.

It is a wideband part (45 MHz at G = 1), and the datasheet gives an overshoot-vs-capacitive-load curve, so layout and decoupling on adapters matter. Community reports of oscillation were not checked (web search unavailable).
Listening impressions depend on genre and circuit (zigsow; Head-Fi notes that op-amp 'sound' is circuit-specific).

families.counterfeit_notes: No counterfeit reports were checked, because web search was unavailable, so this is not a clean bill. Vendor facts that help spot odd parts (rev L and the 9-Nov-2025 addendum): no DIP package is listed. The OPA2211A comes only as SO-8 PowerPAD (DDA, top marking 'OPA 2211 A', NiPdAu, MSL1) or 3×3 mm SON (marking 'OBHQ'). The SOIC single is marked 'OPA 211' (high grade) or 'OPA 211 A'. In VSSOP ('OBCQ') and SON ('OBDQ') both grades share one marking, so the grade cannot be read from the part. Any 'OPA2211' in a DIP-8 body is an adapter module or a remarked part. A DDA body with no exposed pad on its underside would also be suspect (inference from the package definition). Buy from authorized distributors, and on adapter modules check that the pad is soldered to V− (the datasheet says it 'must be connected to V–').

reputation.summary: Tangent (tangentsoft) made the OPA2227 the default op-amp for his PIMETA/CMoy headphone-amp guides. He described it as sounding very like the OPA132/OPA134, minus the bass bloom, and called it a good upgrade path. He found the decompensated OPA228 more resolving and 'lively' than the OPA132, but it oscillated in his low-gain CMoy, so he preferred the OPA227. On Head-Fi the OPA2227 divides opinion: some call it 'horribly dull and laid back', while the OPA2228 is 'waaaay better' and 'pleasant sounding', beating the AD8066 when gain is 5 or more or the part is compensated. Japanese C-Area wiki rates the OPA2228 as flat, high-resolution, smooth and realistic, more accurate than the OPA2134 or OPA2604. It describes the OPA2227 as OPA2134-like but leaning to the low end (Zigsow: 'bass stands out'). No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurements were located in this run.
sonic_descriptors: neutral, OPA132/OPA134-like without bass bloom (Tangent, OPA227)
flat, high resolution, smooth continuity, realistic (C-Area wiki, OPA2228)
more lively and resolving than OPA132 (Tangent, OPA228)
typical_uses: CMoy / PIMETA headphone amplifiers (DIP-8 OPA2227PA / OPA2228PA)
DAC output / line stages and preamps with low source impedance (datasheet: best below ~20 kohm source)
Op-amp rolling in socketed DIP-8 audio gear
Professional audio equipment (named in datasheet applications)
Low-noise reference / supply buffering in DIY DACs, e.g. OPA2227 buffering a 2.5 V reference in a diyAudio DAC project
caveats: OPA228/OPA2228 is decompensated (G>=5). It can oscillate in unity- or low-gain sockets or with capacitive load. The datasheet recommends a feedback capacitor CF for G=+2/-2, which raises output noise.
Back-to-back input clamp diodes: large fast input steps in a follower can drive destructive current. The datasheet limits input current to 20 mA, and 'subtle damage' can shift offset and noise.
Not rail-to-rail. Output needs about 2 V headroom (3.5 V into 600 ohm) and Isc is about 45 mA, so it is marginal from a 9 V battery into low-impedance headphones without a buffer.
Input bias current is cancelled internally; TI says a bias-balancing resistor raises offset and noise and is not recommended.
Iq about 3.7 mA per amplifier, which matters for battery life.
A-grade vs non-A grade differs only in DC precision, which is irrelevant for audio (Tangent).

families.counterfeit_notes: No counterfeit reports specific to OPA227 or OPA228 were found, but search coverage in this run was limited. Genuine TI marking per the 2014 package addendum: DIP parts read 'OPA2227P', with an extra 'A' line for PA grade; SOIC parts read 'OPA' over '2227U' or '2227UA', and the same pattern applies to 227/228/2228. General advice, not specific to this family: Burr-Brown audio op-amps are widely remarked in grey-market channels, so buy from authorised distributors. Suspect parts can be caught by slew rate (about 2.3 V/us for OPA227 vs about 10 V/us for OPA228; a mismatch means the wrong die), noise (3 nV/rtHz) and Iq (about 3.7 mA per amp).

reputation.summary: The AD712 was a mainstream 'better' audio dual in the late 1980s and 1990s. The rec.audio FAQ (v1.5, June 1993) lists it among the better op amps for audio, next to NE5532, LM833, AD827 and OPA2604. ADI marketed it as an 'enhanced replacement for LF412 and TL082', so DIYers used it as a drop-in upgrade for TL072/TL082 sockets in CD players, DACs and preamps. Its strengths are 0.0003% THD, 120 dB crosstalk, 20 V/µs slew and pA bias, which suit high-impedance line stages and filters. It is now a tier-C legacy part, eclipsed by lower-noise JFET parts. No modern measurements (Audio Science Review, Samuel Groner) were found this session, and no verified sonic descriptors were collected.
typical_uses: Drop-in TL072/TL082/LF412 upgrade in CD-player and DAC output/filter stages
High-impedance line buffers and active filters (the data sheet includes second-order and 9-pole Chebyshev filter examples)
DAC/ADC buffers and I/V stages that need fast settling (the data sheet shows AD565A/AD7545 settling examples)
Photodiode and electrometer preamps (pA bias, with guarding)
caveats: Voltage noise of 18 nV/√Hz at 1 kHz is high next to bipolar parts (NE5532, OP27) and modern JFETs (OPA1642, OPA827). It is a poor choice for low-impedance or MM-phono inputs.
Output phase reversal if either input goes more negative than about -14.1 V at ±15 V supplies. The CM range reaches only -11.5 V, so avoid large negative input swings (data sheet footnote).
Needs at least ±4.5 V supplies and is not rail-to-rail, so it does not suit low-voltage portable or USB-powered gear.
Output is about 25 mA. It is not a headphone driver.
Loads above about 1500 pF need a 100 Ω isolation resistor (data sheet Figure 46).
JFET bias current doubles every 10 °C. Hot chassis raise bias and offset errors in DC-coupled designs.
Pinout is the standard dual (AD712) / single (AD711); check the single-channel pinout before rolling.

families.counterfeit_notes: No documented counterfeit AD711/712/713 parts were found. The discovery hint that 'AD711-class dies are found in remarked fake OPA627s' is only partly supported. The widely cited ZeptoBars decap (2014, also covered by Hackaday) found an AD744 die under an OPA627 marking. The AD711 attribution comes from forum summaries and is unconfirmed (low confidence). Electrical clues: an AD711-class die would slew about 20 V/µs, far below the OPA627's roughly 55 V/µs. Its supply current would also be well below the ~7 mA per channel that the OPA627 counterfeit checks use; AD712 Rev. I gives 5.0 mA typ for two amplifiers. Data sheets before Rev. D (9/2001) carried a metallization photograph, which is useful for comparing decapped dies. Buy AD712 from authorised distributors. Genuine current production uses Z (RoHS) suffixes for PDIP/SOIC.

reputation.summary: More of an instrumentation legend than a mainstream op-amp-rolling part. It combines 2.9 nV/rtHz white voltage noise with only about 6.9 fA/rtHz current noise, so it stays quiet with both low and very high source impedances. That makes it a reference choice for hydrophone, piezo and charge-amplifier front ends and for low-noise measurement. For example, Rubiola picked the AD743 over the OPA627 for AM-noise detector amplifiers because of its lower voltage noise. In audio it has a niche following in MM phono/RIAA stages and high-impedance mic or piezo preamps, where the cartridge's inductive impedance makes current noise matter. Community sound descriptors and ASR-style measurements could not be retrieved in this run because the web search budget was already used up.
typical_uses: MM phono / RIAA preamp input stage (niche following; per discovery notes, not web-verified)
Hydrophone and piezo-film charge amplifiers (e.g. AD745 charge amplifier for PVDF film in a Taiwanese thesis)
Low-noise measurement front ends (AM/phase-noise detector amplifiers, Rubiola arXiv:physics/0512082)
Cryogenic bolometer readout / precision bias circuits (AD743 in arXiv physics/9902042 circuit)
High-impedance sensor and accelerometer preamps
caveats: Single op amp only: not a drop-in for the dual (5532/TL072-style) DIP-8 sockets used in most op-amp rolling. Two parts per stereo pair plus an adapter are needed.
The surface-mount part is a 16-lead wide SOIC (R-16), not SOIC-8, so an adapter or custom footprint is needed.

AD745 is decompensated (dominant pole 4.8x higher than AD743 in ADI's models) and must run at a noise gain of about 5 or more (exact minimum gain to verify in the datasheet). It is not a unity-gain buffer.

Large JFET input capacitance (20 pF in the model). With high-value feedback resistors this adds a feedback pole and raises noise gain at high frequency (e_n x C), so a feedback capacitor may be needed.
About 8 mA quiescent current per amplifier, high for a JFET op amp, so it runs warm in DIP.
Minimum supply is about +/-4.8 V (9.6 V total); not a 5 V single-supply part.
Low-volume, relatively expensive ADI part; which grades/packages remain in production was not verified.

families.counterfeit_notes: No fakes sold as AD744 were found. The concern runs the other way: genuine AD744 dies have been remarked as OPA627. In the ZeptoBars 2014 teardown (Habr post 218571, also covered by Hackaday on 2014-04-10), a DIP 'OPA627' bought on eBay for $2.70 including shipping held an ADI die marked 'AD' and 'B744'. It matched the die photo in ADI's AD744 datasheet. It had only 1 laser-trimmed resistor, against at least 4 on a genuine OPA627 die (a metal-can OPA627 bought for $5 was the reference). The AD744's compensation pad was not bonded out. ZeptoBars thought the counterfeiter bought AD744 bare dies and packaged them as OPA627. How to spot an AD744-based fake: (1) about 3x higher noise and higher offset (0.5 mV vs 0.1 mV) than a genuine OPA627; (2) lower supply current. My inference is that the AD744 draws about 3.5 mA against 7-7.5 mA for the OPA627, a figure used in Head-Fi/diyAudio OPA627 guides; this is not verified. (3) A decap shows the 'AD'/'B744' marks. When buying a genuine AD744/AD746, use authorized distribution. No marketplace remarking of these parts was documented.

reputation.summary: A niche cult part from the mid-2000s op-amp-rolling era. Head-Fi users call it punchy and intimate, with a rich timbre and thick texture that suits female vocals and strings. Some rate 2x AD825 on an adapter above other options ('AD825 is the best and nothing will change it'). Others hear it as flat or unemotional in some DACs, and as more coloured and a bit closed-in than the AD797. The LME49990 was reported as smoother with a firmer low end than the AD825. LC Audio Technology sold AD825 upgrade parts. Audio Asylum and diyAudio threads name it, for its FET input and high open-loop bandwidth, as a better replacement for the AD712 that John Curl called the weak link of the Parasound HCA-2200 MK-I. No objective audio measurements (ASR, Samuel Groner) were found. All sonic claims are forum folklore.

flat / unemotional in some DACs (dissenting view)
coloured and a bit closed-in compared with the AD797 (dissenting view)

typical_uses: Op-amp rolling in DAC and CD-player analog stages, on SOIC-to-DIP adapters (two AD825s per dual socket)
Drop-in upgrade for AD711/AD712-class JFET op amps, e.g. the Parasound HCA-2200 MK-I input stage (forum discussion)
Headphone amplifiers (Tangentsoft / Head-Fi)
LC Audio Technology upgrade kits
caveats: Single-channel and surface-mount only (SOIC-8 / SOIC-16). Replacing a DIP dual needs an adapter carrying two chips.
It is a 41 MHz part, so adapter wiring and local decoupling matter. This is general high-speed practice: no AD825-specific oscillation reports were found in the sources available.
It needs more supply headroom to swing 2 V into 330 ohm (8.6 V minimum in the Tangentsoft test) than parts such as the AD823 (6.1 V), though it drives 33 ohm well (4.7 V).
The praise is subjective forum opinion. No published THD+N or noise measurements of AD825 samples were found.

reputation.summary: This is a niche op-amp for rolling in CD players, not a mainstream audio legend. In the Audio Asylum 'tweaks' forum and on diyAudio, users who swapped it into CD-player output and I/V stages called the sound 'much cleaner, more open, and more detailed'. They also reported more precise instrument placement than the AD827, and in one Audio Asylum comparison it was 'almost as good' as the OPA637. Its appeal is video-class speed (50 MHz, 350 V/µs) combined with unconditional stability into capacitive loads. No independent measurements (Audio Science Review, Samuel Groner) were found. A 2005 translation of Tangent's op-amp notes (DiyEden/Soomal) put the AD826 on its list to test, but no review followed.
typical_uses: CD-player analog output stage op-amp swap
DAC current-to-voltage (I/V) converter
Video and line drivers (the designed use)
Buffers driving cables or capacitive loads
caveats: The evidence is thin: a few forum posts from the discovery notes, which this pass did not re-read. There are no published measurements.

This is a 50 MHz video part. Tight decoupling and short leads are sensible when socket-rolling, although ADI rates it stable into any capacitive load. This is engineering inference, not a reported failure.
Input bias current is high (3.3 µA typ, 6.6 µA max), which can cause DC offset with large feedback or source resistances.
Voltage noise is moderate at about 15 nV/√Hz, well above NE5532- or AD797-class parts.
It draws about 6.8–7.5 mA per amplifier (about 14–15 mA per package), so it runs warmer and drains batteries faster than audio duals.
The Tangent/DiyEden headphone-amp notes argued that ultra-high-speed op-amps are generally a poor fit for simple headphone amps.

reputation.summary: A niche cult part with split opinion. DiyEden published a Chinese translation of an English headphone-amp op-amp study on Soomal (2005). It quotes an article called 'The best op-amp I've heard' naming the AD843 the only op-amp that can rival the OPA627. The author found it smoother than the OPA627, trading some resolution for smoothness, with 'boldness, charm, vitality and passion'. A pair cost about half as much as a pair of OPA627s. The same study rates the AD845 as less detailed and says to upgrade to the AD843, and rates the AD8610 as having more detail and smoothness than the AD843. Head-Fi opinion (via an earlier search summary) is largely negative: 'harsh and unpleasant', 'no competition for OPA637', 'stay away from this - bad offset, oscillation, etc.', 'a nasty chip'. One user found 2x AD843JN on an adapter 'really good' but warm, because of the high quiescent current. It also appears in Maverick TubeMagic D1 op-amp rolling lists. No objective measurements (Audio Science Review, Samuel Groner) were found.
sonic_descriptors: bold / energetic ('气魄、神韵、活力和热情')
typical_uses: headphone amplifier op-amp rolling (CMoy-style, single-channel sockets)
DAC output stage rolling, used in pairs on dual adapters
replacement for OPA627 in single sockets
caveats: High quiescent current: about 10.7 mA typical in ADI's model. It runs warm and is poor for battery amps.
Needs a high supply voltage: measured minimums of 8.2 V and 12.2 V. The sound degrades quickly as the supply voltage drops.
Head-Fi reports of bad offset and oscillation. It is a 34 MHz part, so it is sensitive to layout and decoupling.
Single only: dual-socket use needs two chips on an adapter.
The surface-mount version appears to be a 16-lead SOIC ('-16' suffix), not a standard SO-8. This is inferred and unverified.

Measure quiescent current (about 10-12 mA expected from ADI's model); a much lower Iq points to a substituted die such as a TL071-class part. Also check the offset against the grade limits: 2 mV for J, 1 mV for K.

reputation.summary: A niche ADI JFET single with thin enthusiast coverage. The only located source is a Chinese translation (DiyEden, published on Soomal 2005) of an English headphone-amp op-amp survey. That single reviewer calls the AD845 'a very interesting chip': smooth, with less detail than the AD843, and a slightly valve-like feel (有点电子管的感觉) while keeping ADI's punch. The reviewer recommends it for mains-powered systems and smooth-sound lovers, or as a cheaper stand-in before moving to the AD843. Discovery notes also claim a cult following for DAC I/V and line stages. This has not been verified and should not be treated as established.

families.name: AD847 / AD827 (single / dual high-speed bipolar video op amp)
families.tagline: ADI's 50 MHz, 300 V/us video op amp. In the 1990s it became a favourite CD-player and DAC upgrade, praised for fast, dynamic sound with strong bass.
families.technology: A bipolar, voltage-feedback, high-speed op amp (50 MHz unity-gain bandwidth, 300 V/us). It is internally compensated to be stable at unity gain and is rated to drive unlimited capacitive load. ADI's SPICE macro-model uses an NPN differential input pair. According to ADI's electronics textbook, the AD848 (stable at G>=5) and AD849 (stable at G>=25) are basically the same design with different internal compensation. The AD827 is the dual version of the AD847. The fab process name (complementary bipolar or otherwise) was not verified this run.
