reputation.summary: A niche-cult op amp for 1990s-era swaps. The AD847/AD827 were ADI video amplifiers that audiophiles fitted into CD-player output stages, DAC I/V and filter stages and headphone amps. The rec.audio FAQ listed the AD847/AD827 among 'the better op amps for audio'. Chinese reviewers (Soomal) group the AD847 with the AD797 as famous for big dynamics, a 'grand' sound and powerful bass. Western and Japanese listeners describe the AD827 as warm and slightly sweet, with a sharp attack, forward vocals and clean highs; some find it a little coarse or thin in the bass. It is still named as a rolling option: Fosi Audio lists the AD827 as compatible with the ZA3. No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurements were found this run.
sonic_descriptors: a bit too sweet (AD827, Audio Asylum)
huge dynamics / grand sound (Soomal: 动态大，声音大气)
ADI 'both ends lifted' tonal tilt (两头翘, Soomal)
vocals forward, clean highs, slightly coarse (Japanese reviews)
fast, clean square-wave response without overshoot
typical_uses: CD-player analog output stage upgrades
DAC I/V conversion and output filter stages
headphone amplifiers and preamps
op-amp rolling in consumer gear (e.g. Fosi ZA3)
original design use: video and line drivers, cable driving (unlimited capacitive load)
caveats: Bipolar input with microamp-level bias current (about 3 uA per the ATE-25 table): DC offset rises with high-impedance or unmatched source resistances. Check DC-coupled stages.
A 50 MHz part in sockets or adapters needs tight supply decoupling and short leads. This is general high-speed practice, not a documented AD827-specific failure.
Needs at least about 9 V total supply and draws about 5 mA per amp, more than audio parts such as the NE5532-class alternatives.
The AD827 SOIC appears to be a 16-lead package (AD827JRZ-16), so only the DIP-8 version is a drop-in for standard dual sockets.
Some listeners find it too sweet, or light and loose in the bass. One Japanese headphone-amp test reported reduced gain below about 200 Hz and a 'sparse' impression (anecdotal).

reputation.summary: This is a niche, engineer-oriented part rather than a roller's legend. ADI markets it for low-power, low-noise audio. ADI app note AN-1429 recommends it for the I-to-V stage of current-output audio DACs, in both the 'High Performance' and 'Quality performance by low power consumption' columns. Commercial use is documented in the Matrix Audio Mini-i Pro 2S: LME49720 for I/V, ADA4075-2 for the low-pass filter, and ADA4075-2 driving a TPA6120A2 headphone stage. Soomal's review groups it with the LME49720 as a 'very high-end, low-distortion op amp'. The project discovery note calls it a low-power drop-in upgrade for the NE5532, but that was not independently verified. No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurements, and no Head-Fi or diyAudio listening impressions, were retrieved this run.

caveats: Minimum specified supply is 9 V total, so it is unsuitable for single 5 V or +/-2.5 V rails (AN-1429).
Output is not rail-to-rail: about 2 V headroom to each rail limits swing on low supplies (AN-1429).
It has bipolar input current noise. A Japanese measurement-ADC designer dropped it for the FET-input OPA1656 because the 3.3k/4.7k resistor network would make current noise significant.
It is SMD-only (SOIC-8/LFCSP-8), so socket rolling needs a DIP adapter.
Check the maximum supply before using an NE5532 socket at +/-18 V. The SPICE header lists '9/30V', but the datasheet maximum was not verified.

reputation.summary: This is a niche-cult part in DIY DAC circles. On diyAudio it is a favourite for current-to-voltage (I/V) conversion after current-output DACs, and it is recommended in 'best dual I/V op amp these days' threads. Measurement-minded builders like its very low voltage noise, its bandwidth, and headroom up to ±16 V. It is also a common choice for instrumentation LNAs and photodetectors, including Gerhard Hoffmann's 'lono' parallel-op-amp LNA. A Japanese/English audio review site names the ADA4898-1 as the cheap 0.9 nV/√Hz equivalent of the LT1115. The praise quotes come from the discovery notes and were not re-checked this run.
sonic_descriptors: deep, tight and impactful bass (diyAudio, I/V use)
typical_uses: I/V converter after current-output audio DACs
DAC output buffer / reconstruction filter
Low-noise preamp / LNA front ends (parallel arrays, as in Hoffmann 'lono' and aewallin ADA4898_LNA)
Photodiode transimpedance and servo loops (TU Darmstadt APQ photodetector/PDH/MTS modules)
caveats: Comes only in SOIC-8 with an exposed pad (RD-8-2). There is no DIP version, so op-amp rolling needs an adapter board, and the exposed pad must be connected as the datasheet says (rail not verified here).
Draws about 8 mA per amplifier, so a dual dissipates about 0.48 W at ±15 V. It runs warm on DIP adapters that have no copper under the pad.
Needs at least ±5 V, so it does not suit low-voltage portable designs.

Current noise is fairly high (2.4 pA/√Hz). The noise-optimal source impedance is about 375 Ω (0.9 nV divided by 2.4 pA), so it works best with low-impedance sources such as I/V stages and low-R feedback networks.

General high-speed caution (engineering inference, not a specific report): with 65 MHz of bandwidth, layout, decoupling and capacitive loading matter. Socket or adapter wiring can cause peaking or oscillation.

reputation.summary: Historically important more than currently praised. The LF156/LF356 was National's first BI-FET op amp (1975) and the first monolithic JFET-input op amp. Walt Jung's 1978 Electronic Design survey groups the 355/356/357 as 'second-generation FET' op amps with clearly better drift and offset than general-purpose parts, and notes the OP-15/16/17 were 'patterned after' them. National's own 1978 Electronics article stresses its low noise (12 nV/√Hz), fast settling and stability with capacitive loads up to 10,000 pF. In current Hi-Fi/DIY communities evidence of praise is thin. Tangent's headphone op-amp notes (read here in a 2005 Chinese translation) call the LF355 a 'Walkman' op amp with specs very like the TL071 and unsuitable for low-impedance headphones: it needed 14.9 V to put 0.5 V into 33 Ω. It survives in vintage synth VCO/VCF designs, sample-and-hold and I/V circuits, and lab front ends. No modern distortion measurements (ASR, Groner) were found this run.
typical_uses: DAC current-to-voltage converters and fast D/A or A/D buffers (fast settling)
High-impedance buffers, photodiode and electrometer front ends
Integrators, sample-and-hold, log amplifiers
Active filters and vintage analog synth VCO/VCF circuits
1970s–80s 'Jung-era' audio/line stages as a low-noise FET single
caveats: If an input goes past the negative common-mode limit (−12 V typ, only −10 V guaranteed for LF35x at ±15 V) the output is forced high, so the phase reverses. An input taken below V− can destroy the part (datasheet Application Hints).
Fitting it backwards in a socket, or reversing the supply, can fuse internal conductors (datasheet warning). This matters when op-amp rolling.

Supply current is high for a FET single: 5 mA typ, 10 mA max for the LF356. Self-heating raises input bias current, which doubles every 10 °C; the datasheet recommends a heat sink when minimum IB matters.
The LF357/LF157/LF257 is decompensated and stable only at AV≥5. It will oscillate as a follower or unity-gain stage, so it is not a drop-in for an LF356 socket.
Offset trim uses a 25 kΩ pot with the wiper to V+, not V−; pins 1 and 5 are BALANCE. Some third-party summaries get this wrong.
Poor at driving low impedances: Tangent found it unsuitable for low-impedance headphones.
It is a single (DIP-8 single pinout), so rolling it into dual-op-amp sockets needs adapters.
The earliest LF156 (1975 New Products page) labelled pin 8 'current source reference' and required pin 8 to be tied to pin 7 when offset adjust was unused. Later datasheets show pin 8 as NC.
Specs are guaranteed at ±15 V for LF35x. There is no low-voltage specification.

revision_history.changes: First announcement: metal-can LF156 only. Pin 8 was a 'current source reference' that had to be tied to pin 7 (V+) when offset adjust was unused. Typical slew rate 15 V/µs and settling 1.4 µs.

Full LF155/6/7 series with A and B grades and LF255/6/7 industrial parts, in H, J (ceramic DIP) and N packages. DIP pin 8 is NC. Slew rate 12 V/µs typ (7.5 min for LF156/256/356B). Capacitive loads 10,000 pF. Schematic note 'C = 2 pF on LF157'.

Reduced to LF155/LF156/LF355/LF356/LF357. Dropped the A grades, LF355B/LF357B, LF255/256/257 and the J package. Added SOIC LF356M/LF356MX. LF357N no longer offered. The feature list now says 5,000 pF, and the schematic note becomes '3 pF in LF357 series'. Package power ratings changed; the N package is now 670 mW / 130 °C/W, versus 500 mW / 155 °C/W in 1980. DC and AC limits are unchanged from 1980 for the non-A grades.
Re-added LF256 and LF257 (TO-99, −25 to +85 °C) to the title, tables and order list. Electrical limits unchanged.
Known only from the Rev D history ('Revision B (March 2013)'). Content not seen.
'Changed layout of National Data Sheet to TI format.' No electrical changes are listed.

Added the Pin Configuration and Functions section, ESD ratings (±1000 V HBM), Thermal Information table, Feature Description, Device Functional Modes, Application and Implementation, Power Supply Recommendations, Layout, Device and Documentation Support, and Mechanical/Packaging/Orderable sections. Removed the THIGH parameter as redundant. No electrical-limit changes. The package addendum dated 8-Jan-2026 lists only the LF156 (H, /NOPB, MD8 die), LF256H(/NOPB) and LF356M/MX/N /NOPB as Active.

families.counterfeit_notes: This run found no documented counterfeit reports; web search was unavailable, so forums were not checked. The following are generic screening heuristics, not reported cases. Remarked LF351/TL081-class parts are the obvious risk. A genuine LF356 draws about 5 mA typ (10 max) at ±15 V; an LF351 draws about 1.8 mA (National JFET macromodel header). A genuine LF356 has a GBW of about 5 MHz, and offset nulls with a 25 kΩ pot on pins 1/5 with the wiper to V+. Current genuine TI marking is 'LF 356N' (PDIP) or 'LF356 M' (SOIC), per the SNOSBH0D addendum. Treat marketplace 'NS LF357H' metal cans and 'National' parts with post-2012 date codes as suspect. A metal-can LF357 that is stable as a unity-gain follower is also suspect, because the real part is decompensated and needs AV≥5.

reputation.summary: A fast 1970s bipolar op-amp (15 MHz, 50-70 V/us). In the late-1970s slew-induced-distortion/TIM debate (Walter Jung and co-authors, Audio magazine) high-slew parts such as the LM318 were favoured for audio. Today it is a niche/cult part in DIY circles, used for fast buffers and DAC I/V stages. Community evidence is thin. It is not a low-noise audio design and has no published noise spec in any source seen. Some hobby write-ups wrongly call it a 'dedicated audio op-amp'. Audio-DIY SPICE modellers (s-audio.systems) keep separate National, TI and LTC LM318 models, a sign of interest in vendor-to-vendor differences.
typical_uses: DAC output buffer / I-V stage (DIY)
fast line buffers
active video filters and composite-video receivers
function generators / oscillators
fast D/A output amplifiers, pulse amplifiers
class-D amplifier control loop (academic paper)
caveats: High-speed part: needs 0.1 uF bypass capacitors right at pins 4 and 7. It is prone to oscillation with stray capacitance on the inverting input and with long socket/adaptor leads.
Pins 1/5/8 are compensation/balance pins. Circuits that use feed-forward caps on these pins are not drop-in with parts where pin 8 is NC or pins 1/5 are offset null (and vice versa).
Feed-forward compensation (>150 V/us) only applies to inverting configurations.
Quiescent current about 5 mA typ (10 mA max) per amp.
Needs at least ±5 V supplies. A hobby simulation needed >5.3 V to operate.
No noise specification. Not a low-noise part compared with NE5534/LME49710-class devices.
Several different dies are sold under one name (National vs TI-legacy vs LTC), so behaviour may differ by maker.

families.counterfeit_notes: No specific LM318 counterfeit reports were found (web search was unavailable). General precaution for cheap marketplace DIP-8 LM318N parts: remarked slower op-amps are common in this segment. A quick check is a unity-gain square-wave test at ±15 V: a genuine part should slew at least 50 V/us and have about 15 MHz small-signal bandwidth, while a remarked 741/4558-class part slews under 1-2 V/us. This is generic advice, not a documented LM318 case.

families.name: LME49880 (National / TI Overture E-Series dual JFET-input audio op-amp)
families.tagline: National's late Overture E-Series JFET dual (7 nV/√Hz, 0.00003% THD+N). It came only in PSOP, is now obsolete, and Japanese op-amp rollers run it on DIP adapters.
families.technology: Dual JFET-input audio op-amp from National's LME 'Overture E-Series' (siblings: LME49720, LME49860, LME49990). The datasheet says the JFET process was used to lower flicker noise and the noise corner frequency. Supply range is ±5 V to ±17 V. It is unity-gain stable, drives capacitive loads up to 100 pF, and has typical input bias of 5 pA. The only package is an 8-lead PSOP with an exposed pad (MR suffix; TI's package addendum calls it 'SO PowerPAD').

part_numbers.notes: Generic dual. No single, quad or vendor DIP version has been seen. TI discontinued it as part of a process-technology end-of-life and names OPA1642 as the replacement (TI E2E thread 565578, about 2016-2017).

Lead-free orderable in the 8-lead PSOP with exposed pad. A 2014 package-option addendum listed it as ACTIVE ('SO PowerPAD', 8 pins); it is now OBSOLETE (TrustedParts, TI E2E). Whether a tape-and-reel MRX/NOPB version existed is unconfirmed.

reputation.summary: Linear Technology's dedicated ultralow-noise audio op amp. It is a long-standing enthusiast favourite for low-source-impedance stages: MC/MM phono (RIAA) preamps, MC head amps and microphone preamps. The 1990s rec.audio FAQ put it among the 'highly recommended' singles and said the LT1028 and LT1115 'are very well received for phono preamps, head amplifiers, and microphone preamplifiers'. diyAudio members call it 'very interesting sounding' and group it with the LT1028 and LT1122 as the LT parts worth trying. Japanese hobbyists call it the most monitor-like LT part, with exceptional resolution; it appears in Japanese phono-EQ builds and on Zigsow alongside the AD797, THS4631 and LME49990 as a famous single. A srad.jp commenter noted its datasheet noise equals the AD797's at about half the Mouser price. It is still used in new DIY designs, e.g. an LT1115 + LT1010 MC/MM phono preamp (2021-2025). No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurement was located this run.
typical_uses: MC/MM phono RIAA equaliser / preamp
moving-coil head amp
microphone preamplifier
low-noise line / measurement preamp with low source impedance
single-op-amp socket rolling in DIY gear
caveats: Single only (no dual or quad), so dual sockets need an adapter.
The only corroborated SMD version is a 16-lead wide SOIC (SW16) with a non-standard single pinout; no SO-8 was found.
Expensive: about 20 USD per Frieve, versus about 2.7 USD for the ADA4898-1 with similar noise.
Bipolar input with noise optimised for low source impedance, so it offers little benefit with high-impedance sources.

The high-GBW (tens of MHz) part can oscillate in careless layouts or sockets. The rec.audio FAQ claimed the LT1115 is 'not unity gain stable'. This is unverified: the LTC macromodel describes it as internally compensated. Check the datasheet for the minimum stable gain before using it as a follower.

families.counterfeit_notes: No documented counterfeit analysis was found, but web search was unavailable this run. Marketplace spam pages advertise 'free shipping 50pcs LT1115CN8' lots. Cheap bulk lots of a part that sells for about $20 each through ADI channels (per Frieve) are a strong red flag for remarked parts or pulls. Buy from ADI or authorised distributors. reputation.summary: A niche, cult-level pick with no mainstream following. Head-Fi op-amp rollers name the LT1122 as a candidate alongside the LT1361, LT1364 and LT1469 in threads on DAC output stages; one thread also prefers the LME49720 over the LM4562. diyAudio members group it with the LT1028 and LT1115 as the Linear Technology chips worth trying, and call the LT1122ACN8 'a good chip'. Tangent's widely translated op-amp listening notes (Chinese translation on Soomal, 2005) list the LT1122 among chips he had on hand to test later, but give no verdict. No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurements were found; web search was unavailable in this pass. Outside audio, a KiCad reproduction of the HP 3458A 8.5-digit DMM A3 analog board uses an LT1122 as unity-gain buffer U404.
sonic_descriptors: 'a good chip' (diyAudio, general praise; no specific sonic descriptors were verified)
typical_uses: DAC output and reconstruction-filter stages (Head-Fi recommendations)
Single op-amp rolling in DIP-8 sockets (LT1122ACN8 / CCN8)
Fast-settling buffers for DACs and data conversion (the design intent in its datasheet title)
Precision instrument buffers: HP 3458A A3 board, U404 unity-gain buffer (KiCad reproduction)
caveats: Single channel only: dual-op-amp sockets need an adapter carrying two of them.
Relatively high quiescent current, about 7-7.8 mA per amplifier (distributor and datasheet-derived data), so it runs warmer and drains batteries faster than TL07x-class parts.
A fast JFET part (about 14 MHz GBW). Stability in any given socket or layout was not verified; treat it like other fast op-amps (decoupling, short leads).
Grades A-D probably differ in DC or settling guarantees (not verified). For audio the grade is unlikely to matter, but the A grade costs more.
Its noise density and distortion specs were not verified in this pass, so do not assume it is a low-noise audio part.

families.tagline: Lower-bias, 2 mA/amp sibling of the LT1364, rated 25 MHz and 600 V/µs. A niche sound-card buffer pick that listeners call warm, bright and tonally rich.
families.technology: Bipolar, built on Linear Technology's complementary bipolar process. It uses the single-stage topology of the LT1354–LT1365 family: matched high-impedance voltage-feedback inputs with current-feedback-like slewing. It is sold as a C-Load part, stable with any capacitive load. Linear's LT1364 datasheet calls the LT1358/LT1359 the 'Lower Power Version of LT1364/LT1365' at 2 mA per amplifier.
manufacturers: Analog Devices (acquired Linear Technology in 2017; current vendor)

N8 = DIP-8, S8 = SO-8, C = commercial temperature grade, #PBF = lead-free. LT1357CS8#TRPBF also appears in a Mouser-derived dataset. The ADI lifecycle status was not checked.

It belongs to LTC's C-Load high-speed family (LT1354 to LT1365), is unity-gain stable and is meant to drive capacitive loads. With an LME49720 elsewhere in the chain, users describe the LT1361 as giving an 'extremely clear and airy sound'. Xonar discussions rank it among the best I/V op amps, alongside the LT1028, OPA627 and OPA827. Head-Fi posts list it with the LT1122, LT1364 and LT1469 as alternatives to the LME49720. Users call it forgiving of poor bypassing and tolerant of a wide supply range, so it can stand in for most bipolar duals. No bench measurements were found (Audio Science Review, Samuel Groner or similar). All praise is subjective forum opinion.

A 50MHz, 800V/us part: needs a tight layout and short decoupling. Socket adapters add parasitics, although the C-Load design tolerates capacitive loading.
Supply current is about 4 mA per amplifier. Distributor output-current data (34 mA) points to limited ability to drive low-impedance headphones directly.
Descriptors come from a small number of subjective posts; no measurements were found.

reputation.summary: A niche but well-regarded MUSES model in the Japanese DIY and portable-audio community. It is the MUSES pick when a low-voltage or battery supply rules out the higher-voltage parts. A Zigsow user review ('低電圧で使えて優しい音質', 'usable at low voltage, gentle sound') finds it gentler than the OPA2134 while keeping MUSES-like transparency. A Stereo magazine blog article groups it with MUSES8820 and MUSES8920 as the mass-production MUSES models. No English-language objective measurements (ASR, Groner) were found.
sonic_descriptors: gentle / soft (優しい音質), per a Zigsow review
typical_uses: battery-powered portable headphone amplifiers
portable audio devices and smartphones (vendor-stated targets; leadless KW1 aimed at mobile)
high-end audio equipment (vendor-stated)
low-voltage single-supply (+2.7 V and up) audio stages
Audio-Technica AT-PHA100 portable DAC/amp, reportedly (only from an AI-generated review repo; low confidence)
caveats: There is no vendor DIP8 version. DIP8 'units' (for example Audiophonics) are SOP8 dies on adapter boards, and adapters add their own layout and stability risk.
It is a low-voltage part. The listed operating range tops out at about 13 V total, and the maximum is about 15 V per parametric data. Do not roll it into +/-15 V equipment.
Almost all praise comes from Japanese subjective reviews. No independent measurement data was located.

reputation.summary: Too new (October 2025) for a settled enthusiast consensus. Most of the praise is the vendor's own claim, repeated by Japanese and international trade press: MUSES flagship sound-tuning methods were applied to MUSES8920/A by reviewing the signal and power paths and optimising element placement. Japanese DIY blogger new_western_elec compared it with NL8902 (Oct 2025) and published a listening post, 'MUSES8921を試聴しました' (Apr 2026). Per a search summary of that post, he treats MUSES8920 -> 8920A -> 8921 as step-wise version upgrades of the JFET MUSES line, and hears 8920A as slightly shallower and narrower in space than 8920 but wider in bandwidth. His specific MUSES8921 verdict was not captured. No ASR, Groner or other independent measurements were found. The headline typical specs equal MUSES8920A's, so any improvement is a sound/layout claim, not a spec gain.
sonic_descriptors: Vendor marketing only: 'true sound that resonates with the heart' (心に響く"真実の音") (Macnica/Nisshinbo launch headline)
Vendor claim: better sound than MUSES8920/A through signal/power-path review and element-placement optimisation
new_western_elec (per search summary, Apr 2026): part of a step-wise 8920 -> 8920A -> 8921 evolution; detailed MUSES8921 descriptors not captured
Predecessor MUSES8920, NOT MUSES8921 (JP community folklore, not re-verified): clean and dry, high resolution, no harshness
typical_uses: DAC I/V converter (5 pA input bias; the vendor says it is ideal for this)
Preamplifier / line amplifier
Active filters
Headphone amplifiers, including portable (vendor target market)
PC, desktop and portable audio (vendor target market)
Op-amp rolling via the Kyoritsu MUSES8921AN-DIP conversion module
caveats: Different part number from MUSES8920/MUSES8920A; do not treat it as the same die.
Headline typical specs (8.0 nV/rtHz, 0.0004%, 25 V/us, 11 MHz, 5 pA, ±3.5 to ±17 V) match MUSES8920A's; measured benefits are unproven.
No independent measurements or ASR/Groner data found.
Retail 'DIP' units seen in Japan are the SMD MUSES8921AN on an adapter board (Kyoritsu MUSES8921AN-DIP), not a native DIP8, so check the height and fit in sockets.
Costs more at retail than MUSES8920AE (about ¥1,700 vs ¥1,200 in Japanese listings; the MUSES8921 price probably includes the adapter).

Long-term supply of the MUSES line is uncertain. new_western_elec reported (2024-06 factory visit) that MUSES05 and MUSES03 were dropped, and he voiced concern after Nisshinbo HD news in Dec 2025 (earlier pass, not re-verified).

families.counterfeit_notes: No counterfeit reports specific to MUSES8921 were found; the part has only been on sale since October 2025. General Japanese community advice (earlier pass, not re-verified) is that MUSES01/02 fakes are common on Chinese marketplaces; genuine parts are laser-marked and fakes are often ink-printed. Buy from authorised channels such as Akizuki, Kyoritsu Eleshop/Digit, Mouser and DigiKey. Be sceptical of any bare 'MUSES8921D' or native-DIP8 MUSES8921: only the EMP8 MUSES8921AN is confirmed, and retail DIP units seen are Kyoritsu adapter modules (MUSES8921AN-DIP). Relabelled MUSES8920/8920A or generic JFET duals are a plausible but unverified risk. There is no same-number silicon change: MUSES8921 is a separate part number and a vendor-described derivative of MUSES8920/A.

Japanese retailers market it as a Hi-Fi op-amp (Akizuki: '2回路入HiFiオペアンプ'), and one auction seller calls it 'MUSESの量産型'. The only listening report is the guiblo blog comparison (2023). caveats: Evidence is thin: one subjective, unblinded blog comparison and a YouTube shoot-out that was not checked. No measurements were found.

NJM8901E is SMD (EMP8 = SOP8 150 mil), so DIP8 sockets need an adapter.
Typical offset is 2 mV and the maximum is 10 mV. That is high for DC-coupled stages, so use coupling capacitors or a DC servo where needed.
Supply is ±4 V minimum, so the part is not suited to low-voltage single-cell rails.
Lifecycle is uncertain: one distributor (Profusion) flags NJM8901E-TE2 as obsolete.

The blogger new_western_elec compared it with MUSES8820 in September 2025 ('MUSES8820とNL8802、MUSES8920とNL8902を聴く'). A ranking of OPA2604 < MUSES8820 < MUSES8920 < NL8802 < NL8902 appears in the Japanese comparisons found, but it is unclear whether it comes from nw-electric or from ns-kobo's NS phonoEQ 2 op-amp comparison. reputation.summary: A new part with little coverage outside Japan. Most of the praise comes from new_western_elec (nw-electric.way-nifty.com), a Japanese DIY-audio blogger. In a Sept 2025 A/B session he ranked OPA2604 < MUSES8820 < MUSES8920 < NL8802 < NL8902, and he heard more high-frequency extension and more detail than MUSES8920. His Oct 2025 post compares NL8902 with the new MUSES8921. reputation.summary: Evidence is thin and mostly historical. Bob Neidorff's rec.audio Audio FAQ (part 2, v1.5, last modified 1993-06-04) lists OP249 among its 'highly recommended' audio duals, alongside OPA2604, AD797, LT1115 and HA5112. The FAQ also says FET op amps such as OPA2604 suit line-level, high-source-impedance signals. Today Fosi Audio's ZA3 marketing lists OP249 among compatible DIP-8 duals for op-amp rolling. Synth DIYers (the SOWA 6-input CV/audio mixer) picked it for 'low offset and good dynamic parameters'. Bordodynov's LTspice collection files it under 'AudioOpamp/AD'. No measurement-based audio reviews (Audio Science Review, Samuel Groner) and no community sound descriptors were found in this run.
typical_uses: Line-level audio stages and buffers (FET-input use case described in the 1993 rec.audio FAQ)
Op-amp rolling in DIP-8 sockets (for example the Fosi Audio ZA3)
DC-coupled CV/audio mixers in synth DIY (SOWA mixer)
caveats: The rec.audio FAQ warns that faster op amps swapped into existing gear may oscillate, depending on design and layout. This is a general warning, not specific to OP249.
No datasheet noise, supply-current or output-drive figures were verified in this run, so check the ADI datasheet before using it for headphone drive or low-noise duty.
Reputation rests on a 1990s FAQ plus vendor marketing lists; there is no modern measured evidence of audio superiority.

reputation.summary: An OEM and engineering favourite rather than an op-amp-rolling legend. It comes only in SMD packages, so enthusiasts rarely swap it. It pairs low noise and distortion with modest supply current (2.6 mA/ch). Per a TI E2E thread and Gearspace discussion (not re-checked this run), TI pointed LME49720 users to it after that part's EOL. Reported design wins come from mirrored reviews (Soomal, Frieve) and maker pages: the iBasso DX90 uses a pair of OPA1602 per channel as the DAC I/V stage (with OPA1611 and BUF634), and the Cayin RU3 dongle uses OPA1602 alongside SGM8262 in parallel drive. DIY projects use it as a transformerless balanced line driver, and the quad OPA1604 shows up in multichannel mixers. No op-amp-specific listening tests or ASR/Samuel Groner measurements were found.

Multichannel line mixers and filter banks (OPA1604)
caveats: SMD only (SOIC/MSOP/TSSOP). A DIP-8 socket needs an adapter board.
About ±30 mA output drive suits line level, not low-impedance headphones on its own. The designs above add BUF634s or parallel sections.
Current noise of about 1.8 pA/√Hz (TI figure) makes noise rise with high source impedances, a general bipolar-input trade-off.
No op-amp-specific stability or oscillation reports were found.

families.name: OPA1652 / OPA1654 (TI SoundPlus dual/quad FET-input audio op-amp)
families.tagline: Cheap SMD-only TI FET-input dual/quad (4.5 nV/√Hz, 0.00005% THD+N, rail-to-rail out), used as an OPA2134-class workhorse for I/V and LPF stages in portable DAPs.
families.technology: FET-input, per TI's datasheet and product page. Low-noise folded-cascode input stage, class-AB rail-to-rail output, phase-reversal protection, back-to-back diodes across the inputs, copper leadframe. TI does not say in the datasheet whether the input is JFET or CMOS. A TI E2E engineer groups it with OPA2134 as a 'JFET' audio amp, and the discovery notes call it CMOS. Unity-gain stable. Supply ±2.25 V to ±18 V (4.5 V to 36 V).

reputation.summary: A tier-C 'workhorse' rather than a cult part. Makers treat it as the inexpensive surface-mount successor to OPA2134: FET input, rail-to-rail output, very low THD, 2 mA per channel. A TI E2E engineer says the two have very similar specs and swap in SO-8, but OPA1652 drives much less capacitance (about 230 pF vs 1 nF at G=−1) and has no PDIP. A Japanese zigsow review is titled 'OPA2134の後継 – OPA1652AID' (per an earlier search summary). Head-Fi 'Opamp thread' posters, as summarised by search, call it very good for a JFET-type part and under $2. One poster called it the best-sounding OPA16x2, with a forward, full-bodied presentation that is less detailed than LME49720. Another heard it as close to OPA1656, with the OPA1656 more neutral. A TI designer is quoted there as a fan of its noise performance for the price. Its real footprint is OEM portable audio. Soomal teardowns show it doing I/V and/or LPF in the FiiO X5K, VentureCraft SoundDroid Vantam and Cayin N5 MKII. It also appears in HiBy R6 PRO II / R6 III, HiBy R4 and Cayin BTC-2. The OPA1654 quad appears in Eurorack/synth designs. No independent bench measurements (ASR, Groner) were found. Most enthusiasts now point to the OPA1656 as the higher-performance OPA165x.
sonic_descriptors: Forward, 'spectator-like' soundstage with adequate body and thickness; detailed, but less so than LME49720 (single Head-Fi poster, per search summary)
Similar to OPA1656; OPA1656 a bit more linear (Head-Fi poster, per search summary)
Described as an improved OPA2134 successor (zigsow JP review, per earlier search summary)
typical_uses: DAC current-to-voltage (I/V) conversion in portable players (FiiO X5K, Cayin N5 MKII, VentureCraft Vantam)
Post-DAC low-pass filter and line-out stages
Headphone amp front end/driver ahead of discrete transistor output stages (HiBy R6 PRO II / R6 III)
SO-8 replacement for OPA2134 where the capacitive load is small
Unity-gain buffers with high-impedance sources (FET input, low current noise)
Mixers, effects, musical instruments, Eurorack (OPA1654 quad), guitar pedal output buffers
Op-amp rolling via SOIC-to-DIP adapter modules
caveats: SMD only (SOIC-8, VSSOP-8, WSON-8; quad in SOIC-14/TSSOP-14); no PDIP. Rolling needs a DIP adapter, and adapter/socket parasitics add capacitance.

Weak capacitive-load drive: 100 pF per the datasheet, and about 230 pF max at G=−1 per a TI E2E engineer, versus 1 nF for OPA2134. It is not a blind drop-in where the old circuit relied on OPA2134's cap-load tolerance. Use a series resistor of about 50 Ω.
Output drive is ±30 mA (ISC ±50 mA): not a stand-alone low-impedance headphone driver. OEMs add discrete or buffer stages.
Input common-mode range ends 2 V below V+, so it is not rail-to-rail input. Output swings to within 800 mV of each rail at 2 kΩ.
The sound impressions above come from individual forum posts and are subjective.
Noisier (4.5 vs 2.9 nV/√Hz) and slower (18 MHz and 10 V/µs vs 53 MHz and 24 V/µs) than the later OPA1656.

families.counterfeit_notes: No OPA1652/OPA1654-specific counterfeit reports were found. Counterfeits of sibling TI audio parts are documented: an 'OPA1612' that was a TL082 die (TI E2E, diyAudio) and suspected fake OPA1656 from AliExpress. Hobbyists mostly buy OPA1652 as DIP-adapter modules (AliExpress; Kyoritsu Q5M411 'OPA1652AID-DIP'), where the chip's origin cannot be verified. How to check: (1) TI never made a PDIP OPA1652, which a TI E2E engineer confirms, so a DIP-bodied 'OPA1652' chip is fake. (2) Genuine top marks per TI's 2026 addendum are 'OP1652' (SOIC-8 D and WSON DRG), 'OUPI' (VSSOP-8 DGK) and 'OPA1654' (SOIC-14/TSSOP-14), plus the TI logo and a lot code. (3) Iq should be about 2 mA per channel; input bias should be in the pA range (±100 pA max), and a bias current in the nA range points to a bipolar remark; GBW should be about 18 MHz. (4) Buy from authorised distributors.
alternatives: OPA1656 (dual) / OPA1655 (single): TI's next-generation OPA165x (SBOS901); 2.9 nV/√Hz @10 kHz, 53 MHz, 24 V/µs, 100 mA output. Closest upgrade on the same SOIC-8 pinout.
OPA1642 / OPA1641 / OPA1644: TI JFET-input SoundPlus parts, 5.1 nV/√Hz, THD+N 0.00005%. TI lists them with OPA2134 and OPA1652 as its FET-input audio duals.
OPA1678 / OPA1679: lower-cost TI CMOS audio dual/quad, 4.5 nV/√Hz. Discussed on modwiggler as an alternative to the OPA1654.
OPA1688: 36 V, 10 MHz, high-drive RRO audio op-amp.
OPA2134 (and OPA134/OPA4134): the legacy Burr-Brown FET audio op-amp OPA1652 often replaces; still available in DIP and better with capacitive loads (about 1 nF at G=−1).
OPA1612 / OPA1602 / OPA1662: bipolar alternatives when source impedance is low (lower e_n, higher i_n).

Specs confirmed by the search summary: THD+N 0.00005% at 1 kHz; supply ±2.25 V to ±18 V (4.5–36 V); 2 mA per channel; output swing within 800 mV at 2 kΩ; ±30 mA output drive; 10 pA input bias; 10 V/µs slew rate (https://www.ti.com/product/OPA1652, https://datasheetspdf.com/pdf/1405490/etcTI/OPA1652/1).

A TI E2E engineer says OPA2134 and OPA1652 have very similar specs and swap in SO-8, that OPA1652 has no PDIP, and that it drives at most about 230 pF at G=−1 vs 1 nF for OPA2134 (https://e2e.ti.com/support/amplifiers-group/amplifiers/f/amplifiers-forum/600965/opa1652-replacing-opa2134-with-opa1652).
Mouser lists OPA1652AIDGKR, OPA1652AID and OPA1654AIPW as distributed parts (https://www.mouser.com/ProductDetail/Texas-Instruments/OPA1652AIDGKR?qs=3jfYfyvUSwBBvQAEBFbpyQ%3D%3D).
Head-Fi posters praise its sound for the price and compare it to OPA1656 and LME49720 (https://www.head-fi.org/threads/the-opamp-thread.432749/page-313, per search summary).

reputation.summary: It is not a socket-rolling legend because it is SMD-only. It is well regarded as an inexpensive, rugged all-rounder. A diyAudio member called it 'a very good all-round opamp at a reasonable price, like a 21st century version of the NE5532', with modest 8 nV/√Hz noise. Builders value its 36 V operation, rail-to-rail high-drive output and short-circuit protection, which let it drive headphones directly. One GitHub modder reports it as the final stage of the Topping NX4 DSD, and built an adapter to swap in the INA1620. Other reported uses include DIY headphone amps (HiFiVision build, diyAudio OPA1688/OPA1622 thread), DJ-mixer cue outputs, DAC reconstruction filters and retro-computer audio boards. Forum threads (TI E2E, AudioKarma, Head-Fi) suggest it as an SMD substitute for the discontinued OPA2604AP. TI's own 'next-generation OPA2134/OPA2604 replacement' FAQ is about the OPA1656. No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurements were found.
typical_uses: Headphone driver / output stage (Topping NX4 DSD final stage per one modder; HiFiVision DIY headphone amp; DJ mixer cue output)
Line-level buffers, line-level converters and headphone pre-amps (synth DIY)
DAC output / reconstruction filter (FPGA sigma-delta DAC project)
SMD substitute for OPA2604 / OPA2134 in new designs
Retro-computer and sound-card audio outputs (ZX-Evolution rev D+, Mac NuBus PAS16 daughterboard)
caveats: Voltage noise (8 nV/√Hz) is modest next to OPA1656 (2.9 nV/√Hz), OPA1612 or OPA1602. It is not ideal for low-level sources such as phono or microphone inputs.
SMD only: OPA1688 in SOIC-8 or WSON-8, OPA1689 in SOIC-14 or VQFN-16. There is no DIP version, so socket rolling needs an adapter (WSON is hard to adapt).

Output power into low-impedance headphones is limited. One design note found OPA1688 current insufficient for a 250 mW / 18 Ω target (AarnimM22/HD800-wireless), and Topping NX4 owners swapped in the INA1620 for more drive.
Little independent measurement coverage, so the praise rests mostly on specs and value.

families.name: THS4631 (single high-voltage, high-slew-rate, wideband JFET-input op amp)
families.tagline: A ±15 V JFET-input op amp with 210 MHz GBW and 1000 V/µs slew, used as a cult DAC I/V and buffer part in Japan: airy and transparent once it is stable.
families.technology: JFET-input high-speed voltage-feedback op amp from TI (the datasheet calls the input stage JFET). Unity-gain stable: 325 MHz at G=1 and 210 MHz GBW. Single channel. Runs on ±5 to ±15 V (10–30 V single supply). SMD only: SOIC-8 (D), HSOIC-8 PowerPAD (DDA; 'SOIC-PP' in Rev B) and HVSSOP-8 PowerPAD (DGN; 'MSOP-PP' in Rev B). Standard single-op-amp pinout: 2 = IN−, 3 = IN+, 4 = V−, 6 = OUT, 7 = V+, and 1/5/8 are NC. The TI documents disagree about the thermal pad. Rev B, and the layout section of Rev C, say the PowerPAD is 'electrically isolated from all pins and the active circuitry', recommend tying it to ground, and allow any potential from VS− to VS+. The new Pin Functions table in Rev C says the pad is 'internally connected to V−' and must be soldered to V−.

reputation.summary: A niche cult part in the Japanese DIY and op-amp-rolling scene. It is mostly used as the I/V stage after a current-output DAC, and in headphone amps and buffers via DIP-8 conversion boards. One Ameblo blog titles it 'the rumoured op-amp' (噂のオペアンプ). Shirokuma sells it pre-mounted on a dual 8-pin DIP conversion board, and the maimai-audio blog bought one from Bispa. Users report that when it is not oscillating it gives extended highs, air, transparency and expressiveness. A Zigsow review is titled 'tsundere honours-student character' (ツンデレ優等生キャラ): superb when tamed, difficult otherwise. A cocolog blog compares it with LF357H and OPA627SM, and a Zigsow OPA627AP review lists it with AD797, LT1115 and LME49990 as famous singles. TI's datasheet lists 'Current DAC output buffer' among its applications. No Audio Science Review, Samuel Groner or other audio-band measurements are known to this record.
sonic_descriptors: 'tsundere honours student' (ツンデレ優等生): excellent once stable
typical_uses: I/V conversion after current-output DACs
DIP-8 op-amp rolling via conversion boards (e.g. Shirokuma dual board) in DACs
Headphone amp op-amp swap (e.g. Elekit TU-HP01, per the xgender-isao blog)
High-impedance wideband buffer / line driver
caveats: Oscillates easily in rolling and adapter use; Japanese users report needing an output Zobel network. TI's own datasheet warns that large feedback resistors (e.g. 5 kΩ/5 kΩ inverting) oscillate with the input capacitance and recommends a feedback capacitor, which matters for I/V stages. A non-audio GitHub hardware project (ZS-1100A) also replaced the THS4631 with OPA180/OPA197 'for better stability'.

Runs hot: 12.5 mA typ and 14.5 mA max quiescent per channel in Rev C (11.5 typ / 13 max in Rev B). That is about 0.375 W idle at ±15 V, and a dual adapter carries two chips. Japanese users advise heat management at ±12 V and above.

The thermal pad connection is ambiguous. Rev B says the PowerPAD is electrically isolated, recommends ground and allows VS− to VS+. Rev C's pin table says it is internally connected to V− and must be soldered to V−, yet Rev C's layout section still says isolated/ground. Tying the pad to V− is permitted by both revisions; grounding it is unsafe if Rev C's pin table is right.
SMD only (SOIC/HSOIC/HVSSOP), so socket use needs an adapter. It is a single, so it replaces a dual only on a dual-conversion board.
Noise is specified only above 10 kHz (7 nV/√Hz). The 1 kHz figure, in the JFET 1/f region, is not tabulated, and there is no audio-band THD+N spec.

Parts made after the March 2025 datasheet (Rev C) may be different silicon, with higher Iq, higher output current and re-specified flatness with CF. The listening impressions (c. 2018–2020) predate this.

revision_history.changes: Initial release.

Changed the Related FET Input Amplifier Products table. Differential and common-mode input impedance changed from 10^9 || 6.5 to 10^9 || 3.9 (Ω || pF). Figs 8 and 9 labels corrected from 'RL = 499 Ω' to 'RF = 499 Ω'. Added Figs 23 and 24 (large-signal transient response) and Fig 50, the EVM schematic (Figure 8-17 in Rev C).
Absolute Maximum Ratings: Tstg corrected from '65°C to 150°C' to '–65°C to 150°C'. No electrical changes were listed; the Rev B copy's tables match the Rev A-era values used in TI's 2011 model.

Listed changes: new TI format (numbering, Device Information and Pin Functions tables, separate ESD Ratings table). Related Products OPA656 values updated (7 to 6 nV/√Hz, 290 to 400 V/µs). 0–70 °C columns deleted. 0.1 dB flatness with CF=8.2 pF changed from 38 to 6 MHz typ, and 20 MHz typ without CF added. Static output current sourcing changed from 80 to 90 mA min over temp, 90 to 120 mA min at 25 °C and 98 to 180 mA typ; sinking changed likewise to −90/−120/−180 mA. Iq max changed from 13 to 14.5 mA (25 °C) and 14 to 15 mA over temp (the history says '–40°C to +125°C'; the table says −40 to 85 °C). 'Updated graphs with new silicon data to the latest standard.' The noise graph now shows voltage and current noise, the Ios-vs-temperature graph was deleted and merged into the Ib-vs-temperature graph, and CF=0 pF was added to the typical conditions. Changes not listed, found by comparing the Rev B copy: Iq typ 11.5 to 12.5 mA; the new pin table says the thermal pad is 'internally connected to V−' where Rev B said the PowerPAD was 'electrically isolated'; package names SOIC-PP/MSOP-PP became HSOIC/HVSSOP.

silicon_changes.when: Published in SLOS451C (March 2025). TI was still serving Rev B, with the legacy limits, in a PDF generated 2019-03-21, and TI's PSpice model dated 2020-11-02 still uses the Rev B Iq and Isc values (11.5 mA; +98/−95 mA). The re-characterisation therefore went public between 2019 and March 2025. No PCN was located, and the physical change date is unknown.
silicon_changes.identification: By datasheet only. SLOS451C (Rev C, March 2025) says 'Updated graphs with new silicon data' and carries new limits; SLOS451B (Aug 2011) describes the legacy part. The top marking is unchanged ('4631' on D/DDA, 'ADK' on DGN, the same in the 2017 and 2025 addenda), so the marking cannot tell old from new. No date-code cutoff or PCN number was found. The '.A'/'.B' orderable suffixes in the 2025 addendum are a TI-wide addendum convention (they also appear on NE5532, TL071, LF353, OPA1652 and OPA1611), so they are not evidence of a THS4631 die change.
silicon_changes.summary: Rev C re-characterises the THS4631 on 'new silicon data'. Output current rises sharply (typ 98 to 180 mA; min at 25 °C 90 to 120 mA), and quiescent current rises (typ 11.5 to 12.5 mA; max 13 to 14.5 mA). The 0.1 dB flatness with an 8.2 pF feedback capacitor is re-specified from 38 to 6 MHz. The new pin table also describes the PowerPAD as tied to V− instead of electrically isolated. Headline specs are unchanged: 7 nV/√Hz, 20 fA/√Hz, 210 MHz GBW, 1000 V/µs, ±500 µV Vos max, 100 pA Ib max. The spec changes are vendor-documented. That they reflect a new die, process, fab or leadframe attach is an inference; TI does not say so. The pattern resembles other TI legacy-part refreshes of 2024–2025.

silicon_changes.audio_impact: No listening or measurement comparison of old and new lots was found. In practice: more idle heat, already the main known problem in DIP-adapter use; much stronger static drive, useful for low-impedance and headphone loads; and a different AC response with feedback capacitance. That last point matters because the THS4631 is already oscillation-prone in I/V stages, so Zobel and CF values tuned on old parts may need re-checking. The Japanese sound impressions (c. 2018–2020) were formed on pre-Rev-C silicon.
silicon_changes.compatibility_risk: medium: pinout, package and headline AC specs are unchanged. But higher Iq and heat, a changed compensated-loop response, and the ambiguous thermal-pad potential (grounded pad vs. internal V− tie) can upset marginal stability or thermal designs, or adapters that ground the pad. Tie the pad to V−, which both revisions allow.

families.counterfeit_notes: No THS4631-specific counterfeit reports were located; no web search could run in this pass. Genuine markings are the same in TI's 2017 and 2025 package addenda: '4631' on SOIC-8 (D) and HSOIC-8 PowerPAD (DDA), and 'ADK' on HVSSOP/MSOP-8 PowerPAD (DGN). A DDA part must have an exposed pad underneath; a '4631' SOIC without a pad is the plain D package. Because the part is SMD-only, hobbyists usually buy it pre-mounted on DIP adapters from small vendors (e.g. Shirokuma), or as bare DDA parts from shops such as eleshop.jp. Prefer authorized distributors or known adapter makers over anonymous marketplace sellers. The marking cannot tell pre- and post-2025 silicon apart.
alternatives: THS4601: TI ±15 V FET-input, 180 MHz, 100 V/µs, 5.4 nV/√Hz, unity-gain stable. Listed in the THS4631 Related Products table.

OPA627: ±15 V difet, 16 MHz, 55 V/µs, 4.5 nV/√Hz. The audiophile benchmark it is compared with (OPA627SM); listed in the THS4631 Related Products table. OPA637 is its decompensated sibling and is not in that table.
OPA656: ±5 V FET-input, 230 MHz, 400 V/µs, 6 nV/√Hz (Rev C table; Rev B said 290 V/µs, 7 nV). Low-voltage only.
OPA657: ±5 V FET-input, decompensated (min gain 7), 1600 MHz GBW, 700 V/µs, 4.8 nV/√Hz. Not a drop-in for unity-gain I/V use.
LF357 (LF357H metal can): the classic decompensated JFET part the Japanese community compares it with.
OPA828: modern ±18 V JFET-input audio/precision part (catalogued separately). A calmer, lower-power choice for ±15 V I/V stages.
open_questions: No WebSearch ran in this pass: the session's WebSearch budget (200/200) was exhausted, and the GitHub code-search API returned HTTP 429. Verification relied on primary TI PDFs, model files cloned from GitHub (Rev C and a newly found Rev B copy) and earlier search-result listings in the session logs.

Five archive_seed_urls were seen in the documents: the ths4631.pdf symlink, https://www.ti.com/lit/pdf/SLOS451, the /product/THS4631 page, the ?qgpn variant and the part-details URLs (all embedded as links in the Rev C PDF). The rest are INFERRED from TI URL patterns: /lit/gpn/, the revision-specific /lit/ds/slos451x/ paths, the legacy focus.ti.com paths, and /lit/zip/sloc051 (from the model filename sloc051a.zip in werner2101/spicelib).
Is Rev C's 'new silicon data' a real die, process, fab or leadframe change? Is there a PCN, and from which date code?
Is the DDA/DGN pad really internally tied to V− on current parts? Rev C's pin table says yes, while Rev C's layout section and Rev B say it is electrically isolated.

Rev C is internally inconsistent in three places. The Features list says 'High output current: 95 mA' against a table value of 180 mA typ. The revision history's '–40°C to +125°C' conflicts with the table's −40 to 85 °C. And the absolute maximum output current (150 mA) is below the 180 mA typical static output current.
e_n at 1 kHz (JFET 1/f region) is not tabulated. It would have to be read from Figure 6-12 of Rev C or from the older noise graph in the Rev B copy.
No copies of SLOS451 (Rev *) or SLOS451A were located. Distributor mirrors (e.g. mouser.com/datasheet/2/405/…) were not checked.
When exactly did THS4631D, THS4631DGN and the E4/G4 variants become obsolete (after Aug 2017, before May 2025), and was there a PCN?
There are no Audio Science Review, Samuel Groner or other audio-band distortion measurements. It is also unknown whether Japanese adapter vendors now ship Rev C silicon.

families.technology: BiFET. The input is a P-channel JFET differential pair: both TI PSpice macromodels (level 1 /301, level 2 /302) use PJF devices J1/J2. The TI macromodel catalogue calls it 'high speed, biFET', and the MicroSim/TI symbol library calls it 'Excalibur Low-Noise High-Speed JFET-Input Operational Amplifier'. It belongs to TI's 'Excalibur' TLE20xx generation. A third-party parts database says Vos is trimmed on-chip. Single (TLE2071), dual (TLE2072) and quad (TLE2074), each also in a tighter A grade. The March 2000 datasheet also covered a TLE207xY chip (die) form. reputation.summary: A niche budget favourite, not a legend. Head-Fi CMoy/portable-amp threads (c. 2007-2009) rate the TLE2072 highly: one user tried about 20 op-amps and voted it the best cheap op-amp for a 9 V CMoy. Users rated it above the OPA2132, OPA2134 and OPA2227 at low supply voltage and said it drew less battery current. Listeners describe a forward presentation with a tipped-up, lively midrange, bass with weight and texture, and treble that 'pulls off cymbals with conviction'. Forum lore says the TLE2072 has the better DC specs and the sister TLE2082 the better AC specs, although TI's macromodels for the two are identical. It is also used in open-hardware audio: the ohdsp PCM4202 ADC input filters and ADAU1966 DAC differential-to-single-ended buffers (2016) use the TLE2071/TLE2072. Their designer lists them as examples of 'good quality fast audio grade devices', interchangeable with the NE5532, OPA1652 and OPA1642. No Audio Science Review, Samuel Groner or other distortion measurement was found; the search budget was exhausted.
sonic_descriptors: treble that pulls off cymbals with conviction
typical_uses: 9 V battery CMoy headphone amplifiers (op-amp rolling)
Audio ADC input filter/driver (ohdsp ADC-PCM4202 and ADC-PCM4202-SE boards)
DAC differential-to-single-ended output buffers (ohdsp BUF-DiffToSE-ADAU1966)
Low-noise JFET charge/transimpedance preamps on 9 V batteries, e.g. the CERN DIY particle detector (TLE2072CP/ACP)
Upgrade for TL071/TL072/TL081 sockets needing more bandwidth and slew
caveats: The praise rests on a handful of Head-Fi CMoy posts. The sound descriptors are forum folklore and no published measurements were found.
JFET voltage noise of about 11.6 nV/rtHz typ (17 max) is well above bipolar audio parts. This matters in low-impedance, high-gain stages.
Output current is modest (about 25 mA per LISO; the macromodel limits near 45 mA). Low-impedance headphones need a buffer.
The common-mode range reaches V+ but stops several volts above V- (model: -11.3 V at +/-15 V). Keep inputs away from the negative rail.
Offset-null pins are bonded out only on the ceramic JG package (per partinfo). Plastic DIP/SOIC pins 1, 5 and 8 are NC, which is harmless in TL071-style sockets.

It is a 10 MHz, ~40 V/us part, so use short decoupling and watch capacitive loads when dropping it into circuits designed for slower TL07x parts. This is general engineering caution, not a documented report.

reputation.summary: This is a niche, budget-tier favourite rather than a legend. Head-Fi CMoy/portable-amp threads (c. 2007–2009) group it with its sister TLE2072 among the best cheap op-amps for 9 V CMoys. Users say the TLE2072 has the better DC specs and the TLE2082 the better AC specs. They describe the TLE2082 as 'lively, clean, detailed' with 'great highs and lows' and a good midrange, and say it 'shines for budget-fi'. No Audio Science Review, Samuel Groner or other published distortion measurement was located, because the web search budget ran out before a dedicated search.
typical_uses: 9 V battery CMoy headphone amplifiers (op-amp rolling)
Input/gain stage and driver for discrete-transistor headphone output stages. Example: the ohdsp AmpTwo (2017) uses TLE2082 input stages and TLE2081s driving BCP53/BCP56 output devices.
General fast JFET-input buffering and filtering, e.g. oscilloscope front ends (the SampleScope project)
Proposed as a replacement for the MC33182D in the Gameboy DSO project
caveats: The evidence base is small: praise comes from a handful of Head-Fi CMoy threads. Measurements are not documented.
JFET-input noise (11.6 nV/rtHz typ) is well above bipolar audio op-amps such as the NE5532 (about 5 nV/rtHz). This matters in low-impedance or high-gain phono/mic stages.
Output current is about 25 mA (LISO library). Low-impedance headphones need a buffer or a discrete output stage, as the AmpTwo design uses.

It is a fast (10 MHz, 40 V/us) amplifier. This is general engineering caution, not a documented report: use short decoupling and watch capacitive loads and long leads when socket-rolling it into circuits designed for slower parts such as the TL07x.

reputation.summary: TI's ready-made current-feedback headphone driver was widely used in the 2009-2016 Chinese and PC-audio boom. Examples: the Asus Xonar Essence STX (Soomal 2009, whose packaging touts support for 600 Ω headphones), Musiland Monitor sound cards, FiiO E9, and Sony PHA-1/PHA-2. It is still used in current DAC/amps (SMSL, Sabaj, Aiyima, WiiM, FiiO, Shanling). Enthusiasts rate it for strong current drive, very low noise and distortion figures on paper, and low cost. It is also a common output stage inside an op-amp + CFA composite loop (e.g. OPA1612 or OPA2134 driving a TPA6120A2). Soomal says it had tested at least 10 (later 16) products using the chip. Soomal notes results vary widely with the design, and that designers had become better at using it by 2016. The measured reputation is mixed: implementations with series output resistors show about 10 Ω output impedance (ASR on Sony PHA-1; Roland UA-M10). High-end composite designs measure very well, e.g. the Topping L30 II on ASR, which Frieve says uses the TPA6120A2.
sonic_descriptors: powerful drive, including high-impedance (600 Ω) headphones (Soomal)
coarse or grainy, lacking finesse, in a high-output-impedance implementation (Soomal, Sabaj A20d 2022)
typical_uses: Sound-card headphone outputs: Asus Xonar Essence STX/ST, Creative Sound Blaster ZxR / E5 / X7 / BlasterX G5, Musiland Monitor 01 PS / 03 US / 03 PS
Portable amps and DAPs: Sony PHA-1 / PHA-2, OPPO HA-2, FiiO E9 and X7 AM5 module, Topping NX3, Shanling M5 Ultra
Desktop DAC/amps: SMSL SAP-9 / M20 / DO400, Sabaj A20d, Aiyima DAC-A10, WiiM Ultra, Roland UA-M10, Rupert Neve RNHP
Current buffer inside a VFA-CFA composite loop (with OPA1612, OPA2134, NE5532)
DIY headphone amp kits and boards (pavouk.org, Head-Fi TPA6120 thread)
caveats: TI's typical application uses series output resistors (bsikar/ra8p1-ereader-kicad notes this conflict). Many products therefore have high output impedance, e.g. about 10 Ω on Sony PHA-1 (ASR) and Roland UA-M10. Soomal also criticised Sabaj A20d results for this reason.
Very high drive can damage low-impedance headphones or IEMs if gain is not limited. Soomal warned about this on the Musiland Monitor 01 PS.
Very wide-bandwidth CFA: sensitive to layout, feedback resistor value and capacitive loads. Composite loops need careful compensation and a scope above 300 MHz to verify stability (PWieland/SCAM).
The PowerPAD must be soldered to a thermal via array (Zeren/Automobile-PMR layout checklist).
Surface-mount only (PowerPAD SOIC-20 / QFN-14), so it cannot be swapped in a DIP socket.
Needs rails up to ±15 V; Soomal reports performance improves at higher supply voltage. Portable designs need boost converters.

reputation.summary: A cult part among Japanese modders rather than a Western audiophile legend. The C-Area wiki describes it as NEC's audio op-amp developed from the 4558, like the JRC NJM4580. Comparing it with the NJM4580DD, the wiki says it has tighter bass, similar treble and possibly slightly lower resolution, and calls this a matter of taste. It appears widely in Japanese CD players, AV receivers, mini-systems and Tascam multitracks. The Tascam 424 MKI channel sound is partly credited to its UPC4570 + NJM4565 op-amps (JHS 424 Gain Stage). No independent measurements were found.
sonic_descriptors: tight / firm bass (compared with NJM4580DD, per C-Area wiki)
possibly slightly less resolution than NJM4580 (subjective)
typical_uses: CD player output and filter stages (Japanese domestic players)
AV receiver audio paths (Yamaha AV-S70, µPC4570G2)
mini-system audio (Sony HCD-GRX80, UPC4570C-1)
cassette multitrack channel preamps (Tascam Portastudio 424 MKI; Tascam 238S uses µPC4570HA)
preamps and tone-control kits (e.g. AIYIMA boards sold with UPC4570C)
op-amp rolling in Japanese DIY as an NJM4580 alternative
caveats: The DIP-8 µPC4570C is reportedly a maintenance (保守) product, and aftermarket supply goes through channels such as Rochester Electronics.
Minimum supply of about ±4 V (not re-confirmed) makes it unsuitable for low-voltage single-rail designs.
The SIP-9 (HA) and SOP-8 (G2) versions are not drop-in replacements for DIP-8 sockets.
The sound claims are Japanese-community folklore, and no independent distortion or noise measurements were found.

families.counterfeit_notes: No reports of counterfeit µPC4570 parts were found. The DIP µPC4570C is reportedly a maintenance product and is sold through surplus and hobby channels, such as Suzusho and AliExpress tone-control kits advertised with 'UPC4570C'. DigiKey Marketplace lists UPC4570C-A through Rochester Electronics, an authorized aftermarket source. Remarked vintage Japanese op-amps are a general risk from hobby channels. The LCSC/EasyEDA 'NEC4570G2' part has an unverified origin. The actual top-mark formats were not seen.
alternatives: NJM4580 (JRC / Nisshinbo): the closest functional counterpart, also described as 4558-derived
NJM2114 (JRC / Nisshinbo): low-noise bipolar dual used in similar Japanese equipment
NE5532 / LM833: pin-compatible generic low-noise bipolar duals
OPA1602 (TI): modern low-noise bipolar dual
LM4562 / LME49720 (TI): modern low-distortion bipolar dual
open_questions: What changed between R03DS0135 Rev.1.00 (2019-01-17) and Rev.2.00 (Feb.27.25)? Does the Renesas datasheet still list the C (DIP) and HA (SIP) packages, or only G2?

Was the 2019 renumbering from NEC G10528 to Renesas R03DS0135 purely editorial, or did it come with a fab or process change? No PCN was found, and no silicon change is recorded (unverified rather than proven).
The printed dates of the NEC editions G10528EJ7V0, EJ8V0 and JJ8V0, and the earlier editions 1 to 6, are unknown.
Which mirror holds which edition (Reichelt, alldatasheet 6770 and 1689631, Verical, datasheet4u, Scribd, datasheetq) was not seen.

The lifecycle status of each part number (C-A, G2-E1-A, HA) is unconfirmed, and no Renesas EOL notice for the UPC4570 was found. The maintenance-product status of the DIP comes only from Japanese retailers.
The ±4 to ±16 V recommended supply range was not re-confirmed in this pass.
GBW is specified at 100 kHz, so the OrCAD macromodel's unity-gain crossover of about 7 MHz is not necessarily inconsistent. Check whether the datasheet gives a separate unity-gain frequency.
Not captured: i_n, THD, quiescent current, output current, Vos and absolute maximum ratings.
The meaning of the -1 (Sony) suffix is unknown, and the lead-free meaning of -A is unconfirmed.
The introduction year is unknown.
The origin of the LCSC 'NEC4570G2' part is unknown.
The reputation sources (C-Area wiki and others) were not re-checked in this pass.

refuted_claims: The draft said it was unknown whether Renesas issued a new datasheet number or only re-covered NEC G10528. This is refuted: Renesas issued R03DS0135 (Rev.1.00 on 2019-01-17, Rev.2.00 on Feb.27.25).

The inferred URL https://www.renesas.com/en/document/dst/upc4570-data-sheet was not found. The real Renesas URLs are /en/document/dst/upc4570-datasheet and /en/document/dst/upc4570-data-sheet-g10528ej8v0ds00, so the inferred URL was removed from the archive seeds.

claims_confirmed: The current Renesas datasheet is R03DS0135EJ0200 Rev.2.00, dated Feb.27.25, 11 pages: https://www.renesas.com/en/document/dst/upc4570-datasheet
An earlier edition, R03DS0135EJ0100 Rev.1.00, is dated 2019.1.17 (search summary): https://www.renesas.com/en/document/dst/upc4570-datasheet
Renesas serves the NEC datasheet G10528EJ8V0DS00 behind its 'Old Company Name' cover: https://www.renesas.com/en/document/dst/upc4570-data-sheet-g10528ej8v0ds00
A 7th edition, G10528EJ7V0DS00, exists: https://www.renesas.com/en/document/dst/upc4570-data-sheet-g10528ej8v0ds00
The datasheet gives e_n = 4.5 nV/√Hz, SR = 7 V/µs, GBW = 15 MHz at 100 kHz, with internal compensation: https://datasheet4u.com/datasheet/NEC/UPC4570-368239
Packages are µPC4570C (8-pin DIP, 7.62 mm), µPC4570G2 (8-pin SOP, 5.72 mm) and µPC4570HA (9-pin): https://datasheet4u.com/datasheet/NEC/UPC4570-368239
The datasheet claims 3x lower noise and 7x higher GBW and slew rate than the 4558: https://cdn-reichelt.de/documents/datenblatt/A200/upc4570.pdf

The Renesas UPC4570C product page and UPC4570C-A part-details page are live: https://www.renesas.com/en/products/upc4570c/part-details/upc4570c-a
